en: Now begins the second chapter.
"If it be argued that there would follow the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis, we say no; for that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. (BS 2.1.1)

To demonstrate the connection between the two chapters that have been completed and those yet to be commenced—characterized respectively by the reconciliation of contradictions and the establishment of systematic harmony (samanvaya)—and for the sake of easy comprehension, he states the essential purport of these two in brief: "In the first chapter...

By means of this definition, there exists a relationship of subject and object (viṣaya-viṣayibhāva), because objections are raised and resolved regarding the reconciliation established by the natural sense of the Vedānta passages, which are independent [of other means of knowledge].
For the subject matter has the sense of the previously mentioned definition, because it is the domain of both the objection and its resolution; and this [subject] is that very domain.
Having thus introduced the chapter (*adhyāya*), he introduces the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) which is a constituent part of it, beginning with the words "In that regard, first of all...
The term *tantra* refers to that by which the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana*) is systematized (*tantryate*) or explained (*vyutpādyate*).
That which has this very name is the Smṛti known as Tantra, composed by the supreme ṛṣi Kapila, the primordial knower;
other Smṛtis composed by Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and others follow it.
Indeed, no other scope for these Smṛtis can be asserted, except for their illumination of the means to liberation, as is the case with the Smṛtis of Manu and others.
If they were not to assert even that [the self is the agent], then the Upaniṣads, having no other scope, would result in being non-authoritative.
Therefore, the Vedāntas must be interpreted in some way so as not to contradict that [fact].
He raises an objection against the prima facie view: "But how [can this be known] from the words 'He who sees,' etc.?"

This has indeed been established in the *Dharmamīmāṃsā* at the point where it says, "But in case of contradiction, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded, for there is no inference when [the Veda] is absent.

Just as Smṛtis that contradict the Śruti are to be disregarded due to their weakness, it is therefore not proper to describe the stronger Śrutis as being subject to the weaker Smṛtis; rather, it is proper that the Śrutis, whose status as valid means of knowledge is self-evident, simply sublate the weaker Smṛtis.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣī) provides a resolution: "This may be so.

The meaning is that even though a matter has already been established, it is being established once more for those who are dull-witted due to a lack of faith. Having stated this initial resolution, the proponent states the ultimate resolution: "And the [scriptural] authority of Kapila and others is also [to be accepted]."

This is the intended meaning [of the Sūtra]: since Brahman has been stated to be the cause of the scripture in the aphorism "Because it has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*), this entire collection of the Vedas, being originated from Brahman, is preceded by an intellect whose scope is restricted solely to objects that are naturally established and unobstructed.

In the same manner, the Smṛtis of Kapila and others—who are renowned in Śruti and Smṛti as having a naturally established status—must also originate from an intellect that has all things as its unobstructed object.
Thus, there is no distinction between these [Vedic passages] and the Śruti texts;
nor can these passages, which clearly intend to establish the Pradhāna and so forth, be interpreted otherwise.
Therefore, the Śruti texts themselves must be explained in some way so as to conform to them.
Moreover, even reasoning (tarka) conforms to the Smṛti of Kapila and others; therefore, for this reason as well, this very [conclusion] is established.
This being the case, he says: "Its application."
For while there is no contradiction among the Śrutis regarding Brahman due to the uniformity of their purport,
there is no such lack of contradiction regarding the Pradhāna among the Smṛtis;
this is because many of those [Smṛtis] are seen here and there to be devoted to establishing that Brahman is the material cause.

Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the meaning found in the Śruti alone is to be accepted, and not that which is found in the Smṛti due to its contradictions. [An objection is raised: "In that case, would all Smṛtis be rejected simply because they contradict one another? To this, he says: "And in the case of conflicting Smṛtis...
and "Nor regarding objects beyond the senses... [and so forth].
[The opponent] suspects [this] according to the intention of those with limited vision, saying: "It is possible for Kapila and others [to have such knowledge]. [The author] refutes this: "No."
Regarding the phrase "even from [the attainment of] perfection":

Kapila and others were certainly not *siddhas* by birth like Īśvara; rather, for them—who had ascertained the authority of the Veda and practiced it—their perfection was attained in this life through their practice in a previous existence.
For this very reason, they are said to be "innately perfected" (*ajānasiddha*).

This is because in this present life, no means for attaining perfection has been practiced by them; rather, those perfections have arisen from the practice of the meaning of the Vedas in previous births.
Thus, for those who have ascertained the authority of the Vedas, any statement of a meaning contrary to them is sublated and is simply non-authoritative.

Furthermore, it is not proper to cast doubt upon the meaning of the Veda on the basis of something that is itself unauthoritative (*apramāṇa*), because that [meaning] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus,

having stated that a statement concerning an established fact is unauthoritative when it contradicts the Veda, he reminds us of what was said previously— that there is no confidence in the word of even those who are established when they contradict one another— by saying, "even in the case of a conceptualization based on the authority of the perfected ones" (*siddhavyapāśrayakalpanāyām api*),
thereby awakening those who are dull-witted due to blind faith, using the phrase "even for one whose wisdom is dependent on others" (*paratantraprajñasyāpi*).
Now, if the Śruti indeed makes known the excellence of the knowledge of Kapila and others as having for its object the reality that is free from obscuration, how can their word be invalid?
For if it were invalid, it would follow that the Śruti itself would also be invalid. To this, he says: "But as for the Śruti... [and so forth].
First of all, the mutually contradictory statements of perfected beings (siddhas) cannot constitute valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there can be no conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) regarding a real entity (*vastu*), because such an alternative is untenable once the entity is established.
The performance [of ritual] is conceptualized as something to be produced in the future, not as something already established; for that [performance] is yet to be determined.
Therefore, the delusion arises merely from the similarity of the word "śrauta" (Vedic), such that the Sāṃkhya founder Kapila is [erroneously] considered to be one who follows the Śruti.
It might be argued:
"Kapila alone is authoritative based on the Vedas, not others such as Manu and the rest;
therefore, their Smṛti, being in contradiction with Kapila’s Smṛti, should be rejected. To this, he says: "And there is another [Smṛti] of Manu."
And he states the corroboration of this by another scripture with the words, "In the Mahābhārata also. He says,
"And the Śruti," meaning that not only is Manu’s Smṛti in agreement with other Smṛtis, but it is also in agreement with the Śruti.
He provides the summary: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

It might be argued as follows: "Granted that the Kāpila doctrine contradicts the Veda; nevertheless, since both originate from human intellect, what is the decisive reason (*vinigamanā-hetu*) whereby the Kāpila doctrine, which contradicts the Veda, is not to be respected? To this [he replies]:
He says: "For the Veda is independent.

This is the intended meaning: it is true that God has the scripture as His source; nevertheless, He does not possess independence in the composition of the scripture, as is the case with Kapila and others.
For that Blessed One composed the scripture in this creation in accordance with exactly what He had composed in the previous creation.
Thus, by following the precedent of what precedes, and by following the precedence of what precedes that, this causal relationship between the scripture and the Lord is beginningless.

In that regard, the Lord’s composition of the scripture is not preceded by his knowledge of the scripture's meaning, such that his independence would be compromised as it is in the case of Kapila and others.
Furthermore, although his knowledge of the scripture's meaning manifests spontaneously, it does not constitute the cause of the scripture.

Because both [the Veda and the Smṛti] manifest simultaneously [without succession], and because the Śāstra (Veda) is intrinsically informative, it is free from the suspicion of defects due to the absence of human autonomy; thus, being independent, it is a direct authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own subject matter.
The words of Kapila and others, however, were composed by independent authors such as Kapila and are preceded by their recollection of that [Vedic] meaning.

And those recollections of meaning are preceded by the experience of that meaning; therefore, while the validity of those [recollections] is being determined as a subordinate factor for the cognition of meaning— requiring both recollection and experience— the meaning is already determined by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) itself, which possesses an intrinsically established status as a means of valid knowledge and thus requires no dependence on them, acting with far greater speed.
It is logical that the meaning of the Smṛti is sublated by the Śruti. //1//
START BsVBh_2,1.1.2:
And because the others are not perceived. BBs_2,1.2:
First, regarding the *pradhāna*, there are observed in certain parts of the Veda what appear to be [authoritative] statements; however, no such [statements] are found for the others.
But those [elements] do not even connect with their modifications, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest.
Furthermore, unlike the elements and the sense organs, the Great Principle and the others are not established by worldly consensus.

Therefore, because there is no ultimate corroboration by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the Smṛti lacks a foundational source despite its claim to be rooted in such a source, it is non-existent—just like the memory of a daughter's daughter belonging to a barren woman.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that the knowledge of the Ṛṣis serves as the foundation for this [view].
Therefore, it is established that the world does not have primordial matter (pradhāna) as its material cause according to the Smṛti of Kapila. //2//
START BsVBh_2,1.2.3:
By this, Yoga is refuted.
(BBs_2,1.3) By this, the validity of the Yoga treatises of Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others is not rejected in every respect.

However, it is said that there is no validity regarding the independent *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as the material cause of the world, nor regarding its transformations—the *mahat*, the *ahaṅkāra*, and the five *tanmātras*.
Yet, by this much alone, it does not follow that these [scriptures] must be invalid;
for they would incur invalidity only if they were intended to establish those very things [in which they lack authority].
Nor are these [treatises] intended to establish the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth;
rather, they are intended to explain the nature of yoga, its means, its intermediate results in the form of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*), and its ultimate result, which is liberation (*kaivalya*).
And since that [explanation] must have some basis for its exposition, *pradhāna* along with its transformations has been taken as that basis.

Just as in the Purāṇas, where the accounts of primary creation, secondary creation, genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the histories of dynasties are intended for the purpose of establishing those [topics],

yet they are not what is primarily intended to be expressed; and just as even from a text whose primary aim is something else, another meaning might be accepted if it is perceived there for its own sake.
If it were not contradicted by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it would be authoritative];
however, it has been stated that this [Yoga system] is indeed contradicted by the Vedāntic scriptures.
Therefore, even though the Yoga-śāstra is a means of valid cognition, the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth is not established by it.
For this very reason, the venerable Vārṣagaṇya, the author of the Yogaśāstra, said: "The supreme form of the guṇas does not come within the range of vision;
that which has reached the path of vision is merely illusion, utterly insubstantial."
Thus, by one desiring to explain yoga, the qualities have been mentioned here merely as signs,
but not in their actual nature.
The meaning is that these [entities] lack ultimate reality (*atāttvika*).

It is logical that even non-worldly entities such as *pradhāna* and so forth—which have been imagined through fallacious reasoning in beginningless prior disputations—are objects of restatement (*anuvādya*).
With this intention, he says: "By this refutation of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, the Yoga Smṛti also should be understood as refuted, since it likewise has *pradhāna* and so forth as its subject matter."

He raises an objection regarding the commencement of another topic: "But this being so, [it follows] by the same logic... He replies: "There is a further doubt here: let it be granted that the existence of *pradhāna* is not known from the Sāṃkhya treatises."
However, the existence of *pradhāna* and other principles will be made known from the *Yogaśāstra*, for a great deal of agreement between the *Yogaśāstras* and the Veda is observed.
Furthermore, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is the means of the Upanishads, requires *yoga*;

indeed, the direct realization of the Upanishadic self-reality can never arise without abandoning the external means prescribed by the *Yogaśāstra*, such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), and without the internal means such as concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

Therefore, because it is not sublated by the knowledge of reality derived from the Upaniṣads and because of its great degree of internal consistency, the Smṛti on Yoga is authoritative like the Smṛti concerning the Aṣṭaka and other rites.
Consequently, since the Pradhāna and other principles are understood from this authoritative source, they are not "unscriptural" (aśabda).
Nor is that [Yoga-smṛti] non-authoritative with respect to the Pradhāna and so forth.

And it is logical that [the Veda] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the restraints (*yama*) and so forth; for if it were not authoritative in those cases, there would be no confidence in anything else either.
As they have said: "For as long as monkeys do not find a foothold anywhere..."
Those piśācas do not attack him as long as he remains within their own domain.

Thus, this demoness of the invalidity of yoga—which has gained its footing in the case of the Pradhāna and so forth—would be impossible to ward off anywhere; therefore, by one who seeks to block its progress, the Pradhāna and such must be accepted.
This is the meaning of the doubt: "The Pradhāna is not without scriptural authority."
Even this suspicion regarding the evening [of the treatise] is dispelled by the extended application [of the same reasoning].
He states the reason for its removal: "even when there is agreement on a portion of the subject matter.
If the Yoga-śāstra were concerned solely with the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth, [the objection would hold].
It would be invalid due to contradiction with the direct Vedic scriptures of the Vedānta;
and thus there would be a lack of confidence even in the restraints (yamas) and other practices prescribed therein.
Therefore, that [scripture] does not have the primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth as its primary subject.
However, it has been stated that [the scripture], taking that [the self] as its motive, is primarily intended for the exposition of yoga.
Furthermore, the lack of authority regarding what is not its subject matter does not undermine its authority regarding its own subject matter;
for the eye, though lacking authority with respect to taste and so forth, cannot likewise lack authority with respect to form.

Therefore, because it contradicts the Vedānta scriptures, the Pradhāna and other such principles are not its subject matter; however, the ultimate point is that this does not imply a lack of authority [for the scriptures].
This might be so:
there exist thousands of Smṛtis concerning the inner self (adhyātma) belonging to the Buddhists, Ārhatas, Kāpālikas, and others.

To the question, "Why are those [traditions] not also rejected? he says: "Even though they exist. Indeed, since those [traditions] mostly contradict the meaning of the Veda, are disregarded by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), and are accepted only by certain base individuals—such as barbarians (*mleccha*) who are like animals—there is not even a suspicion that they are rooted in the Veda; thus, they have not been rejected.
"But the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya and Yoga are contrary to that," meaning they are set aside because they are intent upon Pradhāna and other such [entities].
"Not by means of Sāṃkhya knowledge independent of the Veda" means not by means of that which has Pradhāna and so forth as its object.
For those Sāṃkhyas and Yogas are indeed dualists; the meaning is that they explain their own scriptures by treating the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth as the ultimate reality.
They are called Sāṃkhyas because they proceed by means of *saṃkhyā*, which is right understanding (*samyagbuddhi*) based on the Veda.
Thus, yoga is meditation (*dhyāna*), because one intends to express the non-difference between the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*).
For yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*), and its means is meditation, which is one-pointedness of cognition (*pratyayaikāgratā*).
This [identification] is merely an illustration.
Other means of yoga, both external such as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), and internal such as concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth, should also be understood.
By this, it is intended that for those who accept the authority of the Vedas—such as the followers of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda—all their systems of logic and traditional codes (smṛtis) are included.
The rest is easy to understand. //3//
START BsVBh_2,1.3.4:
"Not so, because of its having different characteristics, and because of the word [of scripture] that it is such.
(BBs_2,1.4) He states the intermediate connection: "Regarding this position that Brahman is the efficient cause and the material cause of this world..."
He raises an objection with the words, "But from where [does this arise]?
For contradiction would exist only if there were identity of object;
and here, there is no identity of object.

The meaning is that, like Dharma, Brahman is also not an object of other means of knowledge; because it is beyond reasoning (*atarkya*), it is the exclusive domain of the independent Vedic revelation (*anapekṣāmnāya*). He provides the solution: "This might be so," [meaning] "It is not an object of another means of knowledge, since that [other means] investigates an already established entity."
Dharma must be [known] through its nature as something to be accomplished, whereas Brahman is established as the object of perception.
Therefore, because they have the same object, there is scope here for reasoning (*tarka*). [Objection:
Let there be a contradiction; nevertheless, what is the reason for relying on reasoning? To this, he says: "And just as in the case of the Śrutis..."

The meaning is this: just as many scriptural passages (*śruti*) that have scope (*sāvakāśā*) are interpreted in accordance with a single scriptural passage that lacks scope (*anavakāśa*) when there is a contradiction between them, so too, when there is a contradiction with a single reasoning (*tarka*) that lacks scope, even many scriptural passages must be explained through the postulation of secondary qualities (*guṇakalpanā*) and so forth, in order to conform to it.

Furthermore, the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), by removing beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) through its very nature as its opposite, is accepted as the means to liberation (*mokṣa*) in a perceptible manner.

In this context, since the direct realization of Brahman is the primary means for attaining liberation, inference—whose object is the unseen (adṛṣṭa) through its similarity to the seen (dṛṣṭa)—is more proximate in terms of its objective content;
whereas verbal knowledge, which has an entirely imperceptible (atyantaparokṣa) domain, is extrinsic.
Therefore, even by virtue of its proximity to the primary goal, inference alone is stronger, as he says: "And by way of similarity to the seen."
Moreover, he states that reasoning is also respected regarding Brahman by means of scripture itself, saying "Scripture":
this objection concerning Brahman’s being the material cause of the world is now further introduced through reasoning: "The similarity of modifications with their material cause is established;
yet the world is not similar to Brahman, and thus there can be no modification of Him."
The Brahman is pure consciousness, while the world is insentient and characterized by impurity;
therefore, because of its similarity to the Pradhāna, it is the Pradhāna itself that undergoes transformation.

For instance—a single female body, by virtue of its nature consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, simultaneously produces pleasure, pain, and despondency for her husband, her co-wives, and Caitra who does not possess her; and by this, all states [of existence] are explained through the example of the woman.

Therefore, because it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and because it manifests as the diverse multiplicity of high and low states such as heaven and hell, the world is both impure and insentient.
But Brahman is conscious and pure, because it is unsurpassed;
therefore, it is logical that the world is a modification of the primary matter (pradhāna), which is impure and unconscious, and not of Brahman.

To those, however, who claim that the world is conscious because it is a modification of the conscious Brahman, he says: "And this world is insentient. He raises an objection regarding inconsistency: "But is not [the master] also conscious? He replies: "Not even in the case of the master and the servant."

[Objection: "Granted that a conscious being might not directly assist another conscious being, it may nevertheless assist by means of directing its organs, intellect, and so forth, which are its effects. To this, he says: "For consciousnesses are unsurpassed and non-agents.
"Surpassing" (*atiśaya*) consists in the connection with attributes subject to arising and passing away.
The absence of that [agency] is their state of being unsurpassed.
For this very reason, because they are devoid of activity, they are non-agents;
therefore, the meaning is that they also lack the capacity to employ the intellect and other faculties.

The challenger exposes the seed of the latent tendency (*anuśaya-bīja*) with the words "even that which... He states a provisional resolution by way of concession with the words "by him also, in some way...";
however, he introduces the very passage from the Sūtra to state the ultimate proof: "And even the other [form] is not of a different character."
He states the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) of this portion of the Sūtra: "For this [consciousness] is indeed not understood [from the word alone]" and so forth.

Indeed, the consciousness of earth and the other elements, which is understood from the meaning of the words because their nature is sentient, would—being corroborated by another means of knowledge (*māna*)—subvert the lack of consciousness even if it were heard directly [from the text].
Or, in the absence of another means of knowledge, the literal sense of the word must be set aside by the sense of the scriptural passage.
The meaning is that the sense of the Vedic revelation (śruti) must not be altered on the strength of that [inferential reasoning]. //4//
In order to introduce another sūtra (BsVBh_2,1.3.5), he raises an objection: "But surely sentience also exists in some cases.
It is not the case that consciousness belongs to earth and the other elements only by way of primary derivation (*mukhya*).
However, the meaning is that this is the direct sense of many scriptural passages. He introduces the aphorism: "To this, he recites the following reply:
'But there is a designation of the presiding deities, on account of distinction and conformity. (BS 2.1.5)
He analyzes [the passage] with the word "but" (tu):

these scriptural passages do not directly state that clay and the like, or speech and the like, possess consciousness; rather, they refer to the presiding deities who are of the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, on the strength of this scriptural authority, one should not suspect that clay and the like, or speech and the like, possess consciousness.
But why is it so? To this he says: "Because of distinction and conformity" (viśeṣānugatibhyām).
Therein, he explains the distinction: "For the distinction... and so forth.

Because the enjoyers are those who are benefited and the elements and senses are those that benefit, such a distinction would be untenable if there were identity; furthermore, it would contradict what is well-known to all people and the Vedic scripture stating, "And it became consciousness. The previously mentioned distinction characterized by sentience and insentience would not be possible.

Alternatively, he says that the distinction here is expressed by the word "distinction" (viśeṣa) as being caused by the word "deity" (devatā), citing: "Moreover, the Kauṣītakins [read] 'the colloquy of the vital breaths' (prāṇasaṃvāda)."
He explains the "concomitance" (anugati) with the words "and they are concomitant.
Mantras and other texts designate deities as presiding over all things, such as the elements and the sense organs.

Furthermore, there are many scriptural passages, such as: "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth; Vāyu, having become breath, entered the nostrils; Āditya, having become the eye, entered the eyes," which refer to [deities] residing in specific sense organs.
Deities manifest;
and deities, being distinct from the field-knower (kṣetrajña), are conscious.
Therefore, consciousness does not belong to the sense organs and so forth by their very nature.

Moreover, in the supplementary portion of the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇa-saṃvāda*), [the text] demonstrates the activity of the vital breaths as being presided over by a knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), just like the bodies of ourselves and others;

thus, it confirms that the consciousness of the vital breaths exists through their presiding by the knower of the field. This is what is stated in the phrase: "And in the supplementary portion of the dialogue concerning the vital breaths...
and "Also, 'That fire thought' (*tatteja aikṣata*)."
Although it was described as being secondary (*bhākta*) in the first chapter, it should nevertheless be understood that it can somehow be interpreted as primary (*mukhya*) as well.
He concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). //5//
START BsVBh_2,1.3.6 Siddhāntasūtra—But it is indeed seen. But it is indeed seen. BBs_2,1.6.

Having conceptualized similarity as the reason for the relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), he refutes it with the words, "And if there were absolute similarity.
Having conceptualized dissimilarity as the reason for the absence of the relationship between material cause and modification, he refutes it with the words, "And by the cause of being distinct.
Not conforming to the nature of everything is not incompatible with the relationship between material cause and modification.
Because if one follows that [position], there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*) due to their identity (*tādātmya*).
The middle [alternative] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for the third, however, the meaning is that it is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because of the absence of an illustrative example (*nidarśana*).

Now, one might ask: why is it not argued that the inference [of the world's having a cause] has its object sublated by scripture (*āgama*), since Brahman is understood from scripture as being the source of the world? To this he says: "But there is no contradiction with scripture... He intends to convey that there is no room for any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this Brahman, which is to be known solely through scripture, such that by employing that [other cognition], scripture could be challenged. Thus he says: "As for what was said—that Brahman is already established [and thus does not require inference]..."

For just as, despite the lack of distinction in their being effects (*kāryatva*), injunctions such as "one desiring health should eat wholesome food" and "one desiring a beautiful voice should eat sand" depend upon other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), whereas injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" do not;
what is the reason for this?
Because this distinction of effects is not within the scope of other means of knowledge;
for although there is no difference in their being "become" (bhūta), earth and the other elements are within the scope of other means of knowledge, whereas Brahman, though also "become," is not.
Therefore, the meaning is that [Brahman] is established by Smṛti and Āgama, as its sole province is the sacred tradition (nāya) and it transcends the boundaries of all other means of knowledge.

If Brahman’s being beyond the scope of reasoning is established by Smṛti and Āgama, then how is there an injunction for reflection (manana) distinct from hearing (śravaṇa)? To this he says: "Even though [it is] apart from hearing... and so forth.

For reasoning (*tarka*), by virtue of its function of discriminating the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), serves as their procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) and is dependent upon them; thus, in the absence of the means of valid cognition, it is disregarded because, lacking a basis to support what is to be validated, it is rendered "dry.

However, that which is based on the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*), which discriminates its own object and does not contradict it, is enjoined as "that which is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*).
This is what is meant by "supported by revelation" (*śrutyanugṛhīta*).
It is grasped as the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" procedure) subsequent to the *śruti* (hearing), that is, the act of listening.
Regarding the phrase "as a limb of experience":
for reflection (*manana*), when it is being cultivated, becomes experienced as the object of the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*); thus, reflection is a limb of experience.
"The self's state of non-attachment" means its lack of contact with states such as dreaming;
it means its state of neutrality.

Moreover, for those who maintain that the cause is conscious, it is possible to apply the distinction between "conscious" and "unconscious" to the cause of the world by asserting that, despite the similarity of the effect to its cause, consciousness sometimes manifests and sometimes does not manifest in the effect;
however, for those who maintain that the cause is the unconscious *pradhāna*, this is difficult to reconcile.
For it is not possible for an insentient cause of the world to possess the nature of consciousness.

However, in the case of a sentient cause of the world, since its sentience remains unmanifest even while it exists—as in states such as deep sleep—it is indeed possible, in some way, to attribute to it a lack of conscious selfhood; thus he says: "He who [argues] by the force of the scriptural hearing of a sentient cause..."
However, this would not be tenable for the Sāṃkhya alone, who maintains that the non-conscious *pradhāna* is the cause;
for it has already been refuted that there is a lack of homogeneity [between cause and effect].
This was stated on the assumption that there can be no relationship of cause and effect when there is a lack of homogeneity.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), we do not accept this. //6//
START BsVBh_2,1.3.7:
If it is argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because that would be a mere negation.
(BBs_2,1.7) The effect is not non-different from the cause.
Because if there were non-difference, the status of being an effect would be untenable;
because, as with the cause itself, there is a contradiction in [the effect] acting upon its own self; and because of the association with contradictory attributes such as purity and impurity.

Now, if there were a difference between the conscious Self as the cause and the world as its effect, then this world as an effect would not exist even though the conscious Self as the cause exists prior to its production; and if it does not exist, then that which is non-existent is produced, which contradicts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). To address this, he says: "If [the cause] were conscious and pure... and so forth.
He refutes [the objection] by saying, "This is not a fault.
Why? Because it is a mere negation.
He analyzes this by stating, "For this is indeed a mere negation."
For he will indeed establish this in the section beginning with "The non-difference of that [effect from the cause], on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," etc., as follows:
the effect cannot be defined in its own nature as either existent or non-existent;
rather, it can be defined as existent by way of the form of its cause.

And thus, since the very existence of the cause is the existence of the effect and nothing other than that, how could the effect be non-existent when the cause exists prior to its production? However, regarding that which—prior to production—is either existent in its own nature, or, having been produced, is destroyed, and is therefore indefinable as being either existent or non-existent, there can be no production of what is already existent or of what is non-existent; thus, the refutation of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is without a valid object. This is the meaning.
"In the case of dissolution, there would be the same consequence; therefore, it is inconsistent.
[The author] analyzes this inconsistency: here the opponent says, "If [the soul were to enter] with its grossness... and so forth.

For just as the dissolution of asafoetida, rock salt, and so forth in soups and the like— characterized by non-distinction— colors the soup with its own inherent flavors and so on, even so the world, while dissolving into Brahman which possesses attributes such as purity, would attain non-distinction and thereby color Brahman with its own attributes.
The point is that dissolution cannot otherwise be established in common worldly experience.
He states the inconsistency [of his position] by means of another argument: "Moreover, of the whole...
For no fixed rule is observed regarding the transformation of the ocean into foam, waves, bubbles, and so forth, or the illusory appearance of a snake, a stream, and so on, upon a rope.
Indeed, the ocean sometimes transforms into the form of foam and waves, and sometimes into bubbles and the like.
For instance, regarding a rope, one person mistakes it for a snake while another mistakes it for a piece of cloth;
nor is there a fixed order [of these perceptions].
Thus, this restriction of the distinction between objects of enjoyment and so forth, as well as the restriction of their sequence, is here untenable.
He states the inconsistency by means of another alternative: "Moreover, [regarding] the enjoyers...
He states another alternative preceded by a doubt: "Now, this... (8)
START BsVBh_2,1.3.9:

The sūtra on the established conclusion (siddhānta) states: "But not so, because of the existence of examples" (BBs_2,1.9). Dissolution is not merely non-distinction; rather, it is the non-distinction of the effect within the cause.
And in that case, regarding the coloring of the cause by the properties of the effect, there are thousands of examples;

however, in your view, regarding the dissolution of the effect into the cause, there is not even a fraction of an example for the coloring of the cause by the properties of the effect—this is the meaning.
This might be so if the non-distinction of the effect from the cause were [actually] the case.
To the question, "How can the cause be characterized by the properties of the effect? he says: "Even though they are non-different.
The meaning is that just as the ultimate nature of superimposed silver is the mother-of-pearl, yet the mother-of-pearl is not the silver, so it is in this case as well.

Furthermore, the scripture—which declares the non-difference of the effect from the cause during all three times of its persistence, origination, and dissolution—is beyond doubt for all proponents of the Veda.
In that regard, the refutation concerning persistence and origination is equally applicable to dissolution as well; namely, that the effect is merely superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, he says, "This which is said is too little," meaning that one should not object merely on the grounds of [the effect's] non-existence.
Furthermore, there is this other illustration:
And just as the dreamer is one,
so too is the witness of the three states one— the worldly person.
The three states are origination, persistence, and dissolution.
Regarding the inconsistency [of the previous argument], he provides a resolution by means of another interpretation through the following example: "As for what was said...
The meaning is that because the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*) is determinate, there is a necessity regarding origination.

By this [statement], "by this," the objection that there would be the consequence of the rebirth of liberated beings due to the specific determination of the power of the divisions of false knowledge is refuted,
because of the specific determination that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect.
And because false knowledge, along with its latent potencies, has been destroyed root and branch by the knowledge of reality. //9//
And because of the defect in one's own position:
the difference between cause and effect is indeed the same for both positions.

Although we shall demonstrate later that the consequence of the theory of the non-existent effect prior to its production (*asatkāryavāda*) and the consequence of [the world] being identical [to the cause] at the time of dissolution apply only to the position that Pradhāna is the material cause (*upādāna*), and not to our own position, one should understand that this present argument is made by way of a "sweets-on-the-tongue" (*guḍajihvikā*) tactic to establish their commonality.
[The distinction is: "This is the substrate of pleasure and pain for this person; these are the afflictions, karma, and latent impressions belonging to this [person]."
The rest is easy to understand. //10//
START BsVBh_2,1.4.11:
Also because of the non-establishment of reasoning (tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt).

Regarding an object that is to be known solely through scripture and lies beyond the scope of independent reasoning, one should not employ reasoning based merely on similarity and dissimilarity—as the Sāṃkhyas and others do—by which the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth might be established.
For that [dry reasoning] is indeed unstable because it lacks a firm foundation.
As it has been said: "Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient."
Thus,
no reasoning whatsoever attains stability merely by being embraced by great persons,
because even those very great persons who are logicians are at variance with one another.
In the Sūtra, an objection is raised: "If it were otherwise, the object would be inferable.
This is analyzed as follows: "We shall infer it otherwise.
One should not suspect that there is a fallacy of inference (anumāna-vyabhicāra) based on the deviation of a fallacious inference (anumānābhāsa).
For even in the case of perception and other means of knowledge, that [undesirable] consequence would follow due to their deviation through fallacious appearances (*tadābhāsa*).

Therefore, a skilled inferent must pursue a logical mark (*liṅga*) that possesses an intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*); thus, the Pradhāna will be established without hindrance—this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, that very reasoning by which one asserts the lack of foundation for all reasonings must itself be accepted as being founded; for if that were unestablished, there would be no lack of foundation for the others. Thus he says: "For it is not the case that reasoning itself is unestablished. Moreover, if reasoning were unestablished, there would follow the consequence of the total destruction of the entire worldly course of life.
And he says, "And because all reasoning is unestablished," to show that the determination of the true meaning of scripture does not occur merely by refuting a semblance of its meaning.

Furthermore, reasoning, which consists of inquiry, proceeds by abandoning the previously reasoned prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and accepting the reasoned final conclusion (*siddhānta*). And this [reasoning] operates while the prima facie position remains devoid of establishment.
For in the absence of that [certainty], investigation does not proceed.
This is what he says: "And this very [certainty] is the ornament of reasoning.
He dispels this doubt with the Sūtra: "Even so, there would be the consequence of non-liberation."
We do not disregard reasoning (*tarka*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in other matters;
however, regarding the existence of a cause of the world, there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*) possessing an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*).
As for that which is merely similarity or dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-mātra*), [it is insufficient].
"One is not liberated because of the fault of non-abiding.
By means of another argument, he states the meaning of "non-liberation": "Furthermore, liberation comes from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
For in the world, it is observed that right knowledge—which has the real object as its domain—is established by virtue of having a well-defined entity as its domain.

Just as in the case of perception, this Vedic cognition— which has the conscious world as its material cause, which is produced by the Veda, and whose procedure is determined by reasoning derived from the Veda—

is firmly established. However, for the logicians (*tārkikas*) who, independent of the Veda, seek to establish the diversity of the world's causes through mere reasoning, there is no determination of reality because of their mutual contradictions and the absence of any means for ascertaining the truth.
From that, right knowledge does not arise;
and because of the absence of right knowledge, there is no liberation from saṃsāra—this is the meaning. //11//
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also explained.
(BS 2.1.12) The effect is not non-different from the cause; for if there were non-difference, the status of being an effect would be untenable, as it would possess the very nature of the cause.
And because the meaning of "acting" (karoti) would be untenable;
for its meaning is the manifestation of what has not yet come to be.
And if it were of the nature of the cause, nothing whatsoever would be unmanifested.
If it is argued that this person should strive for the sake of manifestation, we say no;
for even that [manifestation] exists as being of the nature of its cause.
Or, if [the effect] were non-existent, then by the same consequence, the manifest [effect] would also be non-existent, which would contradict its being of the nature of the cause.
For it is not logical that the very same thing should both exist and not exist at that very same time.

Furthermore, what kind of magic gem, mantra, or medicinal herb, or perhaps a lesson learned from a magician’s trick, is this, whereby an effect—though possessing no excellence (atiśaya) yet to be born or already ceased, and being neither obstructed nor situated at a distance—is perceived by that very same sense organ in its identical state?
For a person, [the cognition] is sometimes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and sometimes indirect (*parokṣa*);
by which means, for him, there is at times apprehension through direct perception, at times through inference (*anumāna*), and at times through scripture (*āgama*).
If it is argued that the intervention of another effect is the cause of its being indirect, we say: no.
Because the collection of effects is eternal.
Or, it might be argued that other effects— such as the lump, the shards, gravel, powder, and dust— intervene between [the pot and the observer], and therefore the pot is sometimes out of sight.
That is not so;

for since that causal essence of the class of effects would be eternal, the jar would never be perceived at all due to being perpetually obstructed. Alternatively, if the class of effects were occasional, it could not have the nature of the cause.
Because the conjunction of contradictory properties characterized by permanence and impermanence functions as a differentiator;
and because it has been stated that identity and difference cannot coexist in a single locus due to their mutual contradiction—
for this reason, the effect is absolutely distinct from the cause.

Nor is it correct to argue that the relation of cause and effect is untenable if there is difference, as in the case of a cow and a horse; for it has already been stated that this relation is untenable even in the case of non-difference.
Furthermore, we observe the relationship of efficient cause and effect between a potter and a jar, despite their being absolutely distinct.

Therefore, even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, it is precisely the distinction in their inherence (*samavāya*) that is the cause for the restriction of the relationship between material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*).
That which possesses inherence after having not previously existed is the effect (*upādeya*), and that in which inherence resides is the material cause (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, the status of being a material cause is observed in a cause that is smaller in dimension than its effect.

Just as the threads and other constituent materials of a cloth have a smaller dimension than the cloth itself, it is not possible for the effect to be of an extremely minute dimension when its material cause is the supremely great conscious self (*cidātman*). Therefore, that wherein this gradation of minuteness comes to rest— that from which nothing more minute can possibly exist— is the atom (*paramāṇu*), the fundamental cause of the world.
Furthermore, if there were an infinity of intermediate spaces, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be equal in magnitude, since both possess infinite parts. Therefore, the Śruti—
which declares that the world, as the effect, is non-different from Brahman, the supreme cause— must,

due to its conflict with well-established authoritative reasoning, be interpreted in some secondary sense (jaghanya-vṛtti), just like the word "year" in the context of the *Sahasra-saṃvatsara* sacrifice.
Having thus explained [the previous point], the author extends the refutation of the Sāṃkhya school to one who might raise further objections by means of the sūtra beginning with "By this" (etena).

Its meaning is as follows: we shall refute the difference between cause and effect in the section beginning with "Its non-difference [from the cause], on account of the words concerning the origin" (tadananyatvam ārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ).

Furthermore, we shall disregard the notion of the effect being either less or more than the cause due to the superimposition of ignorance (avidyā), because such a distinction is irrelevant to our purpose.
Since the logic (*tarka*) favored by the Vaiśeṣikas and others is unstable due to its being mere dry reasoning, this sūtra extends the refutation of Sāṃkhya to it as well.

If such is the fate of Sāṃkhya logic— which follows the Veda in some respects and was adopted by cultured authorities such as Manu— then what need is there to mention the doctrine of atoms and the like, which is utterly outside the Veda and disregarded by Manu and others?

"By some part" means that while creation and so forth are indeed the subjects to be explained, they are explained by citing examples—whether real or unreal—that have been imagined through the reasoning of a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa); thus it is said "by some part.
The rest is easy to understand. //12//
START BsVBh_2,1.5.13:
"If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer, [we reply] it would be as in the world.
(BBs_2,1.13) This might be so.
It has been stated that reasoning (tarka) does not have as its object the cause of the world, which is exceedingly profound, and that this [cause] is cognizable through scripture alone;
how then can there be an objection based on reasoning? To this, he says: "Even though scripture is the means of valid knowledge..."
For the Śruti, being inherently authoritative by virtue of its independence, does not depend upon any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, when it proceeds [to convey a meaning], it is displaced from its primary sense and led to a secondary mode of operation due to conflict with reasoning (*tarka*) whose authority is more firmly established;
this is the case, for example, with the Mantras and Arthavādas. This is the meaning.
The commentary has its meaning quite evident.
As for the phrase "just as nowadays":
if this distinction did not exist between the past and future creations, [it would be impossible].
Consequently, that very [perception] would subvert the present division [of time],
just as waking perception subverts dream-vision;
however, this is not the case.
The meaning is that, because their current perception today is uncontradicted, one may infer that those two [past perceptions] were likewise so.
The author of the Sūtras refutes this doubt by merely presenting an example established in common worldly experience without further investigation: "It may be so, as in the world" (Sūtra 1.1.24).
He states the secret of the refutation:
"The non-difference of that [effect] from [the cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'originating material' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. (BS 2.1.14)
He states the division of this undertaking to describe a specific distinction from the previous [section] regarding non-contradiction: "And having admitted this...
It might be argued:

if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is the effect, is non-different from the cause which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then why does the array of defects stated by the Vaiśeṣikas and others not apply? To this he says: "Its non-existence apart [from that cause]."
"It is understood that the effect [is not different from the cause].
Indeed, we do not say "non-difference" in the sense of identity; rather, we are negating difference.
Consequently, the fault of falling into [the position of] non-difference does not follow;
rather, by those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who seek to negate non-difference, assistance is actually rendered to us.
He explains the reason for negating difference: "First, the word *ārambhaṇa*... and so forth.
For in this way, the entire world would be known in its true nature through the knowledge of Brahman, provided that Brahman alone is the reality of the world;
just as when the rope is known, the reality of the snake is known,
for that [rope] is its true nature.
And knowledge of reality is true knowledge; anything other than this is false knowledge, which is indeed ignorance.
On this very point there is a Vedic illustration: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay...
This might be so.
When the clay is known, how can the jar and other objects made of clay be known?
For it has already been demonstrated above that they do not have clay as their essence;
therefore, they are in reality distinct from it.
Furthermore, when one thing is known, another thing does not thereby become known; therefore, the Śruti says: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name;
the entire collection of modifications is merely commenced by speech, but it does not exist in reality."
For this is a mere name, just as "consciousness of a person" or "the head of Rāhu" are mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
As those who know conceptual construction have said: "Conceptual construction is that which follows upon word and cognition, yet is devoid of a real object."
Thus, because it is not a real entity, the collection of transformations is unreal;
"clay alone is real.
Therefore, the reality of jars, bowls, water-pots, and so forth, is clay itself.
Therefore, when the clay is known, the reality of all [its products] becomes known.
This is what was stated: "And it is not otherwise that through the knowledge of one, the knowledge of all is accomplished.
Demonstrating two other illustrations, he concludes: "Therefore, just as in the case of the spaces within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth..."
For those things whose nature is seen and then lost are not real entities, just like the water of a mirage and so forth;
and likewise, the entire collection of transformations is thus unreal.
For that which exists, exists indeed.
Just like the conscious self (cidātman);
for it does not exist at any time, in any place, or in any manner;
rather, it always exists everywhere and in every way, and is never non-existent.

And the collection of transformations is not like this, because it never, in any way, or anywhere, possesses stable existence. For instance, if the collection of transformations possessed an existent intrinsic nature, [it would be permanent].
How could it be non-existent at any time?
If its intrinsic nature were non-existent, how could it be existent in any way whatsoever?
Because existence and non-existence are contradictory as being one and the same;
for form never, nowhere, or in no way whatsoever becomes smell.
Now, if one holds that existence and non-existence are both properties (dharma) of a single thing, [then...]
And since those [modifications] arise depending upon their own causes, they occur only at certain times;
therefore, that entire collection of modifications would be as constant as a staff, and thus no modification would belong to anything.
Or, if it does not exist at the time of its non-existence, [then it is not eternal].
To whom, then, does this non-existence belong as a property?

For it is not logical that the property of non-existence should be present when the substratum (dharmin) itself is not present. Or, if non-existence is not its property, then it must be a separate entity (arthāntara).
What has come to pass for the entity? For when a jar is produced, nothing happens to the cloth.
If it is argued that non-existence is the opposite of existence, we say no.

Because it is logically impossible for that which is non-productive to possess reality; or, if it were productive, then since it would likewise be non-existent there, the same inquiry would apply to it.
Now, what is called its "non-existence" does not arise as some distinct thing, but rather, it simply is not.
As they have said: "Nothing happens to him; he simply does not exist. Now, let this non-affirming negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) be defined:
is that [non-existence] the intrinsic nature of an entity, or is it the intrinsic nature of that entity?

In that regard, according to the former [position], because things possess that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and are thus void, it would follow that the world is empty; and consequently, there would be an absence of the experience of things. According to the latter [position], however, because all things are eternal, the conventional usage of "non-existence" would not occur.

Even if negation has conceptualization alone as its cause, the consequence of the permanence of being remains exactly as it was; therefore, the entire collection of effects exists as something distinct from the cause, yet it is not a real entity.
Consequently, the collection of effects is indefinable and unreal.

Thus, by this means of valid cognition, the unreality of the collection of effects is established; [the text] restates, by way of illustration through the continuous passage beginning with "Only clay is real," the reality of the cause by virtue of its being definable.
The scripture [states]:

"That in which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts is an example (dṛṣṭānta). This sūtra of Akṣapāda intends to show that an example is one established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
it does not, however, intend to imply here that it must be something already established in common worldly usage.
Otherwise, atoms and the like would not serve as examples for them;
for atoms and such are not established for worldly people who lack both innate and acquired excellence of intellect.
Now, he raises the objection of the proponent of manifoldness (anekāntavādin): "But [the object] consists of multiple natures."
Brahman is both one and manifold because it possesses various powers (*śakti*) through which there arise diverse activities and the production of various effects.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "In that regard, by way of its aspect of unity.

For if unity alone were the actual reality, then, due to the absence of multiplicity, the entire worldly and Vedic practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) would be utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, all activities within the sphere of Brahman, such as hearing and reflection, would result in being rendered futile.
Moreover, if Brahman were thus manifold in nature, the analogies of clay and so forth would become appropriate.
He refutes this doctrine of indeterminacy (anekāntavāda) by stating: "It cannot be so."
First, this must be addressed here:
for one who asserts that there is unity in the nature of clay and plurality in the forms of jars, bowls, and so forth, is it intended that there is non-difference between cause and effect,
or rather, difference?

Or [the view] that there is both difference and non-difference. In that case, if non-difference were absolute—as in the case of the nature of clay—then both the two descriptions (as "clay" and as "jar, bowl, etc. and the restriction [of these descriptions] would be untenable. However, if there is difference, both the two descriptions and the restriction are tenable.
However, the claim that "it is the self" is inconsistent;
for one thing cannot be the self of another,
nor is there any doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda).
Even if the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference were equal, there would still be two distinct lines [of reasoning];
however, a restrictive rule [to that effect] is untenable.
For it is not possible that when two substrata—the cause and the effect—are mixed, their properties of unity and plurality should not likewise be mixed.
Furthermore, as long as there is oneness in the nature of clay, there would likewise have to be oneness in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth;
similarly, as long as there is plurality in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth, there would have to be plurality in the nature of the clay.
This very rule implies an absolute distinction between cause and effect.
Or [one might assert] the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of the effect;
we have already exerted ourselves on that point in the first chapter,
so let it rest for now.
He cites a scriptural passage that reiterates what has been refuted by reasoning: "Only clay is real.
This might be argued:
the status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being Brahman is not merely conceptual.
But he is real;

for he is a part [of Brahman], and through knowledge conjoined with action, the state of being Brahman is bestowed upon him. Therefore, [the author] says: "For [he is] self-established" and "of that which is natural and beginningless."

Regarding what was stated—that worldly activity based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) will be established through the aspect of manifoldness—he replies: "And when [the world] is sublated," and so forth.
For as long as there is no sublation, all this worldly activity is like the activity regarding the collection of objects presented in the state of a dream.

And just as that [dream] ceases upon waking due to a sublater, so too does it cease through the sublater which is the direct realization of the identity of the embodied self with Brahman, arising from the ripening of the practice of contemplating such sentences as "That thou art.
This may be so.

By such passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?", it is not meant that worldly activity— characterized by action, agent, and so forth, and dependent upon false knowledge— is removed by perfect knowledge; rather, worldly activity,

which rests upon a particular state, ceases through the attainment of another state, just as the freedom of a child to act, speak, and eat according to his whims ceases upon the attainment of the *upanayana* initiation.

And it is not the case that, for that reason alone, this [state] is based on false knowledge; the same applies here as well. To this he says: "Nor is there an absence of worldly transaction," because [it refers to] the identity of the Self with Brahman expressed in the words "That thou art.
Indeed, this sentence does not state the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman as being restricted to a particular state.
Moreover, it does not refer to that [Self] as eternal in the same way one says, "This is a rope, not a snake.
Furthermore, he states, "And by the example of the thief," because this alone is logical even when expressed through the terms "truth" and "untruth. And [he adds], "Nor in this view... [etc.].
For indeed, the cognition of being coiled in a piece of wood that possesses a staff, a water-pot, and earrings never sublates its possession of a staff or its possession of a water-pot.
Why is that?
Because those things, such as the earrings and so forth, exist in it as real entities.
Similarly here as well, by means of the knowledge of oneness (*ekātmya-jñāna*) which has the real (*bhāvika*) as its object, the reality of multiplicity is not to be negated;
for a thing is not removed by knowledge.
Rather, the meaning is that it was superimposed by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
He objects: "Is it not the case that you are accepting the absolute oneness [of all things]?

[The response is: A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined by the general characteristic of being a means for producing a cognition that is uncontradicted, previously unknown, and free from doubt; thus, perception and the other [means of knowledge] attain the status of valid cognition through the application of this definition.

However, if one accepts the absolute oneness [of all things], then because all of these [means of knowledge] would have as their object differentiation (*bheda*), they would necessarily result in being invalid, since they would be contradicted.

Likewise, even the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions would be contradicted, because it depends upon the distinctions of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), the agent (*bhāvaka*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Consequently, there would be nihilism.

Furthermore, since the rejection of a single part entails the rejection of the entire Veda, the Vedāntas would also lack authority; thus, there is the loss of the position that accepts the absolute non-difference [of Brahman].

The refutation of this treatise on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) does not arise merely from the rejection of injunctions and prohibitions; rather, it follows because its very nature depends upon duality. Thus he says: "Of the treatise on liberation as well. Furthermore, since letters, words, sentences, contexts, and so forth are unreal according to this view, the non-dual knowledge arising from them would be incorrect. Indeed, knowledge of fire (*dhūmaketana*) cannot be correct if it originates from something unreal. Thus he says: "And how [can there be liberation] by means of an unreal treatise on liberation?"
He addresses this with the words "to this it is replied":
although perception and the other means of valid cognition lack ultimate non-sublation,
because they are sublated by both reasoning and scripture.

Nevertheless, because there is no sublation in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), this non-sublation is merely conventional. For no one engaged in the world, having determined an object through perception and the other means of knowledge, is ever found to be contradicted in their practical activity.
Therefore, since they are not sublated, perception and the other means of knowledge do not deviate from the definition of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Because of the establishment of truth," or "because of the establishment of the conceit of truth";
this is a mnemonic verse (*grahaṇaka-vākya*).

He analyzes this: "As long as there is no realization of the oneness of the Self with Truth," [the person] identifies the very modifications such as the body and so forth as the "I" through the state of being the Self, and [identifies] sons, cattle, and so forth as "mine" through the state of being one's own; such is the construction.
And [it is said], "and the Vedic [person]."

He analyzes the argument that the practical application of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and the treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) is like "the practical application of a dream" by saying, "as in the case of an ordinary person who has fallen asleep.

Having restated what was said in the phrase, "And how [can there be liberation] by means of a false treatise on liberation?", he refutes it with the words, "But how [could it be] by means of the unreal?"
It can be argued here that even this collection of knowledge arising from the Vedanta— which begins with the means such as hearing and culminates in the direct realization of the Self— is unreal;
for it too, being of the nature of a mental modification (vṛtti), is a product and thus subject to cessation.
However, that direct realization of the nature of Brahman is not an effect, because its very nature is that [Brahman].
Therefore, this objection—namely, "how can there be the arising of the real from the unreal?"—is not to be raised.
For indeed, that which is real does not arise; how then could it arise from the unreal?
Whatever arises is entirely unreal.

However, conventional reality (*sāṃvyavahārika-satyatva*) is common to both the direct realization of Brahman (*brahma-sākṣātkāra*) in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) and to the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that the objection regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is raised while provisionally accepting the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satyatā*) of the direct realization of Brahman in the form of a mental modification.

Although for one engaged in worldly transaction, truth itself gives rise to fear of death, nevertheless, the cause of that fear—the snake or the cognition thereof—is unreal; thus, it is said that truth arises from the unreal.

And although the cognition of the snake is also real in its own nature, it is not the cause of fear by virtue of being a cognition, but rather by virtue of being qualified by the form of an indeterminable snake.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of fear arising even from the cognition of a rope, since there is no distinction between them as cognitions.
Therefore, it is established that since knowledge colored by an indescribable snake is itself indescribable, the production of the real from the unreal occurs;

yet we do not say that the production of the real from the unreal happens in every case, for otherwise the cognition of fire produced by a "smoke-buffalo"— which is merely smoke superimposed upon something else— would have to be real.
It is not the case that because a true cognition of form arises from the eye, a true cognition of taste and so forth must also arise from it.

For such is the rule regarding true things: that something specific arises from something specific. Likewise, there is also a rule for false things: that from some false thing a true thing arises, and from others a false thing.
Just as it is true that although there is no difference in the superimposition of length and so forth upon the phonemes, people understand the absence of the bowstring (*jyā*) from the word *ajīnam*;
yet, those who understand the absence of the bowstring from the word *ajinam* by means of the superimposed state of length are mistaken.
And there is no distinction whatsoever between the two cases regarding the superimposition of length.
Therefore, it is established that the arising of the real can occur even from the unreal.
He states another illustration: "of one in the state of seeing a dream.
Just as a worldly person, having seen a snake while awake, flees and consequently does not experience the pain of being bitten;
A thirsty person, seeing water, proceeds to drink it; then, having reached it and drinking again and again, he experiences satisfaction.
In this way, everything in the state of dreaming is likewise [unreal]; thus, the accomplishment of an effect arises from what is unreal. An objection is raised: "That effect, too, is indeed unreal."
The meaning is that even so, it has not been stated that the establishment of the real occurs from the unreal.
He provides the rebuttal: "In this regard, we say:
although [it is said] 'of one in the state of seeing a dream'..."
For a worldly person who has awakened from sleep considers the object of cognition to be sublated, not the cognition itself;
therefore, although investigators determine that the cognition—being colored by the indefinable—is itself indefinable, this was nevertheless stated according to the perspective of worldly people.
In this context, he refutes the view of the Lokāyatas with the words: "by this non-sublation of the cognition of the dreamer."

When indeed this Caitra, having awakened from a dream while assuming a hostile body— fierce with wide, gaping fangs, its tail raised and touching the whirling head, its large round eyes fixed and blood-red with rage, terrifying with its bristling horripilation, and reflected in the wall of a crystal mountain— and then perceives his own human body, he then identifies himself as the self pervading both bodies.
One ascertains the self as distinct from the body,
and not as the body alone.
If it were merely that [the dream], there would follow the consequence of an absence of recollective synthesis (pratisaṃdhāna), just as in the case of the body.
And how could this be tenable if the cognition of the dreamer were uncontradicted? But when that is contradicted, there is an absence of recollective synthesis.
He says, "And thus the Śruti," [to show] that the cognition of the real from the unreal is established by scripture and established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Regarding the phrase "thus the letter-forms, etc.": although the nature of the lines is real, nevertheless, according to convention, they are unreal.

For the makers of conventions do not establish a convention such that "this letter is to be understood by means of such-and-such a distinction of lines," but rather that "such-and-such a distinction of lines is the letter *a*, and such-and-such is the letter *ka*. Thus, it is established that the comprehension of the correct letters arises from an incorrect convention. As for what was said—that through the aspect of oneness, the practical activities of cognition and liberation will be accomplished—[that too is untenable].

"But the worldly transaction based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) will be established through the aspect of diversity"—to this he replies: "Moreover, this [monistic principle] is the final means of valid cognition.

For if indeed two transactions based on unity and multiplicity were possible for a single person simultaneously, then for that purpose one might postulate the existence of both; but since they are not, the existence of both cannot be assumed.
But this is not the case;
for there is no worldly transaction based on the cognition of oneness,
because that cognition is the ultimate of all.
For instance, the realization of identity expressed as "That thou art" arises without subverting any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their results, or worldly transactions;
beyond this realization, there exists nothing— whether favorable or unfavorable— that it would need to depend upon.
And since this [cognition] would be rejected by that [which contradicts it], there is nothing further to be desired beyond this, because of the removal of what is favorable and unfavorable;
nor is this comprehension like diluted milk, as he says: "nor is this... and so forth.
It might be argued:
"If this final realization is purposeless, then it would not be undertaken by those possessed of discernment;
or, if it possesses a purpose, it could not be final. To this he says: "And this realization is not without purpose, because the fruit of the cessation of ignorance is observed."
It is not the case that this [knowledge], having arisen, subsequently removes ignorance such that it would not be final;
rather, by virtue of having a nature opposed to ignorance, it arises as the very essence of its cessation.
And the cessation of ignorance is not a fruit by way of being its effect, but rather by way of being desired.
Because the fruit has the characteristic of being desired.
To refute that which is contrary and opposed [to this], he says: "Or it is an error. Why? Because there is a sublater (*bādhaka*).
It might be argued:
let there be no conventional usage based on unity; however, there is one based on plurality, for that alone sustains the entire course of worldly affairs.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing that [plurality], one must assume its reality; to this he says: "And previously.
For the linguistic usage of those who act with prior reflection is established by means of cognition, but not by virtue of its reality.
It has been explained that this is possible even through delusion;
it is "true" because it is non-contradictory,
and it is "unreal" because it cannot withstand analysis and is thus inexpressible.

He concludes the present topic by stating, "Therefore, by the final means of valid cognition," while asserting that the final cognition of oneness possesses subverting power due to its independence, whereas the cognition of multiplicity is subverted because it is weaker, depending as it does upon the apprehension of a counter-correlate.
This might be so.
"We do not postulate the reality of multiplicity for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of multiplicity;
rather, its reality is established by scripture itself"—thus he raises an objection with the words "But [it is said] 'from clay... He refutes this, saying, "It is said: No."
For although some kind of transformation might be inferred by means of the analogy of clay and so forth, it cannot be so inferred; because,
by the definitive statement that "only the clay is real," the unreality of the effect is established through the determination that only the cause is real.
Since there are thousands of scriptural passages that directly establish its immutable eternity, Brahman does not possess the quality of transformation.
Now, as to why transformation does not occur even for that which is immutable, he says: "For [it is] not of one," etc. He raises an objection: "Like staying and moving," etc.

"Just as there is both motion and cessation of motion in dependence upon a single arrow, so too in the one Brahman there will be both transformation and its absence, which constitutes immutability (*kauṭasthya*).
He refutes this by stating: "No, because of the qualification 'of that which is immutably eternal' (*na kūṭasthasya*).
For immutably eternal existence is a constant state, an non-deviation from one's own nature.
How, then, is this not contradicted by [the doctrine of] transmigration?
Furthermore, the property (*dharma*) is not distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*), such that the substratum would remain immutable even when that property arises or perishes;
for if their difference were absolute, the relationship of property and substratum would be impossible, as in the case of a cow and a horse.

But arrows and the like are subject to transformation; they transform through both staying and moving. Furthermore, not even a single syllable of the mass of the Vedas—which has its purpose established by the injunction for Vedic study—can be meaningless, much less this entire collection of sentences which establishes that the world has Brahman as its source.

In this regard, he says: "And not as in the case of Brahman," meaning that when the state of being the source of the world—which is itself devoid of fruit—is mentioned in proximity to the scriptural teaching of the vision of Brahman which possesses fruit, it exists for the sake of that [vision] as a means to it, and not for the sake of some other purpose;
therefore, the meaning is that this [text] does not have transformation (pariṇāma) as its primary purport.
He raises the objection that this sūtra, "non-difference from that," contradicts both the initial proposition and the Śruti, by saying, "for one who maintains that the Self is the immutable Brahman.
He refutes this, saying, "No; because it consists of ignorance."
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are themselves the seed of that [world], and its "determination" (*vyākaraṇa*) is the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*), because sovereignty depends upon that.
