What is meant is this: the omniscience and sovereignty of Brahman are not real (*tāttvika*), but rather have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, the *pratijñāsūtra* (the sūtra concerning the initial proposition) has that [ignorance] as its basis, whereas the *tadananyatvasūtra* (the sūtra concerning non-difference from That) has reality (*tattva*) as its basis.
Therefore, there is no contradiction;
the rest is easy to understand. //14//
And because [the effect] is perceived when [the cause] exists.
(BBs 2.1.15) The existence of the cause means both its being present (*sattā*) and its being perceived; and because the effect is perceived and exists when that [cause] is present.
This is what is meant: the term "object" (viṣaya) refers to both the object and the subject, and the term "subject" (viṣayin) also refers to both the subject and the object;
therefore, the meaning of the sūtra results in the statement: "because of the presence or absence of the perception of the effect, there is the presence or absence of the perception of the cause."

And thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to visual perception which conforms to the presence or absence of light-form, nor is there any deviation with respect to the distinction of smoke which conforms to the presence or absence of fire; this is established.

In that regard, the author of the Bhāṣya begins by stating one part of the aforementioned reason: "For this further reason, the non-difference—that is, the absence of distinction—of the effect from the cause [is established]."
The reason for this is that existence itself belongs to the cause.
He explains its capacity to convey meaning through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by saying, "and not necessarily.
By the logic of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya*), one thing is perceived when another exists.
The meaning is that it is not by way of necessity.

He raises an objection regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in order to qualify the reason (*hetu*), saying: "But even when another exists... He refutes this according to the view of a certain school (*ekadeśin*), saying: "It is said, no..."
Having refuted the partial solution [of the opponent] by means of doubt, he states the ultimate solution, beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
By this, the qualification of the reason (*hetu*) has been stated.
With an alternative reading, he explains this very aphorism as: "Not only from the word alone."
For by the perceptual cognition "cloth," it is the very threads in their state of being stretched lengthwise and crosswise that are apprehended;
a cloth distinct from them is not perceived through direct perception.
However, the unity of the many threads arises from their delimitation by a single purposeful action characterized as a single covering.
Just as many things, such as *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees, delimited by a single place and time, are called a "forest";
and just as things that are individually incapable of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) are seen to accomplish it when combined— without having produced any other distinct entity—
just as stones perform the single function of supporting a cooking pot (*ukhā*).
In this way, even without beginning with a separate object, the threads, when joined together, will produce a single covering;

nor is it correct to say that there is a non-apprehension of difference between two distinct things due to inherence (*samavāya*), because that would involve the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
For difference is established through inherence, and difference [is established] through inherence;
yet there is no other means of proving difference,
since it has been demonstrated that the distinction between purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and designation (*vyapadeśa*) is possible even in the absence of difference.
Therefore, let this be as it may.

And by this same line of reasoning, he states that the root cause, Brahman alone, is ultimately real, while all intermediate causes such as the threads and so forth are indeed indeterminable (*anirvācya*): "And likewise, in the case of the threads... (15).
And because of the existence of another [cause]. He analyzes this by saying: "For the following reason as well."
Not only is there scriptural authority here, but there is also logical reasoning, expressed in the words "that which exists as the nature of something.
For oil does not exist in sand by way of being of the nature of sand, just as a jar exists in clay by way of being of the nature of clay.
For a present jar is perceived as having the nature of clay;
but present oil is not perceived as having the nature of sand.
Therefore, just as oil is not produced from sand, so too the world would not be produced from the Self.
And since [the world] is born, it is understood that "the Self existed by means of the Self. He states another logical argument: "just as Brahman is the cause."

For just as a jar is always and everywhere a jar and never at any time becomes a cloth, so too, that which exists must exist always and everywhere; it cannot possibly become non-existent at any place or at any time, as has been established above.
Therefore, the effect is existent in all three times. If it is asked, "And what follows from this existence? he says: "Furthermore, it is one."
Furthermore, existence (*sattva*) is one and the same for both cause and effect;
for existence does not differ from one individual instance to another.
Consequently, because they are not distinct from that undivided existence, these two also do not differ from one another.
Nor is it logical to claim that the difference belongs to existence itself because it is non-different from those two;
for if that were the case, it would follow that existence is superimposed.

In that situation, when one must conceive of either difference or non-difference as being superimposed, why should one not rather conceive of non-difference, which has real non-difference as its substrate?
Or is it a conceptual construction of non-difference based upon real difference?

We, however, observe that because the apprehension of difference depends upon the apprehension of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and because the apprehension of a counter-correlative is impossible without the apprehension of difference—resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—and because the apprehension of non-difference is independent and thus does not entail such a fallacy, and because difference resides in each individual term and is impossible when one of them is absent, it follows that the conceptualization of difference is necessarily based upon the apprehension of non-difference; this is entirely established.
START BsVBh_2,1.6.17:

If it is argued that [the world] does not exist because of its designation as non-existent, we say no; for [this is said] with reference to another attribute, as indicated by the remainder of the passage (vākyaśeṣa).
Furthermore, the attributes of being determinate and indeterminate are themselves indeterminable.
This Sūtra has been explained by a commentary that requires no further verbal exposition. //17//
[This is established] by reasoning and from another scriptural passage,
because [the self] possesses excellence even in its prior state.
For excellence (*atiśaya*) is a property that cannot exist in an effect that is non-existent.

[Objection: But surely it is not excellence of the effect that is the cause of restriction, but rather a specific capacity (*śaktibheda*) of the cause; and since that exists because the cause exists even when the effect is non-existent, it is indeed existent. To this, he says: "And capacity... [and so forth].
The construction is as follows: it is neither other than cause and effect, nor is it non-existent in the form of the effect.
Furthermore, [it is said] "of cause and effect."
Although this point was already stated under the sūtra "And because it is perceived through existence" (*bhāvāccopalabdheḥ*), it is introduced again here for the purpose of refuting *samavāya*.

For if no relation between *samavāya* and its two relata (*samavāyin*) is admitted, there would follow the consequence of their separation; that is, parts and wholes, substances and qualities, and so forth, would be mutually disconnected.
This is because a *samavāya* that is itself unconnected to its relata cannot connect those relata together.
He raises an objection: "Now, [you might say] inherence itself [is existent].

For just as substances, qualities, and actions are existent through their connection with existence (*sattva*), whereas existence itself is existent by its very nature and thus does not depend on a further connection with another existence; [so too might inherence be].

Likewise, inherence does not require the application of another relation in order to be connected with its two inherent relata, because it is itself of the nature of a relation. He refutes this by showing that it leads to a contradiction with another established doctrine: "In that case, conjunction too... and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that conjunction (saṃyoga) is postulated as inherence (samavāya) because conjunction is an effect, and an effect must arise dependent upon an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), which would be impossible if there were no inherence;
for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that such [dependence] is absent in the case of unproduced conjunction (ajasaṃyoga).
Furthermore:

Inherence, whose definition is dependent upon its relata, does not differ when there is a difference between the two relata, nor does it perish when they perish; rather, it is eternal and one. In that case, conjunction too would be the same.
What is the fault in this?
Now, if out of fear of this consequence, it is admitted that—inherence as well as conjunction—there is a distinction for each pair of relata and that it is non-eternal, [then...]
That being the case, just as [an effect] arises from a single efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), so too conjunction will arise from an efficient cause alone; thus, the two cases are equal.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of the cognition of identity":
for when a relation is understood, it is the cognition of identity that serves as the seed for postulating a relation, not the understanding of identity itself.
"Because of the contradiction regarding its connection with a basis that is both manifold and unitary.

With the analysis of its occurrence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*), he refutes the whole (*avayavin*) as something distinct from its parts by asking: "And how could the effect [arise]? He then says: "The whole... and so forth.
Because the middle and rear parts are obstructed by the front part.
Now, [the opponent might argue] that even though it pervades all the parts, it will be perceived as residing in only a few parts; to this he says: "for there is no plurality.
Or, [he might say], "part by part."

For the number "many" exists by its very nature as a distributed whole across the things to be numbered; thus, even if one thing is not apprehended among those to be numbered, that number is still not apprehended, because its nature consists in being distributed over the totality.
A composite object, however, does not pervade its parts by its own nature.
Rather, it is by way of its parts.

The point is this: just as a thread, while pervading flowers through its parts, does not require the grasping of all the flowers together because it is perceived even in the place of just a few flowers, so too is the case with the whole (avayavin).
He refutes this with the words "even then.
He raises an objection with "like cowness and so forth," and he refutes it with "no."
Although the particulars of the universal "cowness" are inexpressible and not ultimately real— such that one might ask where this [universal] could be fully present in each individual—
nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated as a concession for the sake of argument.
Since it would have no agent, it would therefore be devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*).
For in the absence of a cause, what indeed could an unproduced effect be?
Therefore, the meaning is that it is "selfless" (*nirātmaka*).

If it should be argued that the word "pot" is applied figuratively—on the basis of its being directed toward that purpose—to those parts of the pot which have entered into a temporal sequence through the engagement of activity and are on the verge of producing the pot;

And since they possess agency by virtue of being established entities, the linguistic usage "the jar comes into being" (ghaṭo bhavati) is justified; therefore, he says: "And when the arising of the jar is being spoken of...
For arising (*utpatti*) is not the activity of already established factors such as the potsherds and the potter, which is rather their act of producing (*utpādanā*).
Nor is the act of producing itself identical to arising.
This is because there is a distinction between the operations of the one who causes to act and the one who acts;
otherwise, if there were no distinction, it would follow that just as one says "he produces a jar," one could also say "the jar produces itself.

Therefore, just as in the case of the actions of "doing" and "causing to do," one must accept a difference in locus for the arising and the causing to arise which pertain to the servant and the master respectively, both having the jar as their object.

In this regard, since established agents such as cotton-pickers and potters possess the capacity for production and maintenance (*utpādana-adhiṣṭhāna*), they do not possess the status of being the locus of origination (*utpatti-adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be accepted that the jar itself is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the locus of its origination. Furthermore, since that which is non-existent cannot be a locus, its existence (*sattva*) must be admitted. And thus, in the expression "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), because the activity of the jar is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), its status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) therein is logically established.
Just as in the case of rice grains, when they undergo softening, one says "the rice grains soften";
[the opponent] objects: "Now, origination is simply the connection with the existence of its own cause.
What is meant by this is that there is no such thing as "origination" that constitutes a distinct activity.
By which [property] could one be questioned as to how an unestablished entity can possess agency here;
rather, it is its inherence in its own causes or its inherence in its own existence.
And since that [limitation] is not contradictory even for what is non-existent, he says, "How can that which has not yet attained its own nature [be limited]?

Furthermore, since the effect is non-existent prior to its production, it is untenable to establish a boundary between the absence of the effect and the existence [of the cause]; thus he says, "And of the non-existence..."
This might be argued:
let there be no limit for the absolute non-existence of the son of a barren woman, for he is indeed indefinable;

however, the prior non-existence of a jar does have a limit, since it is definable by means of the future jar. To this, he says: "If the son of a barren woman [were to arise] from the operation of causal factors..."
This has been stated above: just as a jar never becomes a cloth, so too that which is non-existent does not become existent.

Therefore, if the jar were non-existent within the lump of clay, it would be absolutely non-existent. To this, the proponent of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavādin) objects: "But if this is so..."

One might argue that even if the effect is already established beforehand, an operation [of the cause] could still be purposeful for the sake of joining it with its cause; therefore, he says: "And because of its non-difference from that.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault," explaining as follows: just as the reality of the serpent is not different from the rope.
For it is indeed just a rope;
the distinction, however, is conceptual.
Thus, in reality, the nature of the effect does not differ from the cause, for it is simply the very essence of the cause.
However, the effect, being inexpressible, appears as if it were both different and non-different [from its cause].

This is what was stated by the phrase "the otherness of the thing" (*vastv-anya-tvam*): from the standpoint of reality (*vastutaḥ*), that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), otherness does not arise merely from the perception of a distinction.

The meaning is that, in the conventional sense (*sāṃvyāvahārika*), identity and difference indeed exist in some way. For it is precisely by this same method that this section of the text is to be applied.
He states another refutation against the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavādin*): "But for one who... and so forth.

The meaning is that if the effect were non-different from its cause, the operation of the causal agent would possess an object; otherwise, it would not. Having introduced the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "And from another scriptural passage" (*śabdāntarācca*), he explains it: "Thus, by reasoning, [it follows] that the effect... and so forth.
The meaning is not obscure. //18//
And like a cloth;
and as in the case of the vital breath and so forth.
And thus it is explained in the Sūtra by means of a commentary (bhāṣya) that requires no further verbal explanation. //19//

START BsVBh_2,1.7.21:
"Because of the designation as another, there follows the contingency of faults such as not performing what is beneficial" (BS 2.1.21).
Even though the Śrutis speak of the difference between the embodied self and the Supreme Self, nevertheless many Śrutis also demonstrate their non-difference.
Furthermore, difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing due to their mutual contradiction,
nor has it been stated that difference is ultimately real.
Therefore, the embodied soul does not differ from the omniscient Supreme Self in reality.

That very [Self], however, due to the diversity of the limiting adjuncts of ignorance (*avidyopadhāna*), manifests as if divided—like the space within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth. Its conditioned form is the embodied self (*śārīra*); therefore, let it be that individual souls do not experience their own identity with the Supreme Self.
The Supreme Self, however, experiences them as non-different from itself;
for if it did not so experience them, its omniscience would be contradicted.
And if it were to bind these individual souls, it would thereby bind itself alone.
In this regard, it has been said: "Indeed, no one who is not dependent on another enters a prison of his own making," and so forth.
Therefore, the prima facie position is that the world does not have a conscious being as its cause. //21//
"But there is a distinction because of the designation of difference" (BS 2.1.22).
It is true that this Supreme Self, by virtue of being omniscient, perceives the individual souls (*jīvas*) as non-different from Himself in reality; however...
He perceives thus: "In reality, there is no attachment to feelings such as pleasure and pain on their part; rather, it is by the power of ignorance that they have such a conceit.

And so, even while experiencing pleasure and pain, he thinks, "I am indifferent to these," and thus, even if they are cast into a prison, he feels no injury whatsoever, thinking, "It is not mine. Consequently, he does not incur the fault of failing to act for their benefit or other such defects.
This is what was stated [in the commentary]: "Moreover, when [the teacher says] 'That thou art'..."
Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) indicates the coexistence with the previously stated proof, not the introduction of a separate proof. //22//
START BsVBh_2,1.7.23 It might be argued as follows:
if the world has Brahma as its source, [then...]
"Alas! It would follow that everything possesses consciousness just like a living being. To this he says:
"And as in the case of stones and the like, that [consciousness] is not possible" (BBs 2.1.23). This has been explained by the commentary, the meaning of which is not obscure. //23//
If it be argued that [Brahman] cannot be the cause because we observe the withdrawal [of effects into it], we say no; for it is like milk.

Indeed, Brahman—being one and without a second—is accepted as the independent material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, which arises in succession and possesses various diverse forms. This [claim] is untenable.
Indeed, a diversity of effects cannot arise from a single uniform cause,
for that would entail the consequence of their being accidental;
rather, it is the diversity of causes that is the reason for the diversity of effects.
Because we observe a difference in effects— such as sprouts and the like— due to differences in their causes, such as milk, seeds, and so forth,
it is not logical for an effect to arise sequentially from a cause that is non-sequential.
For that which is capable cannot endure delay, and because it is non-dual, it is impossible for it to encounter auxiliary conditions (sahakārins) in a sequential manner.
This is what was stated: "For here in the world...

Each individual factor, such as clay and so forth, is a causal agent (*kāraka*), but their collection (*sāmagrya*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); for it is from that collection that the effect is indeed accomplished.
Therefore, when it is argued that non-dual Brahman cannot be the material cause of the world, it is replied: "Like milk.

First, you must explain this when questioned: is this stated with reference to its real (tāttvika) nature, or with reference to its conceptual (kālpnika) omniscience and omnipotence, which is accompanied by the beginningless seeds of name and form?
In that regard, what indeed can arise from that which is prior, non-dual, and without companion?
For there exists no effect that is a real entity for that whose nature is pure, enlightened, and liberated.
And thus says the Śruti: "Of Him, neither effect nor instrument is found."

But in the subsequent argument, if it is sought to prove that [the Self] lacks a material cause (*anupādānatva*) because of the absence of auxiliary causes entirely distinct from itself— just as in the case of a potter and so forth— then there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to milk and the like.
For these too, independent of external causes such as a conscious agent, undergo a different state of transformation through the mere passage of time by their own nature.
In this case, the reason is being asserted as the independence from intermediate causes; however, that is unestablished,
because [the cause] is accompanied by the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which are themselves indeterminable (*anirvācya*).

And so says the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. Thus, by the sequence of effects, the maturation of that [Māyā] is also to be inferred as being sequential. Furthermore, the production of multiple effects from a single cause possessing diverse powers is observed;
for example, from a single fire come both burning and cooking, or from a single action come conjunction, disjunction, and residual impression (saṃskāra). 24.

But if it is argued that there is no deviation [of the reason] by the case of milk and so forth because of the qualification "provided it possesses consciousness," for we observe that potters and others depend upon external materials such as clay;
And regarding the statement "Brahman is volition," this [scriptural passage] is brought forward:
"Also, as in the case of gods and others, in the world" (BBs 2.1.25).
That by which something is perceived is "loka"; [the word] refers specifically to sound. //25//
START BsVBh_2,1.9.26:
Either there would be the consequence of [Brahman] undergoing transformation in its entirety, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that it is partless.
(BBs_2,1.26) Now, it may be argued that there is no real transformation of Brahman such that it would be subject to the dilemma of being either whole or partial.

However, through a differentiation of form characterized by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) imagined by ignorance—which consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and which is indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality—Brahman becomes the locus for conventional transactions such as transformation;
yet, this imagined form does not touch the actual reality.
For the imagination of a double moon by one suffering from ophthalmia does not bring about an actual duality in the moon.
Or rather, by the impossibility of that [transformation], the moon itself becomes impossible.
Therefore, although the conceptualization of transformation is unreal and untenable, it does not bring about the impossibility of Brahman, which exists in the ultimate sense.
Consequently, since there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), this section (adhikaraṇa) need not have been commenced.
Therefore, he says: "The conscious [principle] is one.

Although transformation is in fact prohibited by hundreds of scriptural passages dedicated to establishing absolute non-duality (*advaita*), nevertheless, by means of the analogies of milk and the deities, there arises again the possibility of its being real; thus, through the reasoning of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), this [objection] is addressed in every respect.

The meaning is that since a [dualistic] position cannot be established— given that the sublated scripture is rooted in words— the meaning of the Śruti, characterized by absolute non-duality, is purified by strengthening the doctrine of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) through the two sūtras beginning with "And thus in the Self" and "For [the powers] are manifold.
Therefore, Brahman exists as unmodified in its true essence.
The objection, "Is it not so even by means of verbal testimony? is raised in order to expose that [the world] is constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
For there is no other alternative between partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and having parts (*sāvayavatva*), because the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.

Therefore, since there is no other mode [of existence], and since the two modes of partlessness and having parts are untenable, the meaning of the objection is that verbal testimony would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), like the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning stones floating on water and the like.
The refutation is easy to understand. //26//
And likewise with respect to the self; for [the cognitions] are indeed diverse. (BBs 2.1.28)
By this, the doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda) is clarified:
for the self that perceives dreams creates chariots and other objects by means of the mind alone, without destroying its own essential nature. //28//
START BsVBh_2,1.9.29 And because of the fault in one's own position. BBs_2,1.29 [The opponent] objects: "Is it not indeed the case that..."
He refutes this by saying "not of such a kind.
Even though a composite whole possesses parts, nevertheless, existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities are individually partless.
For it is impossible that existence alone undergoes transformation while passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) do not.
This is because it is accepted that all [atoms] undergo transformation collectively;

yet, if each partless atom were to transform as a whole, it would follow that its very root is destroyed. Alternatively, if only one part were to transform, the undesirable consequence of having parts (sāvayavatva) would ensue.
"Even for those who speak of such qualities" refers to the Vaiśeṣikas, whose method of production is as follows: from two atoms (aṇu) conjoining, one dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced;
from three of those dyads, one triad (tryaṇuka) is produced.
In that case, the conjunction of two partless atoms would have to pervade both those atoms;
or, if it did not pervade them, it could not exist there.
For it is impossible that the very same thing should at that time both exist and not exist in that place.

And thus, since the six atoms situated above, below, and on the sides would occupy the same location, a mass [of matter] would result in being no larger than a single atom due to the impossibility of extension; or, if they do not occupy the same location, the atom would have six parts, which contradicts its partlessness.
Furthermore, it is impossible to admit that it possesses parts.
If that were so, it would follow that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and a mustard seed would have equal dimensions because they both possess infinite parts;
therefore, the fault is the same. This similarity has been stated merely for the sake of the initial argument.

However, this unavoidable fault applies to those who assert that transformation or the causal relationship exists in a real sense from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), but not to us, the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādins*). Thus he says: "But it has been refuted... (verse 29).

The manifold power of Brahman has been stated; regarding that, the following sūtra is intended to present scriptural authority: "And [Brahman] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture]. (30)
The following sūtra is intended to resolve this objection:
"If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of instruments (vikaraṇatvāt), that has already been answered. (BS 2.1.31)

Just as the distinction between the creation of potters and others—which depends on external instruments—and the creation of gods and others—which does not depend on external instruments but depends on internal instruments—is observed through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and cannot be denied;

and just as the creation of chariots and so forth in a dream—which is accomplished by the internal instrument alone without depending on external instruments, unlike the waking creation which depends on external instruments—is impossible to deny;

even so, the creation of the world by the Supreme Deity, who possesses all powers and does not depend on an internal instrument, as it is heard in scripture, does not deserve to be denied merely on the basis of what is observed in general. //31//
START BsVBh_2,1.11.32:
Not so, because it possesses a purpose. BBs_2,1.32:
To begin with, the process of the world does not proceed from a derangement of his intellect, as in the case of a madman.

Because it is impossible for one who is deluded to be omniscient, this world must therefore have been created by a discerning being. Furthermore, the activity of a discerning being— having as its purpose the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful to oneself and others— cannot be without purpose, even if it involves little effort.
How much more so, then, the great exertion involved in fashioning the delusive array of the world with its immeasurable and manifold high and low diversities?
For this very reason, even "sport" (līlā) is refuted;
for that is accomplished with little effort.
Nor is this [action] purposeless,
because it too possesses pleasure as its purpose;
or rather, because if that [pleasure] were absent, it would be impossible for the primary action to have achieved its objective by being directed toward that end.
Furthermore, because there would be an absence of others to be benefited, activity for their benefit would also be impossible.

Therefore, it follows that the activity of a discerning being is pervaded by having a purpose; since such a purpose is absent [in the case of Brahman as a mere efficient cause], the notion of Brahman being the material cause (upādāna) of the world is untenable. //32//
This being the position reached, it is replied: "But as in the world, there is mere play. (BS 2.1.33)
This would be so if the activity of a discerning person were pervaded by having a purpose; then,
upon the cessation of that [purpose], the activity would cease,
just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* ceases when the state of being a tree ceases.
But this is not the case, because we observe that even among discerning people, there is engagement in certain types of activities even when no purpose has been reflected upon;
otherwise, the prohibition by the authors of the Dharma-sūtras stating, "One should not perform useless exertion," would be rendered without any scope of application.
Furthermore, this sūtra is not meaningful for those who are insane, because it is impossible for them to understand its meaning or to carry out its practice.
Moreover, the activity characterized by inhalation and exhalation, which arises from an unseen cause, is observed among discerning people even without a prior consideration of a specific purpose.
Nor is it correct to argue that consciousness is useless for a conscious being even in this state, because it exists even in the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*);
for even in the state of the *prājña*, consciousness does not fall away.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of inhalation and exhalation occurring even in a dead body.

And just as those who have attained all their desires through the perfection of their own and others' welfare—having accomplished what was to be done and possessing unperturbed minds—do not act with any desire for a purpose that arises as a mere byproduct, even though it exists, nor do they act with that purpose in view; so it is with Brahman.
Thus, the activity of [the Lord] in creating the world is not untenable.

It is observed that what is impossible or exceedingly difficult for those of little strength, vigor, and intelligence is easily accomplished or rendered effortless by others who possess no small strength, vigor, and intelligence; for indeed, the unfathomable ocean was not bound by trees by the monkeys, such as Māruti and others, who were beings of great power.
Nor was this not bound by Pārtha with his stone-tipped arrows;
nor was it not drunk up in a single gulp, as if in sport, by the great sage Agastya, whose birthplace is the water-jar.

And even today, the magnificent palaces and pleasure groves of the illustrious Nṛga kings—which would be difficult for other lords of men to accomplish even in their thoughts—are still visible, constructed as mere playthings.
Therefore, it is logical that the creation of the world by the Lord Maheśvara occurs either by chance, or from inherent nature, or as a mere sport (*līlā*).
Furthermore, this is not a creation in the ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*) for which a purpose could be questioned;
rather, it is based on beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
Moreover, ignorance by its very nature tends toward its effects and does not depend upon a purpose;
for delusions such as the double moon, a whirling firebrand, or a city of Gandharvas do not possess specified purposes.
Nor do their effects—such as astonishment, fear, and trembling—depend upon a purpose for their own arising.

If it is argued that because this [Prakṛti] is permeated by consciousness and is the cause of the production of the world, she is called the "conscious source of the world," he says: "And this [view] does not concern the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Furthermore, even the scriptures do not intend to describe Brahman as the cause of the world in its own nature, but rather they intend to show that Brahman is the self-nature within the world.

Thus, with the intention that since the creation is not intended [as a primary subject], the defect based upon it is indeed without a basis, he says: "The state of being the self of Brahman" (brahmātmabhāva). //33//
[The Sūtra states:
"Inequality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to the Lord] because He has regard [for other factors]; for thus He shows. (BS 2.1.34).
Here, the prima facie argument is not obscure.

The following reply is stated: For the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign— who, aided by the latent impressions of merit and demerit acquired by living beings, fashions the manifold diversity of living entities distinguished by high, low, and middling degrees of pleasure and pain, as well as the various causes of pleasure and pain such as nectar and poison— neither partiality nor cruelty can be imputed.

For a member of an assembly appointed to preside over a court does not become hateful or partial when he says to one who speaks rightly, "You are speaking rightly," and to one who speaks wrongly, "You are speaking wrongly";

nor does the presiding judge become hateful or partial when favoring the one who speaks rightly and censuring the one who speaks wrongly. On the contrary, he is called neutral and free from passion and hatred.
In the same way, God, while favoring those of meritorious deeds and censuring those of non-meritorious deeds, remains strictly neutral; He is not partial.
For in this way, he would be impartial only if he were to favor one who performs evil and suppress one who performs good;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, there is no fault of partiality.
For this very reason, there is no cruelty even in [the Lord] who destroys all living beings;
for that [destruction] is the time for the cessation of the activity of the latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) of those living beings,
and he who would transgress that [time] would be acting improperly.

Nor does the dependence of the Lord upon karma involve a contradiction of His sovereignty; for a Lord who bestows different fruits depending on the differences in actions such as service does not thereby become powerless. Furthermore, [it is said]: "For He alone causes him whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds to perform good karma; He alone [causes him] to perform evil karma... [and so forth].

"By making him do that, He wishes to cast him down"— according to this Śruti, it must be said that the Lord is not the cause [of the world], because the fault of partiality would follow; for having caused good and evil deeds to be performed through his favor and hostility, He leads one to the world of heaven or hell.
Because of contradiction;

for since it is understood from scripture that the Lord creates living beings as happy or miserable after having caused them to perform their respective actions, therefore to say that he does not create is to state a contradiction.
And one should not say: "We are merely pointing out an inequality here, but we do not deny that God is the cause.
What follows from this being so?

Therefore, for those [scriptures] which declare that God does not possess even a trace of afflictions along with their latent impressions (*savāsanakleśa*), the desire to lead some upward and the desire to lead others downward also occurs due to the power of the practice of previous karma of a similar nature belonging to those living beings.
It should be understood in this way,
as they have said: "Whatever— be it generosity, study, or austerity— has been practiced life after life,
by the very force of that habituation, a person practices that very same thing again."
Thus,
having provisionally accepted the reality of creation, this has been stated;
however, one must not forget that even here, creation is actually indeterminable (anirvācya).

And thus, just as for a magician who displays various living beings through the distinction of having complete or incomplete limbs, there is no fault of partiality, nor is there cruelty when he withdraws them suddenly; likewise, for this Blessed One who displays and withdraws the universe—which is an indescribable, manifold, and diverse proliferation—there is no fault whatsoever, whether it be by his very nature or as a sport (*līlā*). //34//
This being established by the previous argument, the following sūtra is intended to resolve a doubt:
"If it be argued that [the world] did not exist because there is no division of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness. (BS 2.1.35)
The doubt and its resolution have been explained by the commentary (bhāṣya) whose meaning is not obscure. //35//
Regarding the statement "because it is beginningless," which was stated as an established fact, the following sūtra is presented for the purpose of proving it:
Moreover, it would follow that [the fruit] both arises and is perceived;
yet if the fruit of an action— whether meritorious or sinful— were to reach the enjoyer even when the action has not been performed,
then the scriptures of injunction and prohibition would become useless, because there would be no engagement in or withdrawal from activity.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the treatises on liberation that ignorance alone is not [the cause];
this is intended to mean dissolution.
The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by distraction (*vikṣepa*), because it is an effect, requires a prior state of distraction for its own production.

This distraction is a false cognition, synonymous with delusion (*moha*), which serves as the primary cause for passion and aversion—the motives for engaging in meritorious and non-meritorious actions.
Furthermore, that [delusion], together with passion and the rest, cannot exist through its own effects without a body as the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, there is no action without passion and hatred;
nor are passion and hatred possible without delusion accompanied by experience;

nor is delusion and the rest possible without a previous body. Thus, delusion and the rest depend upon each preceding body, and each preceding body depends upon each preceding delusion and the rest. Therefore, it is this very beginninglessness that is the venerable truth here.
Regarding this, he says: "However, ignorance (*avidyā*), depending upon karma projected by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), would be the cause of inequality.

Passion, hatred, and delusion are "passion and the rest" (*rāgādayaḥ*); for it is these very things that afflict (*kleśayanti*) a person by making him experience the suffering of saṃsāra, and thus they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).

Their "latencies" (*vāsanā*) are those tendencies conducive to the engagement in karma; "karma projected" (*ākṣiptāni*) means set in motion by them. Ignorance, characterized by dissolution (*laya*), depends upon that [karma].
This might be so; for designation by means of what is yet to come is observed, as in the case of "he winnows the chaff with the cake-potsherd.
To this he says: "And not because it will hold [the offering]," and so forth.

Thus, since beginninglessness has been established, the determination of non-differentiation prior to creation—expressed in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent, one only, without a second"—is intended to negate passion and other qualities in their manifest form;
it does not, however, exclude them even when they are in a state of dormancy. Thus, everything is clear. //36//
START BsVBh_2,1.13.37 And because all phenomena are possible [in that way], [it follows that] he is not omniscient. BBs_2,1.37 / Here, "not omniscient" [is the conclusion].
It is observed that in this world, the activity of everything is indeed presided over by a conscious agent; thus, conformity with worldly experience has been demonstrated.

By the term "possessing all powers," it has been established that [the Lord] is both the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the entire universe. By the term "Great Illusion" (*mahāmāyā*), [it is shown that He possesses the power to manifest the manifold world].
All suspicion regarding the impossibility [of Brahman being the cause] has been dispelled.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the cause of the world. //37//
