Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Removal of Contradictions to the Concordance of the Vedānta through the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the Proponents of Primordial Matter (Pradhāna), and by the Reasoning Employed by Sāṃkhya and Others. __________________________________________________________________________________________ Second Chapter, Second Quarter (Pāda) START BsVBh_2,2.2.1.1:194 [The section concerning the non-origination of the world from the Pradhāna. Now, the following doubt arises: since the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others have been refuted on the grounds that they contradict the Śruti, it might be thought that the Smṛti of Manu and others, which are based upon the Veda, possess authority. Therefore, one might argue that because the Smṛtis of Manu and others are authoritative, their teachings regarding the Pradhāna as the cause of the world must also be accepted as true. To this we reply: even if those Smṛtis are authoritative, they do not contradict the Vedānta texts. Why? Because, like the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others, these too are based on reasoning and are not rooted in the Veda. Furthermore, since the Smṛtis of Manu and others are concerned with the duties of the four castes and the four stages of life (āśramas), they are authoritative only within the sphere of worldly activity (pravṛtti), and not in matters concerning ultimate liberation (nivṛtti). Moreover, there is no evidence whatsoever that the Smṛtis of Manu and others were composed by persons who had directly perceived the meaning of the Veda. On the contrary, there is evidence to the contrary. For instance, Manu himself mentions the names of ancient sages such as Marīci and others, saying, "Whatever law has been ordained for each of them by Manu, that very same law was ordained by me" (Manu 1.34). Since he acknowledges his own dependence on them, it follows that he did not perceive the Vedic truth himself. And since he does not acknowledge any other person who has seen the Veda, it is clear that he had no direct knowledge of its meaning. This being so, how could his Smṛti be authoritative? It is just like the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others. Furthermore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are seen to contradict the Śruti in many places—for example, when they teach that the body consists of the five elements. For the Śruti declares, "This [person] consists of food (earth)" (Chāndogya Up. 6.5.4), and "He consists of water" (ibid., 6.5.4). But Manu says: "In the beginning, the self-existent Lord emitted from his own body the separate bodies of Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu, consisting of the three qualities" (Manu 1.8–9). Thus, because they contradict the Śruti, the Smṛtis of Manu and others cannot be considered authoritative. However, those parts of the Smṛtis which do not contradict the Śruti—such as the rules regarding the performance of sacrifices—are indeed authoritative. This is because they are based on the Veda; for it is impossible for anyone to know the Vedic injunctions without having studied the Veda. Therefore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are authoritative only insofar as they are based on the Veda. But in matters where they conflict with the Śruti, they are not authoritative. Consequently, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world, which is established by the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others, is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative than the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others simply because they are based on the Veda. For even if they are based on the Veda, they are not free from the defects already mentioned. Moreover, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not based on the Veda in the same way that the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others are not; rather, they are based on the Veda only insofar as they deal with worldly conduct. As for the claim that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are based on the Veda because they are composed by persons who have seen the Veda, that is untenable. For there is no proof that such persons exist. Furthermore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are seen to contradict one another—for instance, regarding the number of years in the Kṛta age. One Smṛti says, "Four thousand years is the Kṛta age," while another says, "Three thousand years is the Kṛta age. Since they contradict each other, they cannot both be authoritative. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are accepted by the majority. For even if they are accepted by the majority, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Moreover, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not accepted by all people; for there are many who reject them. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are consistent with reason. For even if they are consistent with reason, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not consistent with reason in all respects—for instance, regarding the origin of the world. One Smṛti says, "From the Unmanifest (avyakta) comes the Great One (mahat)," while another says, "From the Self (ātman) comes the intellect (buddhi). Since they contradict each other, they cannot both be consistent with reason. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are supported by the tradition of teachers. For even if they are supported by tradition, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Moreover, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not supported by an unbroken tradition of teachers; for there is a break in the lineage of teachers. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are accepted by the wise. For even if they are accepted by the wise, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not accepted by all the wise; for there are many wise men who reject them. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are consistent with the Veda. For even if they are consistent with the Veda, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Moreover, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not consistent with the Veda in all respects—for instance, regarding the nature of the soul. One Smṛti says, "The soul is eternal and unchanging," while another says, "The soul is born and dies. Since they contradict each other, they cannot both be consistent with the Veda. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are the work of great sages. For even if they are the work of great sages, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not the work of sages who have directly perceived the Veda; rather, they are the work of sages who have inferred the Veda through reasoning. Since they rely on inference, they are not as authoritative as the Śruti. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are accepted by the world. For even if they are accepted by the world, they are not free from the aforementioned defects. Moreover, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are not accepted by the whole world; for there are many people who reject them. Therefore, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not accepted. Nor can it be argued that the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more authoritative because they are consistent with experience. For even if they are
"And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [for the existence of Pradhāna].
(BBs 2.2.1) This may be so:
for in this section, the arguments of the Sāṃkhyas and others—which are independent, do not rely on the Veda, and have as their object the proof of Pradhāna and so forth—will be refuted.
That is incorrect because it is not an auxiliary part of the scripture (*śāstra*).

For this work does not proceed like a treatise on independent logic (*ucchṛṅkhalatarka-śāstra*), but rather aims to determine, through the presentation of prima facie and conclusive arguments, that the Vedānta passages have Brahman as their ultimate purport.
In that case, what occasion is there for the refutation of independent reasoning as in the case of dry logic? To this he says: "Even though this [work] concerns the Vedānta passages... and so forth.
It is not that the Vedānta passages are being determined for their own sake as objects to be determined;
rather, they are determined for the purpose of generating the knowledge of reality in those seeking liberation.
And just as Brahman is understood from the Vedānta passages to be the material cause of the world, so too [is it established].
Thus, from the inferences of the Sāṃkhya and other schools, it is understood that the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is non-conscious, such as *pradhāna*.
Nor can this [conscious Brahman] be combined with a non-conscious material cause, because of their contradiction. Furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) is not tenable regarding an established reality.
Nor is it correct to say that inference itself does not arise because its object is sublated by scripture;

for since the scriptures of the Sāṃkhyas and others were composed by omniscient beings, they are equal to the Vedic scriptures, and thus an inference stated therein—being like a counterfeit lion—is not sublated.
Therefore, due to conflict with those [scriptures], the concordance of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman is not established, and consequently, the knowledge of reality cannot be established from them.

And since liberation does not occur apart from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is entirely appropriate that even independent inferences (*anumāna*) be treated as fallacious in this scripture.

If this is so, one might ask: why was the refutation of the inferences of others not performed first? To this he replies: "And because of the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta... [and so forth]. Now, one might object: in a discussion among those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*), only the determination of the truth (*tattvanirṇaya*) is useful, and not the disparagement of the positions of others.
He raises an objection, saying: "Does it not bring about the state of being possessed by passion for those who seek liberation?
He answers: "Certainly it does;
nevertheless..."
The discourse of one free from passion culminates in the ascertainment of truth (*tattvanirṇaya*).

Now, since the ascertainment of truth cannot be achieved without refuting the opposing position (*parapakṣa*), even one free from passion refutes the opposing position for the sake of ascertaining the truth; however, it is not done *as* an opposing position [with animosity]. Thus, there is no contradiction in its being a discourse of one free from passion.
Having raised the objection regarding tautology (*punaruktatā*), he provides the resolution: "But [it is so] because of the word 'īkṣati'."
Regarding that, as for "number":
for whatever things are endowed with a certain form from grossness down to subtlety, they are observed to have that as their cause;
just as jars and the like, and necklaces and the like, being endowed with clay and gold respectively from grossness down to subtlety, have those [clay and gold] as their causes.
Likewise, this entire collection of external and internal entities is perceived as being permeated by the nature of pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), and delusion (*moha*);
therefore, it must have as its universal cause that which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Among these, that which is the aspect of pleasure in the cause of the world is *sattva*.

That which is of the nature of suffering is *rajas*, and that which is of the nature of delusion is *tamas*; thus, the existence of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as the cause [of all things] is established.
For indeed, every individual entity is experienced as possessing these three qualities.
Just as Maitra experienced happiness with Padmāvatī, his own wife,
for what reason?
Because of the emergence of the quality of affection toward her.
And there is suffering for her co-wives;
for what reason?
Because of the arising of the quality of passion (rajas) toward them.
But for Caitra, who is dominated by feminine traits and does not obtain her, there is delusion and despondency;
why is that?
Because she arises toward him from the quality of tamas.
And by Padmāvatī, all entities have been explained.
Therefore, it is understood that the entire world, being permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, has that as its cause;
and that is the Pradhāna consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), so called because by it the world is produced or brought forth.
It is called *pradhāna* because the world is deposited (*pradhīyate*) or stored within it at the time of dissolution; or alternatively, it is the primary cause.

And that, like clay or gold, being insentient, proceeds by its very nature to accomplish the purpose of the sentient *puruṣa*, characterized as experience and liberation, but it is not set in motion by anyone else.
For thus they say: "The purpose of the Person alone is the cause; the instrument is not set in motion by anyone.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "from measurement etc.," the grounds for establishing the Unmanifest are understood, namely: "from the activity proceeding from power, from the distinction between cause and effect, and from the non-differentiation of the manifold world."
Having explained these [objections] later, they will be refuted;
thus, he refutes this inference regarding the Pradhāna with the words, "To that we say.
If it is first being established that the insentient Pradhāna proceeds by its own nature alone, without being presided over by a sentient being, then...
That is incorrect;

for the reason of "conjunction" (samanvaya) and so forth is contradictory, because its pervasion (vyāpti) is observed in the subject of the example—such as clay or gold—in terms of being presided over by a conscious agent, which is the opposite of being un-presided-over by a conscious agent. Thus, the reason is contradictory (viruddha).

For clay, gold, wood, and so forth, when not presided over by a potter, a goldsmith, a carpenter, or others, do not produce jars, bracelets, chariots, and the like. Therefore, just as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is contradictory when employed to prove eternity because it is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum,

so too is "homogeneity" (samanvaya) and so on contradictory when used to prove the absence of a presiding intelligent being, as shown by the phrase "because the arrangement is impossible" (racanānupapatteḥ).
If it should be argued that in the subject of the example, an insentient material cause is indeed observed; and although in that case it is seen to be impelled by a sentient being,
nevertheless, that state of being impelled by it is irrelevant to the reason because it is an external factor.
However, it is the internal factor—mere consciousness (caitanya) alone—which, being inherent in the material cause (upādāna), is the efficient cause (prayojaka) of the effect;
as they say: "And of the observed pervasion, some property is the efficient cause.
To this, he replies: "Nor [is it] clay and so forth."
For that which is pervaded, being connected by way of essential nature (*svabhāvapratibaddha*), makes known the pervader;
and that connection by essential nature is ascertained when there is the removal of suspected or superimposed conditions (*upādhi*).
And that ascertainment depends upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
Furthermore, those two— positive and negative concomitance— are not as clear-cut in the case of the insentience of the material cause as they are in the case of being impelled by a conscious agent;
the sense is that there is no need for further elaboration on this internal point.

Even so, one would not have to accept that [the world] is produced by volition (cetanā-prayuktatva) if there were a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); on the contrary, scripture (śruti) is even more favorable [to this view]. Thus he says: "And this being the case... By the word "and" (ca), he adds that the reason characterized by the concomitance (anvaya) with pleasure, pain, and so forth is unestablished (asiddha). Thus he says: "...and because concomitance and so forth are untenable."

Indeed, these internal experiences of pleasure, pain, delusion, and despondency are perceived through direct observation as distinct from external objects such as sandalwood, which are cognized through entirely separate perceptions.
If, however, these [internal states] were of the very same nature as pleasure, pain, and so forth, then, by virtue of their own inherent nature, sandalwood would be pleasant even in winter;
for sandalwood never ceases to be sandalwood.
Likewise, even in the summer heat, saffron paste may be pleasant;
for it is never the case that it is not saffron paste.
In this way, just as a thorn is pleasant to a camel, so too would it be pleasant to other living beings such as humans.
It may be so; for it is not the case that [a thorn] is a thorn only in relation to certain people.

Therefore, it is more reasonable [to hold] that sandalwood, saffron, and the like, though not having pleasure and so forth as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth depending on the species, time, and state [of the person], but they do not themselves have pleasure and so forth as their intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the endowment of entities with the nature of pleasure and so forth is unestablished; thus, the unmanifest cause is not inferred from that nature by this [argument].
This has been stated: "Even though there is no distinction in sound and so forth, it is due to a distinction in mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
Cultivation (bhāvanā) means latent impression (vāsanā) or formative predisposition (saṃskāra); it is because of a distinction in that [cultivation] [that the difference arises].
For karma that brings about birth as a camel manifests only those mental dispositions appropriate to a camel,
such that thorns alone are pleasing to him;
the same should be understood in other cases as well.
He introduces the Sāṃkhya argument "because of limited magnitude" with the words: "thus, of the limited varieties.

For if they were preceded by a combination (*saṃsarga*), then since a combination is impossible in that which is one and non-dual, one must postulate various combined causes inherent in a single object that possesses multiplicity;
and the sense is that these [causes] are precisely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

He refutes this by showing that this "limitedness" (*parimitatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when examined in light of the Sāṃkhya tenets— starting with the words "of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
If limitedness means a finite measure (*iyattā*), then since even space (*nabhas*) lacks such a measure, the reason "because of being limited" (*parimāṇāt*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
Now, we do not say that the dimension of space consists of a measured extent such as a *yojana* or the like; rather, we mean its non-pervasiveness.
And space is non-pervasive with respect to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth;
for an effect does not pervade its cause.
However, the cause pervades the effect, whereas [the ether] is limited because it does not pervade its own subtle element (tanmātra) and so forth.
Alas, even the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas do not mutually pervade one another, nor are these preceded by any other principle; thus, there is a deviation from the rule.
For those [elements] do not enter one another in the same way that they have entered into the collection of effects;
this is because there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect between them.
Furthermore, there is no mutual contact or penetration into the power of consciousness (citi-śakti).
For the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), being immutable and eternal, does not become conjoined with those [guṇas];
consequently, the guṇas do not pervade it and are thus limited.
Likewise, since the power of consciousness is also unjoined with the guṇas, it too would be limited; therefore, the reason "being limited" (*parimitatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, he states that the distinction between cause and effect is also contradictory, just like [the notion of] homogeneity (samanvaya): "But as for the relation of cause and effect... (verse 1).
And because of the activity [of the world] (pravṛtti).

Not only do the various arrangements [of the world] not occur without the superintendence of a conscious being, but also the falling away from the state of equilibrium and the resulting inequality [do not occur].
And thus, that which has arisen as more powerful is the primary factor (*aṅgin*), while that which is subordinate and remains in accordance with it is the auxiliary factor (*aṅga*);
for when such a relationship of primary and subordinate exists, what activity could there be for this [Prakṛti] in effects such as the Mahat?
That [activity] also leads to the conclusion that there must be a presiding intelligent agent (*cetanādhiṣṭhāna*).
For, without a presiding intelligent agent, the wheel, staff, water, thread, and so forth do not remain as subordinate factors upon the primary lump of clay.

Therefore, since activity also establishes a presiding intelligent agent, it has been stated by way of an indirect argument (*vakrokti*) that this Sāṃkhya reason—"because of activity from a capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteśca*)—is indeed contradictory (*viruddha*).
Here the Sāṃkhya objects: "But surely there is activity even for the conscious [principle].

This is the intention: "By you, the follower of the Upaniṣads, having indeed refuted our reasons, you must establish that the conscious principle alone, independent of anything else, is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world; that is incorrect."
"Because the activity of a solitary conscious being is not observed in the subject of the example.

The follower of the Upaniṣads, however, thinking with the intention: "Let this Sāṃkhya first accept that activity has consciousness as its cause; afterwards, I shall refute his own position," said: "This is true;
the activity of a solitary conscious being is not observed."
The Sāṃkhya says: "But not [the activity] of that which is conjoined with the insentient. The word "but" (tu) excludes the Upaniṣadic position.
All observed activity is seen to have the insentient as its substrate, and not even any [activity] whatsoever has the sentient as its substrate.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no inclination on the part of a conscious being toward the creation of the world.
At this point, the Vedāntin, possessing a hidden intention, reflects by means of a question: "But what, then, here?
In the meantime, the Sāṃkhya says: "Indeed, in which..."
A conscious being is not perceived through direct perception either as the substratum of activity or as its instigator;
rather, it is only the activity itself and its unconscious substratum—the body, chariot, and so forth—that are cognized by direct perception.
In that case, the activity of the unconscious entity is caused solely by that [unconscious substratum] itself, and not by a conscious being.
However, in that case, only the mere existence of consciousness is perceived in the living body, owing to its distinction from things such as chariots;
yet, the status of being a cause is not established by mere existence alone.
Let it not be that space is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of produced things like jars, for space exists everywhere.
Thus, it has been stated that even though there exists a conscious principle distinct from the body, that consciousness does not serve as the cause for activity.

And because it is not the cause of activity, for this very reason the Lokāyatikas—observing that activity is seen when the body is present and not seen when it is absent—have concluded that consciousness belongs to the body alone;
and thus it is established that activity is not caused by a conscious self.

Therefore, the follower of the Upaniṣads (the Aupaniṣada) refutes [the objection] that the world’s status as having consciousness as its cause is not established by either its composition or its activity—this is what is being stated: "We do not say so.
For we do not need to establish at this point either the embodied self or the Supreme Self, which are already established through perception, inference, and scripture.
One must state merely that it is the cause for its activity.

In this regard, since activity is not observed in a dead body or in a chariot and the like when they are not presided over by a conscious being, whereas activity is observed when the opposite is the case, it follows through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that consciousness is the cause;
it is not [the cause] by the mere presence of consciousness.
Lest there be an over-extension [of the argument],

he says— "even for the Lokāyatikas"— since there is no dispute even among those who maintain that consciousness is derived from the elements (bhūtacaitanika) regarding the point that the activity of insentient things occurs due to the presiding influence of sentience.
This might be so.
It is reasonable that the body itself—being sentient, possessing hands, feet, and so forth—sets itself in motion through its own activity;

however, it is not reasonable that a conscious being distinct from it—one who is immutable, eternal, devoid of activity, and whose sole nature is knowledge—should be the initiator [of action], because such a being lacks the capacity for engagement. Thus he objects: "But yours...
He replies: "No."
"Like a magnet, and like visible form and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and like visible form and so forth":
according to the Sāṃkhyas, visible form and the other [objects], while remaining in their own location, produce a transformation in the sense faculty.
Therefore, the established position is that the sense organ, having reached its object, transforms into the form of that object.
Now, the opponent reveals his own intention: "Because of oneness.
For those who maintain that there is both the insentient and the sentient, it is appropriate to say that the insentient proceeds when presided over by the sentient.
This is as in the case of the yogins who maintain the existence of a Lord (Īśvara).

However, for those non-dualists (advaitavādins) for whom there exists nothing apart from consciousness, the meaning is: in the absence of anything to be impelled, with respect to what could consciousness possess the quality of being an impeller?
He refutes this, saying: "It is not ignorance.
That which is presented by ignorance—characterized as dissolution and serving as the cause—and by the latent impressions of distraction accumulated prior to creation, that alone is *māyā*;
for it is through the penetration of that [māyā] that this objection has been repeatedly raised.
This is what is meant: this creation is not substantially real, such that it could be questioned by an Advaitin on the grounds of the absence of a second [entity] existing as a reality.
However, in a conceptual creation, there exists a conceptual second companion consisting of *māyā*.
As they say: "The companions are exactly of the same nature as the destiny that is to be."
Thus,
there is no contradiction with Brahman being the material cause (upādāna).

Since Brahman alone, through the entry of its creative power (māyā), is both the material cause and the substratum of the world-delusion—just as mother-of-pearl is the material cause and substratum of the delusion of silver—it is beyond reproach. //2//
START BsVBh_2,2.1.3:
"If it is argued that it is like milk and water, then [the same applies] there as well" (BBs_2,2.3).
The meaning of the objection is this: just as the movement of milk and water occurs by themselves alone, without being presided over by a conscious agent, so too is it for the *pradhāna*.
In that case as well, what is to be proven is the state of being presided over by volition;
nor is there a deviation [of the reason] from the very thing to be proven, for if that were so, it would follow that the entire domain of inference would be destroyed.
Because this is easily accessible everywhere,
it is not impossible to achieve;
for here too, the basis of volition is established by scripture.
And the meaning of [the statement] "there is no doubt of deviation by means of the similar instance (sapakṣa)" is the removal of such a suspicion.
The phrase "the side of the probandum" (sādhyapakṣa) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as "because it is included within the similar instance."

[Objection: But was it not shown in the [sūtra] "Because we see the bringing together" (*upasaṃhāradarśanāt*) that activity occurs independently [of a conscious agent], whereas here it is being established that the activity of everything depends upon a conscious being? How, then, is there no contradiction? To this he says: "Because we see the bringing together.
The meaning is that this was stated in accordance with the perspective of people who perceive only gross objects, but not from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). //3//
START BsVBh_2,2.1.4:
And because [the effect] does not persist through the absence [of the cause], and because [the cause] is independent.

(BBs_2,2.4) Even though for the Sāṃkhyas as well, the *pradhāna* is permeated by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of diverse karmas even during its state of equilibrium, nevertheless the latencies of karma do not have mastery over the creation.

However, when the *pradhāna* itself proceeds toward its own effect, it is unable to produce a creation consisting of happiness because it is obstructed by *adharma*; thus, the obstruction of *adharma* is removed by *dharma*.
Likewise, the obstruction of *dharma* is removed by *adharma* in the case of a creation consisting of suffering.
And the *pradhāna* proceeds toward creation by itself, without depending on anything else.
As they have said: "The efficient cause (nimitta) is not the motivator of the primal natures (prakṛtis); rather, it serves to break the obstruction, like a farmer.

Consequently, since the impressions of merit and demerit (dharmādharmavāsanā) are also present as the means for removing obstacles, there would be no external factor to depend upon; thus, Nature would always transform either in a state of equilibrium or in a state of disequilibrium, and this occasional variation in transformation could not be accounted for.

But for the Lord, who possesses great illusory power (māyā) and is conscious, both the engagement in and the withdrawal from activity are indeed possible—whether through sport (līlā), or by chance (yadṛcchā), or due to the diversity of inherent nature (svabhāva)—as He acts in dependence upon the ripening of karma. //4//
And because it does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth.

For grass, shoots, and the like, when consumed by a cow, transform into the state of milk through their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) without depending on consciousness; the consciousness of the cow is not required for that process.
Because it depends on that [the conscious principle] merely for its application;
thus, the meaning of the objection is: "In the same way, the primary cause (pradhāna) will also undergo transformation by its very nature; what need is there for a conscious agent here?
Is it merely being denied that there is some other efficient cause for grass and so forth when they are consumed by a cow and turn into milk?
Or is it conscious?
First, it cannot be another cause,
because there exists another cause for the distinction between the digestive fire and so forth located within the belly, which resides in the body of the cow.
However, the purpose of refuting the doubt that even in that case an omniscient Lord could be the one acting with prior intelligence is as follows:
this has been stated—“some things are to be accomplished by destiny (daiva). //5//
Even if [the existence of the Self] were admitted, it would follow that there is no object [for cognition],
and consequently, there would be no dependence upon human purpose (puruṣārtha).
This has been stated: "In this way, even some purpose will not be required. Alternatively, it should be construed as "due to the absence of a human goal" (puruṣārtha).
This is what was meant by the statement: "Nevertheless, the purpose for the activity of the Pradhāna must be discerned."
Not only is actual experience impossible for the Puruṣa— who is immutable and eternal and cannot have any excellence added to him—
but there would also follow the consequence of no liberation; for that purpose for which Pradhāna is set in motion must be accomplished by it.
The meaning is that one should pursue only that [pleasure], since it was set in motion by enjoyment, and not liberation, because liberation was not so set in motion;
for if liberation were [the goal], it would have existed even previously.
Because consciousness (*cit*) is eternally pure, it never possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the experience of karma.
Primordial matter (*pradhāna*), however, is the substratum for those beginningless [impressions].
Thus, prior to the activity of *pradhāna*, consciousness is already liberated; therefore, its activity is not even for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*).
And there would follow the consequence of the non-perception of sound and the other objects,
because the Pradhāna does not act for their sake;
this remains true even if one accepts that it acts for the sake of both.
Liberation (apavarga) cannot be the goal to be accomplished, because it is already established merely by the cessation of the activity of the Pradhāna.
Rather, the Pradhāna would proceed for the sake of experience (bhoga).

However, since experience is completed by the mere once-and-for-all perception of sound and other objects, the Pradhāna would not proceed again for that purpose; thus, liberation would be achieved without effort.
Furthermore, because the enjoyment of sound and other objects is infinite, its completion is impossible; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation.

If it is argued that even after providing enjoyment, the *pradhāna* continues to make [the *puruṣa*] enjoy through repeated action until the discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between *sattva* and *puruṣa* occurs, then for what purpose does that which has already begun to act for the sake of the *puruṣa* bring about this discernment of the difference between *sattva* and *puruṣa*?
If it is argued that [the purpose of the *sattva*] is for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*), then alas!

when the *pradhāna*, having accomplished its purpose through a single enjoyment of sound and the other objects, ceases, liberation is established by that mere cessation alone; thus, there is no need to wait for the discernment of the difference between *sattva* and the *puruṣa*.
Nor does this [discernment] exist in its own nature...
[The purpose is] for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*).

Therefore, since the activity of the Pradhāna is not tenable even for the sake of both [the person and itself], it is established that there is no objective (*arthābhāva*). The rest is easy to understand.
He raises an objection: "The power of vision...
For the Puruṣa is indeed the power of vision, and that [power] would be purposeless without an object of vision.
Nor is it purposeful with respect to itself, because of the contradiction of something acting upon itself;
and the primary cause (pradhāna) is the power of creation.

The meaning of the objection is this: since that [power] would be purposeless without an act of creation, it follows that whatever is created by *pradhāna*—namely sound and the rest—becomes the object of the power of vision (*dṛkśakti*). Thus, creation exists for the sake of both [powers].
To refute this, he says: "as the power of creation is not cut off.

For just as the power of creation belonging to *pradhāna*, although its purpose has been fulfilled with respect to one *puruṣa*, continues to operate toward another *puruṣa* because it is never cut off.

In the same way, the power of vision (dṛk-śakti) would also continue to function at all times toward that Puruṣa because it possesses its object and is indestructible; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation (anirmokṣa).

Alternatively, if its purpose were fulfilled by seeing the object once, it would not function again; consequently, the liberation of all beings would occur simultaneously, and saṃsāra would be abruptly cut off. //6//
"If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so,
the remainder [of the argument] is that there is still no escape from the fault."

One might suspect that neither the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) nor the possession of power (*śaktyarthavattva*) acts as the motivator; rather, the *puruṣa* himself—endowed with the power of vision (*dṛkśakti*), like a lame man—will set in motion the *pradhāna*, which is endowed with the power of activity (*pravṛttiśakti*), like a blind man.
To show that this leads to the impossibility of liberation from defects, he says: "First, there is the abandonment of what has been accepted."
It is not only that this involves abandoning what has been accepted;
it is also illogical when examined according to your own view. Thus he says: "And how can [the Self] be indifferent?
He provides the proof for its being inactive: "because it is devoid of qualities."
The remainder has its meaning not hidden [and is thus self-evident]. //7//
START BsVBh_2,2.1.8 And because the status of being a subordinate member is untenable; BBs_2,2.8 / If the state of the Pradhāna were immutable and eternal, [the subsequent states could not arise].
Therefore, there can be no falling away from that [state], because that would entail the consequence of impermanence.
As they say: "The wise call that eternal which is one's own nature (svabhāva) that does not perish.
This is what was meant by the phrase: "for fear of the destruction of the life-force of one's own nature."
Now, there is the "transforming eternal" (pariṇāminitya). As they say: "That whose essential nature is not destroyed even while it undergoes modification—that too is eternal."
Regarding this, he says: "And of the external [world] as well.
How could that very same [nature], which for a very long time remained revolving in a state of equilibrium, come to possess disequilibrium in the absence of the occurrence of a distinct cause?
The meaning is that for that which is independent or even [acts] spontaneously, there could never be equilibrium if there is inequality. //8//
And if there were inference otherwise [than through the effect], it would result in the absence of the capacity for knowledge;
thus, even in this case, [the same applies] to the Pradhāna.
We shall explain that the fault characterized by the impossibility of [the pradhāna] being the principal (aṅgin) cannot be avoided by you;

however, for the sake of argument, we state its non-faultiness even while admitting it. Now he demonstrates the impossibility of its being the principal: "Even those things capable of undergoing transformation... (verse 9).
For the sense-faculty of intellect (*buddhīndriya*) is indeed one, consisting of mere skin and capable of grasping various forms and other objects;
the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are five;
and with the mind (*manas*) as the seventh, there are thus seven sense-faculties.
In some places there are three internal organs—
intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—
while in others there is only one, the intellect (*buddhi*).
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
Here, the Sāṃkhya objects: "But surely for the followers of the Upaniṣads as well..."—the state of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering is simply not possible in a single entity.

For *tapi* (to heat) is not like *as* (to exist), which has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), but rather like *pac* (to cook), which has its state residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*).
Furthermore, the object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit of an action inhering in another [the agent].
And thus, the object of suffering (*tapyam*) must be distinct from the agent of suffering (*tāpaka*), since it possesses the fruit of the action inherent in that agent;

for if they were non-different, it would follow that the object of suffering would not be an "object" (*karman*), just as Caitra—the agent—is not his own object even though he possesses the attainment of the city, which is the fruit of the act of going inherent in himself.

But if there is difference, then the status of being the object of suffering is logically established for the sufferer, just as the city, which is the object of the act of going inherent in Caitra and which partakes in its fruit, is distinct from the agent.
Therefore, since there is no difference [between them], the relationship of the sufferer and the causer of suffering is not tenable.
He states another refutation with the words "And if...
The sense is that an entity cannot be separated from its own nature.
The waves, ripples, foam, and so forth, which are the natural states of the ocean, possess the properties of manifestation and disappearance, yet the ocean is never at any time released from them.

Not only is there a difference between the object of suffering (the sufferer) and the cause of suffering (the tormentor) due to their functional roles, but this is also established by direct experience; thus he says: "And this is well-known.

For instance, even an object of value (artha), because one perceives the defects of its acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, increase, and the harm it causes, becomes a source of misfortune (anartha) and afflicts the seeker.
The object of that [feeling] is the object to be felt and the subject who feels;
these two are recognized as distinct in the world,
and the faults [of their non-distinction] have already been stated.
The meaning is: how can that [bondage] possibly exist in that which is one and non-dual?

Having thus stated that the Upaniṣadic doctrine is inconsistent, the Sāṃkhya establishes liberation within his own system by asserting the difference between the sufferer and the cause of suffering—namely, "but when there is a difference in nature" (jātyantarabhāve tu).
Indeed, the conjunction of the powers of the seer and the seen is the cause of suffering;
its cause is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-discriminative vision.
And that [ignorance] is removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), which is the discernment of the distinction [between Puruṣa and Prakṛti], because it is the opposite of it.
When that [ignorance] ceases, the conjunction caused by it ceases; and when that ceases, the suffering which is its effect ceases.
As it was said by the teacher Pañcaśikha: "By the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction, there occurs this absolute remedy for suffering."
And in this regard, bondage and liberation do not belong directly to the Puruṣa, who is unchanging;
rather, they belong to the intellect-substance (buddhisattva) alone, which has acquired consciousness through the reflection of the consciousness of the Puruṣa.
For it is thus:

The ascertainment of the nature of desired and undesired qualities, having attained a state of non-distinction [with the Puruṣa], is its experience; the ascertainment of the nature of the experiencer is liberation (apavarga),
for by that very means the intellect-principle (buddhi-sattva) itself is liberated.

Nevertheless, just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the lord because of his preeminence, so too bondage and liberation, though occurring in the *buddhi-sattva*, are in some way attributed to the *puruṣa*;
for he is the enjoyer of their fruit due to the state of non-discrimination (*avibhāga*).
Intending this very point, he said: "Perhaps there might even be the possibility of liberation.
To this it is replied: No;
because precisely due to oneness, the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is untenable.
Since the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is not tenable in the case of identity precisely because of that identity,
we must therefore accept that the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is based on conventional differentiation.
For it has been stated more than once that suffering is merely conventional and not ultimate.

This fault would indeed arise if, in the state of being a single self, the sufferer and the causer of suffering were to enter into a relationship of object and subject with one another; this is our position, as is understood from the context.

For even the Sāṃkhya, while asserting that the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is based on difference, cannot claim that the *puruṣa* is the object of the act of suffering (*tapikarman*), because, due to its unchanging nature (*apariṇāmitva*), it is impossible for it to possess the fruit produced by the action of suffering.

It has been stated that only the *sattva* is the object of affliction (*tapyam*) and *rajas* is the afflictor (*tāpakam*). However, because the objects have been presented [to it], the *buddhi-sattva* is afflicted; and through the attainment of non-discrimination from that [intellect], the *puruṣa* also appears as if afflicted, though it is not actually afflicted due to its unchangeability (*apariṇāmitva*).
Furthermore, that attainment of non-distinction is ignorance (*avidyā*);
thus, you must admit that the state of the afflicted and the afflictor is produced by ignorance.
Why then does this very point, which we are stating, appear to you as if it were the case for the *puruṣa*?
Moreover, because the tormentor is admitted to be eternal, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation.
He raises an objection: "Even though the powers of the tormented and the tormentor are eternal...
[The response is: "Because it depends on that conjunction which exists along with a cause, namely, the non-perception [of the power]. This is the meaning.
He refutes this: "No;
[it is] darkness, because it is not seen. It has already been stated that there is no affliction for the Puruṣa.
This [suffering] arises solely from the *rajas* that causes affliction to the *buddhi-sattva*;
and because that *buddhi-sattva*, through its *tāmasa* error, fails to perceive its distinction from the Self (*ātman*), which is the *puruṣa*, there arises the conceit that "the *puruṣa* suffers.
However, the *puruṣa* is not joined even by a grain of the husk of error.
However, that *buddhi-sattva* must have this *tāmasī* non-discriminative cognition (*aviveka-khyāti*) removed by means of *sāttvikī* discriminative cognition (*viveka-khyāti*).
Yet, as long as *tamas* remains at the root, it cannot be eradicated entirely.

Even when severed like a cut jujube tree, it may—having been nourished again by *tamas*, having overwhelmed the *sattva*, and having obstructed discriminative cognition—manifest once more as ignorance with its hundred peaks. Alas, such is this discourse on liberation!
[Otherwise,] one would be forced to abandon asceticism (tapas) altogether.
However, in our own position there is no such fault; thus he says: "But for the follower of the Upaniṣads...

For just as a face, though naturally pure, assumes a state of impurity when its distinct reflection is produced by the limiting condition (upādhi) of a soiled mirror-surface, [so too does the Self appear as diverse].
And that reflection is not actually defiled,
nor is the reflection in reality different from the original object; nevertheless, in that reflection, the state of being defiled finds its footing due to the proximity of the dirty mirror.
Likewise, Devadatta suffers when he perceives his own face as soiled;

however, when—through the removal of the adjunct (upādhi)—he understands by means of conceptualization that the reflection is merely the original image and that it is pure, then his suffering subsides, and he no longer thinks, "My face is soiled.

In the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a semblance of the reflection of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and whose limitation is imagined through the adjunct of ignorance (*avidyā*), suffers due to contact with imagined objects such as sound and the like; but in reality, suffering does not exist for the Supreme Self.

But when, through the culmination of the excellence resulting from the repeated practice of hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on the sentence "That thou art," a direct realization arises for him,

then the individual soul (jīva), experiencing his own self as being of the nature of pure, awakened reality, becomes solitary and established in its own state, with the entire web of afflictions along with their latent impressions completely wiped away. It is not...
Furthermore, he has no fear of saṃsāra because its cause has been eradicated root and branch by means of its unreality;
for the Sāṃkhya, however, since *tamas* is existent, it cannot be utterly destroyed.
This is what was stated: "And because it is heard that the differentiation of modifications is merely a matter of words. (10)

Regarding the doctrine of Primordial Matter as the cause (*pradhānakāraṇavāda*): just as the doctrine of Primordial Matter as the cause is opposed to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, so too is the doctrine of atoms as the cause; therefore, that too must be refuted.
The detailed exposition of the aphorism, "By this, those not accepted by the learned are also explained," is now commenced. In this regard, the Vaiśeṣikas refuted the view that Brahman is the cause.
If consciousness were the material cause of space and so forth, then space and so forth, being produced from that, would themselves be conscious;
for it is observed that qualities are produced in an effect according to the sequence of the qualities of the cause,
just as cloth produced from white threads is white.
It never becomes black;
likewise, space and so forth, when initiated by consciousness, would be conscious and not unconscious.
Therefore, the world has only the unconscious as its material cause.
And that [effect] is insentient; the atoms [are its cause].

Indeed, it is observed that the gross arises from the subtle: as a cloth arises from threads, so do threads arise from fibers; thus, by a process of successive reduction, the causal substance comes to rest as something extremely subtle and partless.
And that [atom] is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).

However, if it were admitted to possess parts, it has been stated that there would follow the absurd consequence that Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed would be equal in magnitude because both would have infinite parts.
In that regard, first of all, motion arises in the atom due to its conjunction with the *kṣetrajña* (the conscious soul) who possesses unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Then, that [atom], having conjoined with another atom, begins a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
However, many atoms, even when conjoined, do not suddenly produce a gross object, because they possess plurality while remaining [in their state of] atomicity.
It is like atoms contained within a jar.
For if the atoms contained within a jar were to originate the jar, then when the jar is being broken down, shards, gravel, and so forth would not be perceived,
because those [atoms] would not have originated [the jar].
However, because the jar itself is composed of those [atoms],
if that were the case, nothing would be perceived when the jar is destroyed by the blow of a mallet, since [the atoms] are not what was composed.
Because the atoms that constitute its parts are beyond the reach of the senses,
many atoms do not possess the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a substance.

Rather, two atoms alone originate a dyad; and its atomic dimension (*aṇutva*) as a measurement is distinct from the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) of the atom. Depending upon the cognition of Īśvara, the number "two" (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*), which has arisen, originates [the dimension of the dyad].
Nor can a substance be originated from two dyads,
because that would lead to the consequence of futility;
for that too would be merely a dyad and not something large.
For the production of magnitude arises from a plurality of causes, from magnitude itself, or from a specific accumulation;
yet there is no magnitude in the dyad (dvyaṇuka), such that a larger [substance] could be produced by those two.
Nor is there a plurality of those two, precisely because they are only two; nor is there a difference in accumulation, as in the case of balls of cotton.
Because its parts lack further subdivisions, it is devoid of the distinction of loose conjunctions between parts.

Therefore, that [whole] must also be minute (*aṇu*), just like its cause, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Furthermore, since there is no excellence in human experience and since the creation of the universe is caused by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), it is for the sake of experience; and since that [experience] is accomplished by the dyad which is its cause, what is the use of a whole based on a dyad?
Because [if it were produced] by another dyad, the act of production would be purposeless;
rather, for the sake of making production meaningful, a triad or a tetrad substance—large or long—must be produced by many dyads alone.
Furthermore, there exists a distinction in experience in each respective case.
Furthermore, there exists a source for the dimension of magnitude (*mahattva-parimāṇa*) produced in dependence upon the cognition of a Lord regarding the number "many.

However, the process is as follows: an effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*) initiated by triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth becomes large either due to the multiplicity of its causes, or due to the magnitude of its causes, or due to a specific aggregation (*pracaya*) of its causes.
By this very same process, the refutation—that qualities inhering in the cause produce another quality of the same genus in the effect-substance—is rendered non-refutable.
He states that [the argument] is inconclusive:
"Or, like the large and the long, [arising] from the short and the spherical. (BS 2.2.11)
Just as a large substance, such as a triad (tryaṇuka), is produced from a small dyad (dvyaṇuka),
yet in the production of the quality of largeness it does not depend on the largeness residing in the dyad, because that [dyad] is small.
Or, for example, that very same triad (tryaṇuka) and so forth arises as long from a short dyad (dvyaṇuka),
yet it does not depend upon the length inherent in that [dyad], because such [length] is absent [in the dyad].
The word "vā" has the sense of "and" (ca), intended to include what has not been explicitly stated.

Just as a dyad (dvyaṇuka)—which is minute and short in dimension—is produced from a spherical atom (paramāṇu) which is non-spherical, so too the insentient world is produced from the sentient Brahman; such is the application of the Sūtra according to the commentary (*bhāṣya*), namely: "But [it is] a specific quality of the atom... and so forth.
The mention of "spherical dimension" (pārimāṇḍalya) is an illustrative indication.

It should also be understood that even "atomicity" (aṇutva) residing in a dyad does not originate spherical dimension belonging to an atom, because the former has its source in the number two (dvitvasaṃkhyā).
The sūtra "from two short [atoms] and from two spherical [atoms]" refers to the substrata possessing qualities (guṇin), not to the qualities themselves.
For when it should have been read as "two by two [form] dyads," one instance of the word "two" was omitted through negligence;
in this way, the formation of the tetrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth is logically established.
For otherwise, that too would be merely a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and not large, as has been stated.
Alternatively, "two" refers to duality, just as in the rule: "The dual and singular endings are used for one and two."
For here the meaning is "in the two [dualities] and the one [unity]";
otherwise, it would have been "in some" (*ekeṣu*), because the things to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) are many.

It should be construed as follows: when those dualities which reside in the substratum of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) initiate a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*), then—because they are the initiators of four dyads, which are the things to be numbered—the two numerical dualities residing in each of them [are the cause].
The meaning is "even in the case of those that are initiators.

When the Vaiśeṣika system is established in this manner, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in its refutation has been stated. But even if it is not so established, the fallacy of deviation remains in that same state; thus he says: "Even when there are many atoms... and so forth.
The construction is: "An atom is not produced, nor is something short produced.
He objects: "Now, you might think that [the production does not occur] because it has been superseded by a contrary dimension through its own causes.
He refutes this: "Do not think so."

The meaning is this: since the qualities residing in the cause do not produce another quality of the same kind in the effect, our desired conclusion is established by this much alone; therefore, one need not weary the mind by pursuing further reasons for that.
Moreover, a [new] size (parimāṇa) occupies a place that already exists; and since no other size exists prior to its production, how could it occupy anything?
Nor does it occupy its own cause.

Intending to show that even spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*), being of the same class as its cause and possessing a cause for its non-transmission due to having equal strength, would result in the non-production of both effects, he says: "And there is no transgression from another dimension.
This means that spherical dimensions and the like are not occupied with the commencement of another dimension.

Furthermore, he says: "And there is no presence or absence of the plurality of causes and so forth in relation to spherical dimension," meaning that there is no presence or absence of the plurality of causes and so forth in the case of spherical dimension during the commencement of another dimension.
He states another instance of deviation with the words "and from conjunction.
He raises an objection: "The substance is the subject under discussion. He refutes it: "No."
Regarding the phrase "by way of an illustration":
this lack of restriction does not apply to us alone, but to you as well; thus he says, "the author of the Sūtras also."
He explains the Sūtra: "Just as in the case of the perceptible and the imperceptible. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //11//
In either case, there is no action; therefore, there is an absence of that [creation].

(BBs 2.2.12) Whether one accepts or does not accept a cause for the initial action of atoms, there is no action; consequently, there is an absence of that [creation], meaning there would be no creation through the sequence of dyads and so forth.

Alternatively, whether the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) inheres in the atoms or inheres in the individual soul (kṣetrajña), in either case, since that which is insentient cannot function without being presided over by a sentient being, there would be an absence of karma; consequently, there would be an absence of creation.
As for the Lord’s status as a presiding agent merely as an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), that will be refuted later on.

Alternatively, action does not exist for the purpose of producing conjunction or for the purpose of producing disjunction; in either case, [creation] does not occur because of the absence of conjunction, which is the cause of creation, and because of the absence of disjunction, which is the cause of dissolution.
The meaning is that there would be an absence of those two, namely creation and dissolution.
He explains this sūtra according to its intended purport: "Now, [regarding] the doctrine of atoms as the cause."
He states the nature of that which is to be refuted, accompanied by its logical justification: "And that is the doctrine (*vāda*).
[The term] "by those inherent" means by those connected to itself.
And here, "connection" refers to inherence (*samavāya*), which is the cause of the cognition "it is here," based on the relationship between the supported and the support.
Because the fifth element is partless, these are called "the four elements.
In that regard, concerning the doctrine of atoms as the cause, this Sūtra is stated.
Therein, he states the first explanation: "of those possessing karma."

By the inclusion of "and so forth" in the phrase "from impact and so forth," impulsion (*nodana*), momentum (*saṃskāra*), gravity (*gurutva*), and fluidity (*dravatva*) are included. Since impulsion and momentum share the same status as impact, and since gravity and fluidity residing in atoms are eternal, it would follow that action (*karman*) would be continuous.
He states the second explanation preceded by a doubt: "Now, the unseen [force] consists of merit and demerit;
[this refers to] the first action."

"And of the self, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), whose consciousness has not yet arisen"— this refers to "by the person possessing the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)"; the meaning is that there is a relation of inherence in the conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya).
"Because of the continuity of the connection.
Although the conjunction between the atom and the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) arises from the motion of the atom, the point is that there is a continuity in its stream.
Furthermore, if [the atom were to merge] with its entire self, there would be no increase in size.

For if there were conjunction by way of parts, then those parts of the two atoms that are in immediate contact would remain unoccupied by the conjunction in their other parts; thus, the first [case] would be possible.
However, if there were immediate proximity in their entirety, then other atoms would fit within a single atom, and thus the first [case] would not exist—this is the meaning.
He raises an objection: "Even though [atoms] are partless..."

Even so, the conjunction of atoms is indeed non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), because such is its very nature. What kind of logical reasoning is this, that "conjunction does not pervade that which is partless"?
This is precisely the logical reasoning: whatever is perceived as being thus, it is accepted as being thus.
He states the following well-founded resolution of this doubt: "The [parts] of atoms are imagined.

For it is impossible for a single partless entity to be simultaneously conjoined with and not conjoined with that very same thing, because existence and non-existence are contradictory within a single, non-dual substrate.
Or, if there were no contradiction, then contradiction would find no occasion anywhere;
yet perception is accounted for even by the postulation of spatial locations.
This is what was stated: "the locations are conceptualized."
And thus, [the author] extracts this [point], saying "this is pure," because imagined things lack reality.
He states the third explanation: "and just as at the time of the first creation.

Now, one might ask: why do striking, pushing, and so forth not exist at the time of the commencement of dissolution as causes for the action that initiates division? To this he says: "for even there, nothing is fixed."
Striking and so forth may occur at some time and in some place,
but not simultaneously in all things;
the meaning is that there is no cause for such a restriction.

"Not for the sake of establishing dissolution" means that although there is the experience of suffering at the commencement of the dissolution of the body and so forth, this statement was made with the intention that such [suffering] does not exist during the dissolution of the earth and other elements; thus it should be understood. //12//
"Furthermore, because of the admission of inherence, there is an infinite regress due to parity. He explains: "Because of the admission of inherence," and so forth.

In the first place, an independent inherence (*samavāya*) that is absolutely distinct from the two related entities (*samavāyin*) cannot join those two together, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it must be joined with the two related entities while itself being connected to them;
and if such a connection of inherence with the related entities were admitted to be by means of another relation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Now, this relation does not require another relation for its connection with the relata, because its ultimate reality consists precisely in the connecting of the relata.
For instance, it is not perceived as independent of the relata even when those relata are distinct;
nor do the two relata become unrelated when that [relation] exists.

Therefore, he raises the objection that inherence belongs to the two inherent things by its very nature and not through another relation, so there is no infinite regress: "But [inherence] is grasped by the cognition 'here'. He answers: "No, it is said."
"Conjunction is also like this.
For instance—conjunction, too, has as its ultimate reality the connection between related entities;
and even if it were distinct, it could not be defined without the two things that are conjoined.
And it is an equal argument to say that while that [conjunction] exists, the two conjoined things do not become non-conjoined;
for if it were said that conjunction is a quality (guṇa), and a quality cannot exist without inhering in a substance (dravya).

And since there can be no inherence (samavetatva) for this [conjunction] without its own inherence, he dispels the doubt that "therefore conjunction must have inherence" by stating: "nor because it is a quality" (na ca guṇatvāt).
If it were to follow that it is not a quality due to the absence of inherence, let it be so; it would cause us no harm whatsoever.
This has been stated [in the verse]: "and because of the definition of the qualities.
However, in the ultimate sense, it is said that [quality] "resides in a substance.
And that [residence] is indeed possible for conjunction by its very nature, even without inherence (*samavāya*).
Nor is it correct to argue that because it is an effect, conjunction must depend upon inherent and non-inherent causes such that conjunction itself is the inherent cause;
for this would entail the undesirable consequence that eternal conjunction is not so.

Furthermore, since inherence also has its existence dependent upon the related entities, and since those related entities—whether one or two—are perishable, inherence itself is perishable and thus an effect.
For it is impossible that there could be a quality or a possessor of qualities, or parts or a whole, such that these do not exist while their relationship does;
therefore, inherence must be an effect.
And thus, just as its production depends solely upon an efficient cause, so too is conjunction.
Now, even if inherence (*samavāya*) also requires both inherent and non-inherent causes, that same infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follows.
Therefore, like inherence, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also does not require another relation.
If it were argued that "it connects the two related things but does not connect itself with the two related things," [that would be incorrect].
In that case, is this [relation] entirely unconnected with the two related entities?
If so, being utterly distinct and unconnected, how could it connect the two related entities?
Or, if it were to connect them, it would likewise connect the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.
Therefore, it must be stated that conjunction is connected to the two conjoined things by means of inherence.
This same [objection] applies equally to the connection of inherence with its inherent substrata, except for one's stubborn insistence [to the contrary].
Thus, the sense is that there would be an infinite regress. //13//
And because it exists eternally, [there would be] either constant activity or lack of activity; this is the remainder of the argument. (BBs 2.2.14)
The commentary on this has its meaning not hidden [i.e., it is self-evident]. //14//
START BsVBh_2,2.3.15:
And because it possesses form and so forth, the opposite [of permanence] is seen. BBs_2,2.15:
Indeed, you yourselves admit that the ultimate cause of the primary elements and their derivatives is the atom (paramāṇu), which possesses form and so forth and is eternal.

If it were admitted that this [atom] possesses form and other qualities, then grossness and impermanence— both of which are contradictory to its being an atom and its being eternal— would follow as consequences;
such is this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding another property when one property is accepted.
For "necessary consequence" (*prasaṅga*) is characterized by an inevitable conclusion;

thus, by means of this *prasaṅga*, the proof (*sādhana*) undertaken to establish the cause of the world is diverted from the establishment of eternal atoms possessing color and other qualities, and is led toward the domain of Brahman.
Having first set forth the Vaiśeṣika position, he says: "Of substances that possess parts... and so on.
Having set forth their proofs for the permanence of atoms, he refutes them with the words: "And as for that which is the cause of permanence.
By saying "existent" (*sat*), he excludes [the atom] from prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*);
by saying "without a cause" (*akāraṇavat*), he excludes [it from things] such as a jar.
As for the second point regarding permanence:
indeed, something that has already acquired a form in one place is what is negated elsewhere.
Therefore, by means of that worldly negation "it is impermanent," one must postulate the existence of permanence elsewhere,
namely in those other atoms;
but that is not so.
Because permanence is also established in the case of the self;
and because we observe that even a designation which is devoid of a basis occurs when it is preceded by a mere conventional notion,
as in the expression, "There is a yakṣa here in this banyan tree."
As for the third reason for permanence, namely ignorance (*avidyā*):
if the non-perception of the cause of existing atoms— which manifest as gross effects— is "ignorance," and by that [ignorance] their permanence is established,
then, this being the case, even the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would possess permanence.

Now, if it were qualified by the condition "being non-substantial" (*adravyatve sati*), then there would be no deviation in the case of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); for since that [dyad] consists of multiple substances, it is impossible for it to be "non-substantial.
Nevertheless, this would result in "having no cause" (*akāraṇavattva*) alone being the ground for permanence.

Since "non-substantiality" (*adravyatva*) is said to mean the absence of a substance that serves as its cause, [the opponent] says "and of that" (*tasya ca*) to point out that it would be redundant. Furthermore,
since the desired conclusion is established by the reason "because of existence while being non-substantial," the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is superfluous.
Now, by the term "ignorance" (avidyā), it is stated that the two causes for the destruction of a substance are absent;
for the cause of the destruction of a substance is twofold— namely, the destruction of its parts and the destruction of the conjunction of its parts—
and neither of these two exists in an atom.
Therefore, the atom is eternal;
nor is there any deviation [from this rule] by means of pleasure and so forth.
He says, "Because they are not substances," [referring to] "even so" (*athāpi*). He refutes this with, "not necessarily" (*nāvaśyam*).
For if the process were established such that many substances, accompanied by conjunction, would originate another substance, then it would be established that there are indeed two substances.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of its destruction":
this is not the case,
because there is a failure to understand the true nature of substance.

It has already been stated above that there is no such thing as a cloth, distinct from the threads and supported by them, which could be produced by the threads acting in conjunction with their combination. Furthermore, he will later refute the six categories of existence.
Rather, the cause itself, undergoing a specific change of state, becomes the effect.
And that [cause] is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*).
For instance, clay or gold is experienced as a universal that persists through all jars, earrings, and so forth;
and it has been stated that these jars, earrings, and the like are not distinct from the clay or the gold.

And we shall explain this further ahead. Therefore, it is precisely the clay and the gold that, transforming into various forms, are designated respectively as "a jar," "a necklace," "potsherds, gravel, and fragments," and "shards, particles,
and powder," because in each case there is recognition of the material cause— the clay or the gold.

However, jars and the like are not recognized in their shards and the like, nor are shards and the like recognized in jars and the like, nor are earrings and the like recognized in their fragments and the like, nor are fragments and the like recognized in earrings and the like—wherein a causal relationship might exist. Nor should it be argued that the momentary state of the shard arises without a material cause (anupādāna) in dependence upon the very momentary state of the jar as it perishes; for what, then, would be the use of recognizing a material cause?
Since this nihilistic methodology will also be refuted later on,
it follows that the particular states, characterized by arising and passing away, are the products (upādeya) of the universal,
while the universal essence itself is the material cause (upādāna).

This being the case, just as a substance such as gold, having abandoned its state of solidity, undergoes transformation into a liquid state— and yet, although the disintegration of parts exists there, it is not the cause of that liquidity, because according to your own view, such disintegration is absent in atoms, making the occurrence of liquidity impossible— so too [is the case here].
Therefore, just as a substance consisting of atoms, through contact with fire, abandons its hardness and transforms into liquidity—
yet neither hardness nor liquidity exceeds the dimension of the atom—
so too clay or gold, which are the common substrates, abandon their state as a lump and, through the activity of a potter or a goldsmith, attain the state of a jar or a golden ornament.
However, jars, golden ornaments, and the like do not deserve to perish through the destruction of their parts or the destruction of their conjunctions;
for the shards and so forth are not its material cause (upādāna), nor is their conjunction its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa); rather, the universal (sāmānya) is the material cause.
And that [space] is eternal; nor is it assisted by conjunction, because of its oneness, since conjunction, being a property residing in two things, cannot exist in a single entity.

Therefore, it is correct that the particular states of the universal—which exists as ultimate reality—are inexpressible and have that universal as their substratum; they possess the nature of arising and passing away, like snakes and other things which have a rope or similar object as their material cause.
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "therefore" (tasmāt). //15//
