And because there is a fault in either case. BBs_2,2.16:
For the earth is experienced as something gross, consisting of smell, form, taste, and touch.
Water consists of taste, form, and touch and is subtle;
fire consists of form and touch and is subtler;
wind consists of touch and is the subtlest.
It is also recorded in the Purāṇa:
"Space, consisting of the subtle element of sound, entered into the subtle element of touch; therefrom arose wind, possessing two qualities, consisting of sound and touch. (1)
For one who likewise enters into form, both qualities of sound and touch [arise];
from that, fire possesses three qualities, and it becomes endowed with sound and touch. //2//
Sound, touch, form, and taste alone entered it;
therefore, water should be known as consisting of four qualities and having taste as its essence. //3//
If sound, touch, form, taste, and smell were to enter into one another, he would describe this earth as a mere mass of fragrance through its singular scent alone. (4)
Therefore, the earth element is seen as gross among the elements; it possesses five qualities, and by that [grossness], its specific manifestations are known as calm, terrible, and deluded. //5//
Because they mutually interpenetrate, they support one another;

thus, the earth and the other elements are joined together by smell and the other qualities. And so, to the extent that there is an accumulation of those things being joined, to that same extent there is grossness in the composite whole.
To the extent that there is a decrease [in grossness], to that same extent there is a gradation of subtlety;
thus, he states—beginning with the word "gandha"—that this matter, established through both experience and scripture, cannot be denied even by the Vaiśeṣikas, though they do not wish it so.

Let it be granted for now that sound [is not a quality of earth, etc.], because the Vaiśeṣikas do not accept it as a quality of earth and the other elements; therefore, [the author] has cited the four elements as possessing four, three, two, and one quality respectively.

Having stated the matter established by experience and scripture, he refutes it through conceptual analysis: "In the same way," meaning "like gross earth and so forth," [the argument applies] to atoms as well.
Because those with accumulated qualities increase through the accumulation of form,
and those being accumulated increase through the accumulation of a composite whole,
it follows that they are not atoms, since they are gross.

But as for one who says that the atom is not a mere aggregate of smell and so forth, but rather a substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of smell and the rest, and that even when there is an accumulation of those substrata— smell and the rest— there can be no accumulation of the substance because they are distinct,
he is addressed [as follows]: "And not without an increase in form," meaning an increase in the essential nature of the substance.
Why?
Because when the elements have undergone an accumulation of qualities in their effects, an increase in form is observed;
for atoms are not perceived by way of their own form, but rather through their effects.
Furthermore, the effect is not distinct from its odor and other qualities;
since it is not perceived as a separate substratum but rather as being identical with them,
and since it is observed to increase when they increase, it must likewise be the case that its causes— the atoms— are of the same nature.

And thus, the meaning is that there would be no state of being an atom because of its grossness. He refutes the second alternative with the words: "But if [the increase and decrease of qualities] were not postulated...
and then, "Or else, all [atoms] would possess four qualities."

Even though in this [opposing] view there would be the undesirable consequence of [all elements] possessing grossness, nevertheless, disregarding that due to its extreme obviousness, [the author] refutes it with the words "tato 'psv api" ("therefore, even in the case of water").
It should also be understood that there would be the undesirable consequence of air being visible (cākṣuṣatva) because of its possession of color-form (rūpavattva). //16//

"Furthermore, due to non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of dependence. (BsVBh_2,2.3.17) This has been explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which requires no further verbal explanation (*nigadavyākhyāta*).
Now, the author of the *Bhāṣya* refutes the Vaiśeṣika system as being contrary to the Sūtra, beginning with the words "Moreover, the Vaiśeṣikas...
Dependence upon substance (*dravyādhīnatva*) means that its definition is dependent upon substance.
For it is not the case that, like cows, horses, buffaloes, and elephants—which are defined independently of one another and are self-sufficient—[qualities and so forth are defined in such a way].

Alternatively, just as smoke and the like, whose production does not depend on fire and so forth, are cognized independently— being themselves determined without depending on fire and so forth— in the same way,
qualities and the like are not determined without depending on substance and so forth;
rather, whenever they are determined, they manifest only in the form of that [substance], for there is no independence in their manifestation.

Therefore, they do not exceed the substance; rather, the meaning is that the substance itself, in its general form, manifests in various ways. Thinking that the dependence of qualities and so forth on substance consists merely in their being effects of substance, [the opponent] objects: "But [is this not true] of other things as well, such as fire? [The author] replies: "Because there is a cognition of difference."
We do not assert that [the cognition] is dependent on that [object] in the sense of having its production dependent on it, but rather that it possesses the form of that [object];
thus, there is no deviation [in the logical rule]. He raises an objection: if it is argued that qualities are dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparable (ayutasiddha).
For where two forms are perceived by means of two distinct forms, they appear either as connected or unconnected through grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya),
such as "curd in this bowl" or "a cow and a horse."
Qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) are not so [independent];

because they lack any other form than that of the substance (*dravya*), they do not exist as distinct from the substance which serves as their substratum, since they lack the status of being formal constituents. This is what is meant by "non-separability" (*ayutasiddhi*).
And thus, the meaning is that they are perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Having thus conceptualized this non-separateness (*ayutasiddhi*), he refutes it with the words, "But as for that non-separateness...
He states, "In the case of non-separateness of location," because [the opponent's] own admission contradicts the claim that there is no difference in location.
However, if "separateness" (*yutasiddhi*) consists in two conjoined effects occupying different locations from their respective relata, then "non-separateness" (*ayutasiddhi*) would be its opposite.
However, for two eternal conjoined things, or for one of them, *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) consists in having separate motion; *ayutasiddhi* (non-separate existence) is the opposite of that.

Thus, *yutasiddhi* is established between ether and an atom, as well as between two conjoined atoms. Furthermore, *ayutasiddhi* is established between a quality and its possessor, such as whiteness and a cloth.
For in that case, the whiteness and the cloth, being related entities, do not have their respective locations elsewhere than in each other;
even though the cloth occupies the location of a different thread, the whiteness occupies the location of the cloth which is its own relatum.
That is not so.
In the case of the eternal conjunction between the self and space, there is an absence of "separate establishment" (yutasiddhi) for both;
for they do not reside in separate substrata because they themselves lack a substratum.
Nor is there separate motion for either one of the two, since both are immaterial and thus devoid of action.
Nor is there an absence of conjunction with the eternal, for that is established by inference;
for instance: space is conjoined with the self, because it is conjoined with corporeal substances.
The inference is: "like a jar and so forth.

Although a form of non-separate existence (*ayutasiddhi*) characterized by not having distinct substrata and supported entities, nor distinct movements—different from the [usual] definition of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*)—does not entail a contradiction with what you accept, it nevertheless cannot account for the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For even if inherence (*samavāya*) were accepted as having such a characteristic, when it is admitted that there is a relation between quality and qualified, the cognition would be "they are connected," not the cognition of identity (*tādātmya*).
And it is for the sake of establishing this that you postulate *samavāya* (inherence).

If, even when postulated, it does not account for this cognition, then enough with that fabrication. Furthermore, the perceptual cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not have *samavāya* as its object.
Because its meaning would be contradictory [to that].
For if it were to have that as its object, the form would be "the cloth is white," and not "the white [thing] is the cloth."
Nor is it correct to say that the word "white" (śukla) conveys its meaning in this way simply because it refers to a substance qualified by a quality;
for perception does not follow the operation of words.
Indeed, a young boy who is metaphorically identified as fire in the expression "the boy is fire" does not appear through perception as having the nature of burning fire.
Nor should it be argued that this delusion of non-difference is based on inherence (*samavāya*), for even in the case of two distinct things;

because, regarding the existence of qualities and so forth and their difference, there is no means of valid cognition other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and if that perception were erroneous, it would follow that everything is non-existent.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a proof of difference, which would serve as its substratum, to arise in contradiction to that [perception].
This has been stated: "Because it is perceived as being identical with that [substance].
Furthermore, the term *ayutasiddha* (inseparable) is primarily used in the sense of non-distinct origination;
and according to your own view, such [non-distinct origination] does not exist between substance and quality.
Because the substance is established first and the quality arises later, he says—"of two things established separately"—to show that this [opponent's] claim is false.
Now, let it be granted that there is separate establishment for the cause; [but what of the effect?]
Anticipating the objection that the effect is non-separately established from the cause because it does not exist apart from it, he refutes it otherwise with the words "even so":
for a relation, whose existence depends upon two related entities, cannot occur if even one of those related entities is non-existent;
and it has already been stated below that inherence (samavāya) is neither eternal nor independent.
Nor can it be said that the production of the effect is non-different from its inherence in the cause;
for if that were the case, since inherence is admitted to be eternal, it would follow that the cause is useless.
Furthermore, if inherence itself were produced, let that alone be the production of the effect—what is the use of inherence?
Furthermore, if there were a relation between two established entities, it would entail the consequence of their being separately established (*yutasiddhi*).
And it has already been stated that no other form of non-separate establishment (*ayutasiddhi*) is possible.
Consequently, the argument put forward by the Vaiśeṣikas—that [the relation exists] because of the absence of separate establishment—is refuted.

The claim that "conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect" would be a poorly stated position, because the very absence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) is itself non-existent. By this same reasoning, the definition that "separate existence consists in non-attainment and conjunction" is also untenable.
Let it not be that there is no relation between cause and effect;
but why should their relation not simply be conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?
To this, one must state that because this [relation] is not conjunction, it is "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhi*).
And so, let that very [definition] be stated; what is the use of this [current one], which is seized by the fault of mutual dependence?
Nor is any other [definition] possible, as has already been stated.
If it were argued that conjunction is the attainment preceded by non-attainment, or that it is produced by the action of one or by the action of both—
It is not like the relationship between a post and a hawk, or between two wrestlers; for the relationship with the threads occurs at the very moment the cloth has arisen.
Therefore, [the author] says "and just as of that which has just arisen" to show that this is indeed inherence (*samavāya*).
For even you admit that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) can be produced by another conjunction, and not only produced by action (*kriyā*);
nor is conjunction merely the attainment of what was previously unattained.
Because that [conjunction] is absent in the eternal conjunction between the self and space,
and because a newly produced effect lacks contact with its cause for a single moment;

furthermore, if a relation were established as something distinct from the nature of the related entities, then one might resort to different definitions for its various sub-types, but such a relation distinct from the related entities is itself unestablished.
For it has been stated further on that a relation distinct from the two related entities, being itself unrelated, cannot be intended to join those two related entities;

Therefore, by both reasoning and experience, the effect is not something other than the cause.
Rather, this is simply an inexpressible modification (*pariṇāmabheda*) of the cause itself.
Therefore, since the effect is not distinct from the cause, what could be connected with what?
And since conjunction is not distinct from the two conjoined things, what could be their conjunction? To this he says: "Nor [is there a conjunction] of the conjunction," and so forth.

The occurrence of various cognitions and designations with respect to even a single entity is possible by depending on the distinctions between its various indescribable particular states;

for it is not the conjunctions of the parts of the lump that perish,
but rather, while remaining conjoined, they are pushed apart by the expansion and thus come to pervade a larger space.

In this way, through contact with fire, the constituent parts of the substance gold attain a state of liquefaction while remaining in conjunction; they do not, however, become separated from one another.
Therefore, just as a lump of gold is destroyed even without the destruction of the conjunction between its parts, [so too is the case here].

Furthermore, just as liquidity arises in gold without the production of another conjunction, so too atoms will perish and others will arise even without the destruction of the conjunction of their constituent parts; thus everything is clarified. //17//

Even if the aggregate were caused by both [factors], that [result] would not be attained. BBs_2,2.18:
He states the intermediate connection:
Regarding the phrase "the established tenet of the Vaiśeṣikas":
the Vaiśeṣikas are indeed partial nihilists (ardhavaināśika).

For they accept the eternity of atoms, space, direction, time, self, and mind, as well as generality, particularity, inherence, and certain qualities; yet they maintain the total, traceless destruction (niranvayavināśa) of all remaining things.
Therefore, they are "half-nihilists" (*ardhavaināśika*).

Consequently, the presentation of that [view] serves to remind one of all nihilists (*vaināśika*) by way of their commonality in being nihilists; thus, the refutation of the nihilist doctrine follows immediately after.
For those half-nihilists who maintain the existence of stable entities, the commencement of a composite whole might indeed be possible.

However, we shall demonstrate that for those who maintain the doctrine of momentary existence (*kṣaṇikabhāvavāda*), this [objection] is utterly remote; therefore, it was said "all the more so. Now, in order to refute this, he sets forth the nihilist's (*vaināśika*) position and states its various divisions, saying: "And that is of many kinds."
Indeed, due to the diversity of proponents,
some adopt the tenet of the existence of all things, some the existence of consciousness alone, and others the emptiness of all things.

Now, if it is argued that a difference in the realization of reality cannot exist for those venerable omniscient ones because reality is of a single nature, [the author], being dissatisfied with this, says: "Or [it is due to] the difference in those to be trained (*vineya*).
For disciples possess inferior, middling, or superior intellects.

In that regard, those of inferior intellect are introduced to emptiness by means of the doctrine of the existence of all things, in accordance with their disposition; those of middling intellect are introduced to emptiness by means of the existence of mere cognition;
but for those of superior intellect, the reality of emptiness is taught directly.
As it is said in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*: "The teachings of the Lords of the World follow the inclinations of sentient beings;
they are divided manifold in the world through many skillful means. (1)

Although the teaching is differentiated by way of the distinction between the profound and the superficial, and sometimes possesses both characteristics, it is undifferentiated in that emptiness has the characteristic of non-duality. //2//
Thus,

although there exists a difference in their internal views between the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, nevertheless, since they are in agreement regarding the existence of all [dharmas], they are presented here as a single group.
And thus, the triad is established:
earth has the nature of solidity,
and water has the nature of moisture.
Fire has heat as its intrinsic nature;
wind has motion as its intrinsic nature. Motion means impelling.
Having spoken of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), he speaks of the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caittika*) with the words "likewise, form" (*tathā rūpa*).

By the etymologies "that by which things are manifested" (*rūpyante ebhiḥ*) and "those which are manifested" (*rūpyante*), the sense-faculties together with their objects constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Although earth and so forth, when being manifested, are external, they nonetheless become internal because they reside within the body or because they are connected to the sense-faculties.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is that which has the aspect of "I," or which, directed toward objects such as form, arises from the sense faculties and so forth, and exists as a continuous stream.

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is that particular state of the mind which arises upon contact with pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral objects, characterized by pleasure, pain, or that which is devoid of both.
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) is a conceptual cognition whose appearance is suitable for association with a name.
It is of such a kind as "Ḍittha, who is wearing earrings, fair-complexioned, a Brahmin, is walking.
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) consists of the afflictions (kleśa) such as attachment (rāga) and so forth,
as well as the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) such as pride (mada), conceit (māna), and so forth.
And [it consists of] merit and demerit.
Thus, the collection of these is the five aggregates. In that [collection], even though it has both as its cause—

When the external [collection]—the aggregate of primary elements and derivative matter caused by dyads—and the internal collection, which is intended as being caused by the aggregates such as form and consciousness, are considered, that [collection] is not attained; that is, its logical consistency is untenable.
Why?
Because that which is a composite lacks consciousness.
For it is observed that a conscious potter and others, having gathered all the clay, staff, and other materials, fashion a jar consisting of a composite whole.
Indeed, in the absence of a wise potter who operates the clay, staff, and so forth, the unconscious clay, staff, and other materials never fashion a jar by operating on their own.
And when there is no weaver, the loom, threads, and so forth do not weave a cloth;

therefore, the production of an effect depends upon the conjunction of causes conducive to it, and in their absence, it does not occur. Furthermore, the conjunction of causes conducive to the production of an effect depends upon the observation of an intelligent agent; in the absence of such observation [of an intelligent agent], it does not occur.

Since it is not possible [for the effect to arise otherwise], the production of an effect is pervaded by its dependence upon the observation of an intelligent agent; thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the production of the effect, being excluded from causes that are not presided over by an intelligent agent, remains restricted to those cases where there is indeed the presiding of an intelligent agent.
In this way, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
If it should be argued that the production of an effect is certainly dependent upon volition (*cetanā*), yet there exists a mind (*citta*) which is volitional, and that—
upon contact with the objects of the sense faculties and so forth— it flares up, [causing] that causal complex to become as fit for the effect as it is; thus it is.

[The opponent claims that] the conscious [Self], presiding over unconscious causes, brings about the effect; to this, he replies: "And because the manifestation of consciousness depends upon the accomplishment of a complex [of conditions].
Indeed, there is no manifestation of consciousness without the accomplishment of an external and internal complex."

Therefore, one who desires that [result] would fall into a circular argument that is difficult to resolve. Furthermore, the illumination of the mind belonging to a previous existence does not bring about the formation of the subsequent aggregate,
because at the time of formation, it has long since passed away and thus lacks efficacy.

This is because, unlike our own established conclusion, you do not admit the existence of another intelligent being— whether as an enjoyer or a ruler— who is permanent and the creator of the aggregate;
for it is only one who knows the specific arrangement of causes who can be a creator,
and one cannot know that specific arrangement of causes without [the knowledge of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, that which is momentary—failing to persist through the time of positive and negative concomitance—is incapable of cognizing those very concomitances;
therefore it was said: "of the stable.
If it were argued that causes, being independent of one another, will produce the effect even when not assembled together, [the response follows].
To the objection that there must be an intelligent agent who brings [the causes] together here, he says: "And even if one admits an independent activity.

If it is argued: "There exists the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the locus of the ego-sense and the synthesizer of the preceding and succeeding; that itself will be the synthesizer of the causes," [the response follows].
Regarding this, he says: "Of the mental disposition (āśaya) as well.
For if that which is indeed one were maintained to be stable, then it would be the self itself under another name;
but if it is momentary, [then...]
Consequently, the aforementioned fault would ensue:

if that continuum is distinct [from the self], the self is accepted under another name; if it is not distinct, it is simply consciousness itself, and since that is momentary, the aforementioned fault ensues.
The *āśaya* (basis) is the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), because the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the experience of karma reside within it.
Furthermore, *pravṛtti* (activity) is the operation of the constituent members [of the causal complex].
Furthermore, activity is not tenable for things that are momentary.
For in the world, activity is well known to depend upon an agent and to have that agent as its cause.
Therefore, that which possesses activity must exist prior to the activity and also at the time of the activity.
Otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be the states of being a cause and a substratum;

for there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things that exist at the same time, nor is there a relationship of container and contained between two things that exist at different times.
And thus, there would be a loss of momentariness; so he says: "And because of the admission of momentariness. (18)

If it is argued [that the sequence of the aggregates is established] because they are mutually dependent (itaretarapratyayatva), we say no, because they are merely the causes for the arising [of one another] (utpattimātranimittatva).
This is expressed by the words "even though" (yadyapi).
This is the meaning: in brief, the characteristic of dependent origination was stated by the Buddha as "this is the fruit of conditions.
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains fixed;
it is the stability of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, and the conformity to dependent origination."
Furthermore, this dependent origination occurs by way of two causes: connection through cause (*hetūpanibandha*) and connection through condition (*pratyayopanibandha*).

It is, moreover, of two kinds: external and internal. Therein, the causal connection of external dependent origination is as follows: from the seed comes the sprout; from the sprout, the leaf; from the leaf, the stalk; from the stalk, the stem; from the stem, the bud; from the bud, the awn; and from the awn, the flower.
"From the flower comes the fruit":
when the seed is absent, the sprout does not arise; likewise, up to the point that when the flower is absent, the fruit does not arise.
But when the seed exists, the sprout comes to be,
up to the point that when the flower exists, the fruit comes to be. In this regard, it does not occur to the seed to have the cognition, "I am producing the sprout."
Even for the sprout, there is no such cognition as "I am produced by the seed.
Likewise, up to the flower, there is no such thought as "I am producing the fruit.
Similarly, even for the fruit, there is no such thought as "I am brought forth by the flower."
Therefore, even in the absence of consciousness (*caitanya*) and even in the absence of another presiding agent, the fixed law of cause and effect is observed among seeds and the like.
The causal nexus (*hetūpanibandha*) has been explained; now the conditional nexus (*pratyayopanibandha*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is being stated.
Condition (*pratyaya*) is the conjunction of causes.
Because other causes depend upon each respective cause, this state of those [causes] as they so depend is called a condition.
This refers to the sense of "assemblage" (samavāya).
Just as a sprout arises from the assemblage of the six elements (*dhātu*) with the seed as its cause,
therein the earth element performs the function of cohesion for the seed, whereby the sprout becomes solid.
The water element moistens the seed;
the fire element ripens the seed;
the wind element brings forth the seed from which the sprout emerges.
The space element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed,
and the season also brings about the transformation of the seed;
thus, when these elements are present without deficiency, through their conjunction, the seed germinates and the sprout arises, and not otherwise.
In this regard, it does not occur to the earth element, "I perform the function of supporting the seed," nor does it occur to the season, "I bring about the transformation of the seed."
Even for the sprout, it does not occur thus: "I am produced by these conditions.

Likewise, internal dependent origination occurs through two causes: connection by way of cause (*hetūpanibandha*) and connection by way of condition (*pratyayopanibandha*). Among these, its connection by way of cause is as follows: "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to conditioned by birth are old age, death, and so forth. If ignorance were not to exist, the formative forces would certainly not have arisen.
Thus it continues up to birth (*jāti*).
If birth were not to exist, then aging, death, and the rest would certainly not arise.
In this regard, ignorance (*avidyā*) does not think, "I bring about the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)."
It does not occur to the formative forces (saṃskāra) that "we have been produced by ignorance.
Likewise, it does not occur to anything up to birth (jāti) that "I am producing old age, death, and so forth.
Nor does it occur to old age, death, and so forth that "we have been produced by birth and the other factors."

Moreover, even though ignorance and the other factors are themselves insentient and are not presided over by another conscious being, the production of formations and so forth occurs—just as sprouts and the like arise when seeds and such are present, despite being insentient and lacking the supervision of another conscious being.
This is because we observe only this much: that "having depended upon" (pratītya) or "having reached" (prāpya) this, that arises; and no presiding consciousness is perceived.
This is the causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) of internal dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Now, as for the conditional connection (*pratyayopanibandha*): the body arises from the conjunction of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
Among these, the earth element of the body produces solidity.
The water element moistens the body;
the fire element digests what has been eaten and drunk by the body;
the wind element performs the functions of respiration and so forth for the body.
The space element (ākāśadhātu) creates the state of internal cavities within the body.

That which brings about the sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), conjoined with the activity of the five consciousnesses and being associated with outflows (sāsrava)— namely, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna)— is called the consciousness element (vijñānadhātu).
For when the internal elements, such as earth and the rest, are complete, then from the conjunction of them all, the arising of the body occurs.
In that process, it does not occur to the elements of earth and so forth, "We are producing the hardness and other qualities of the body.
Nor does it occur to the body, "I am produced by these conditions."
Thus,

the body arises from insentient elements such as earth and the rest, which are not presided over by another conscious being, just like a sprout. This dependent origination, being directly perceived, is not to be otherwise conceived.
In this regard, among these very six elements, there is the notion of unity, the notion of a solid mass, and the notion of permanence.
the perception of pleasure, the perception of a sentient being, and the perception of a person;
the perception of "human being," the perception of "mother" or "daughter," and the perception of "I-making" and "mine-making."
This ignorance (avidyā) is the root cause of the entire mass of misfortunes in saṃsāra;
when this ignorance exists, the formative forces (saṃskāras)—namely, passion, hatred, and delusion—operate toward sense objects.
Consciousness (vijñāna) is the representation of things as objects.
From consciousness arise the four formless aggregates of clinging; that is "name.
Depending upon these, form is produced.

When these are condensed together as one, it is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). The stages of the body, such as the embryo (*kalala*) and the bubble (*budbuda*), are name-and-form. The sense-faculties, which are mixed with name-and-form, are the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The coming together of the three—name-and-form, the sense-faculties, and consciousness—is contact (sparśa).
From contact arises feeling (vedanā), such as pleasure and so forth.
When feeling exists, there occurs an attachment (adhyavasāna) thinking, "I must again experience this pleasure," which is craving (tṛṣṇā).
From that, grasping arises, which consists of the activities of speech and body.
From that, existence arises; "existence" refers to merit and demerit (dharma and adharma), from which birth occurs.
Birth is the manifestation of the aggregates caused by those [merits and demerits].
Subsequent factors such as aging and death have birth as their cause.
Aging is the maturation of the aggregates that have been born;
death is the destruction of the aggregates.
The internal burning of a dying fool who is attached to his children, wife, and so forth is grief (*śoka*).
The lamentation arising from that is: "O mother! O father!"
Alas! This lamentation for my children, wife, and so forth;
the suffering experienced in conjunction with the five types of sensory consciousness when encountering the unattainable;
and mental suffering, which is dejection.
And such types of means are included among those secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

These—ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, which have birth and so forth as their cause, and birth and so forth, which have ignorance and so forth as their cause—are mutually causal and revolve incessantly like a waterwheel. Thus, it is by these factors beginning with ignorance that the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is projected.
He refutes this as follows: "That is not so; why?
Because [the cause] is the sole occasion for origination.
This is the intended meaning: indeed, that effect which is bound to its cause may well arise independently of anything else, since its production depends solely upon the cause.
The collection of the five aggregates, however, is dependent upon conditions; its arising is not governed by causes alone, but rather is born from the convergence of various causes.
And it has been stated that there is no other agent besides consciousness to bring these causes together.

Because even the arising of a sprout from a seed— which is dependent upon conditions— is itself subject to dispute and thus falls within the scope of the thesis; and because if one were to point out a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of the thesis itself, it would lead to the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of invalidating all inference.
It might be argued as follows:
soil and the other factors, having reached their final moment, initiate the sprout independently;
however, their mutual conjunction occurs by virtue of the conditions for their approach.

Nor should it be said that since the effect is established from a single cause alone, what is the use of other causes? For it is not the case that the effect is established merely by following immediately after a cycle of causes; nor is it logical to claim that even if one [cause] is capable of producing the effect, others may remain indifferent.
For they are not so wise as to deliberate thus: "Not even one among us is capable of this task; therefore, our presence is useless.
Rather, because their mutual proximity arises dependent upon the conditions for their approach, they are neither able to fail to arise nor able to remain absent.
And depending upon all of them, being independent [of any one], the effect also ought not to fail to arise.

Nor is it the case that, although all [causes] produce their effects by virtue of their own power, they do not desire various effects, because their capacity exists only for those specific effects. Furthermore, there is no difference in the effect resulting from a difference in the causes,
because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is a single unity.
And since the differentiation of that [cause] is the cause for the multiplicity of effects, as is observed to be the case;
that is not so.
For if, having reached their final moment, they were independent in the production of their own effects, [then...]
Indeed, by this sequence, all [preceding moments], each in turn, are independent in the production of their respective effects.

Thus, even though there is no difference in their being located within the granary, that seed-moment situated in the granary which must produce—through a succession of its own effect-moments—a seed-moment capable of generating a sprout, is itself entirely independent in the production of its own effect; and so it is for every [subsequent moment].

If the seed-moments occurring in immediate succession were independent [of their predecessors], then a farmer would achieve his purpose simply by placing a seed in a granary; he would have no need for the laborious work of farming, which involves so much suffering.
For that very seed-moment by which a sprout is to be produced through its own series of moments, that independent series of moments would produce the sprout right there in the granary.
Therefore, it must be stated that the final, intermediate, or initial moments arise as an effect only through mutual dependence.
As they have said: "Nothing arises from a single [cause]; everything arises from a causal complex (sāmagrī). And this is as follows:
The conjunction of causes is observed to be preceded by an intelligent being who understands their specific arrangement and its purpose; therefore, it cannot arise from that which is insentient.
This is what was stated: "A composite would be possible if some cause for the composite were understood.
This also applies to the case of mutual dependence (*itaretarapratyayatva*).
The meaning is: "even though they are mutual causes.
Not understanding the intended implication (abhisaṃdhi), the opponent objects: "But surely [the series] is implied by implication through ignorance and the rest. He replies: "To this it is said:"
Regarding the phrase "yadi tāvat":
does "impelling" (ākṣepa) mean production, or rather making known?
In that regard, a cause does not produce an effect because it would otherwise be impossible; rather, it does so by its own inherent capacity.
Therefore, it must be explained as a process of making known.
And thus, another producer must be stated for that which has been made known;

and even in the case of a permanent [entity], such a thing is not possible without a conscious presiding agent, despite the existence of an enjoyer— how much less so, then, in the case of momentary entities?
The aggregate might perhaps be impelled by the experience of an experiencer;
however, he shows that such an experiencer does not exist at all, thereby demonstrating its complete dismissal—by the phrase "in those devoid of an experiencer.
Furthermore, many things, existing in a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor, produce an effect.
Furthermore, on the view that things are momentary, there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, because a momentary entity cannot be a locus for benefit;
since a moment is indivisible, it is impossible for it to be either unbenefited or benefited.
Or, if that [arising] were possible through a difference in time, it would contradict momentariness;
this is what he means by saying, "and in cases devoid of a substratum and a superstratum.
Now, this is the intended meaning:
For if dependent origination were a connection based on conditions (*pratyaya*), then an intelligent presiding agent might be required;
however, it is not a connection based on conditions, but rather a connection based on causes (*hetu*).
And thus, no presiding agent is needed.

The intention is that the cause will produce the aggregate of effects by its very nature alone. Granting for a moment that an effect does not arise from a solitary cause, the author—intending to show that this position entails the fallacy of mutual dependence—says: "How [can it be] that very [cause]?"
Now, having set aside dependent origination as it relates to conditions (*pratyayopanibandhana*), he raises an objection: "If you think that they are merely aggregates (*saṃghāta*)," [he replies:
"For even unstable entities always arise and pass away only in combination;
they do not, however, remain fixed apart from that state and then be gathered into a heap by anyone."
And thus, the sense is that this was brought about here by a conscious creator;
by the word "beginningless," he eliminates the fallacy of mutual dependence.
Having thus formulated this [position], he refutes it with the words: "Even so, because of the aggregate" (*saṃghātāt*).

That continuum of formations (*saṃskāra-saṃtāna*) called merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), which exists as a series of aggregates, must produce pleasure and pain accordingly either by itself, without depending on any adventitious factor, or else by depending on one.
If it were produced without dependence, it would always produce pleasure and pain;
for that which is capable and independent cannot be delayed. If it is produced through dependence, then a cause for that attainment must be accepted by one who possesses discernment.
Thus, dependent origination is not based on conditions.

Therefore, one must maintain that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) belongs solely to the continuum of the aggregation when it is independent of adventitious factors, whether in producing a similar [effect] or a dissimilar one.
And in this case, the refutation stated in the Bhāṣya applies.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the aggregate exists for the sake of experience":
it is established by personal experience that one who has not yet attained experience, being desirous of experience and wishing to obtain it, engages in the means to achieve it.

This engagement is postulated only when there is a stable experiencer distinct from the experience itself—one who persists through the time of the experience and its means; it is not postulated when such a subject is unstable.
Nor is it [possible] in the case of that which is not other than enjoyment;
for enjoyment does not serve for the sake of enjoyment, nor does one thing serve for the sake of another's enjoyment.
The same should be understood regarding liberation as well.

In that case, if one who desires enjoyment and one who desires liberation were to remain fixed [in their respective positions], there would be an abandonment of what has been accepted; or, if they were unstable, it would follow that activity would ensue—this is the meaning.
However, a composite entity (saṃghāta) cannot be established because of the absence of an enjoyer.
Because activity is untenable in the absence of an enjoyer, there is an absence of an agent;
consequently, due to the absence of action, the composite whole cannot be established—this is the meaning. //19//
And because of the cessation of the preceding [moment] upon the arising of the succeeding one (BBs 2.20).
He states the connection of this [sūtra] with the preceding sūtra: "This has already been stated."

Having accepted dependent origination as a causal connection (*hetūpanibandhana*), dependent origination as a conditional connection (*pratyayopanibandhana*) has been refuted; the meaning is that he now refutes even that causal connection. He states the refutation: "Now this... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is ceasing":

the state of being in the process of ceasing (*nirudhyamānatā*) cannot be accepted by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*)—who assert that destruction is causeless—as being the presence of a cause of cessation, as the Vaiśeṣikas do, because that is not their position.
Therefore, "the state of being in the process of ceasing" must be said to mean either being seized by destruction or having just recently ceased.
And what is intended by "ceased" is "ceased for a long time";
thus, since both are seized by non-existence, the status of being a cause is untenable. He raises an objection: "But if it is an existing entity..."

For the existence of a cause at a time prior to the production of its effect is purposeful, but not at the time of the effect; the point is that since the effect is already established at that time, the existence [of the cause] is useless for the sake of establishing it.
He refutes this very point from the perspective of worldly experience with the words "of that which has become an entity" (*bhāvabhūtasya*).
For generally, in the world, entities are seen to perform their functions only after having come into being and having become active;
and thus there is stability [of the entity], otherwise there would be contradiction with worldly experience.
He raises an objection again: "But [it is] existence itself. As they say: "For those things, existence itself is the action, and that very same thing is called the causal factor (*kāraka*).

It is true that there is thus possession of activity; nevertheless, he states that even so, momentary things lack the nature of being causes: "Even so, the causal status of a momentary thing is simply not tenable."
For jars and the like, as well as necklaces and the like, are experienced as having the nature of clay and gold respectively, due to their causes being clay and gold.
If the cause were not present at the time of the effect, how could there be an experience of those effects as having that [causal] nature?
Nor should it be said that the effect merely resembles the cause, but does not possess identity with it.
For if there were no persistence of any form, similarity itself would be untenable; or, if there is such persistence, that very [persistence] is the cause,
and thus its identity with the effect is established— this is the meaning of the non-momentariness [of things].

But if there were total dissimilarity, the relation of cause and effect would result even in the case of threads and a jar, which would lead to the fallacy of over-extension; thus he says, "or even without [it].
Nor is the fact of its existence [when the other exists] the regulator, because that cannot be grasped in a single moment.
The meaning is that the universal (sāmānya) is not a cause;
or, if it were a cause, its momentariness would be lost, which would result in the undesirable consequence of favoring our own position.

Furthermore, even among the three alternatives regarding arising and ceasing, there is the consequence of the entity being eternal; thus he says: "Moreover, as for what are called arising and ceasing..."
Even if one were to establish [the self] as a synonym [for the aggregates], it should be understood that this entails its permanence.
Since it would be unassociated with the arising and ceasing of things, it follows that the thing itself is eternal;
for even in the case of association, association with what is non-existent is logically impossible.
It should also be understood that if one accepts the existence of a sentient being (*sattva*), there would be the consequence of eternalism (*śāśvatatva*).
The remainder is explained by its literal meaning. //20//
START BsVBh_2,2.4.21:
If it were non-existent, there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity.
(BBs_2,2.21) For a consciousness that lacks the appearance of blue acquires its blue aspect from the blue object as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
From the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), which is the prior consciousness, comes the nature of cognition;
from the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), which is the eye, comes the specific determination of grasping form;
and from the causal cooperative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*), which is light, comes the clarity of the object.

In the same way, for mental factors such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, which arise from causes non-different from those of the mind, these very four causes apply. This proposition— that mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes— would be contradicted if non-existence were considered a cause.

Now, [if it is argued that] "it remains for as long as the production of subsequent moments occurs," then production is non-different from the entity being produced; and if that were so, there would be a loss of momentariness, which constitutes a failure of the thesis. //21//
START BsVBh_2,2.4.22:
The non-attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation [is established] because there is no interruption. BBs_2,2.22:
"Pratisaṃkhyā" (analysis) is a cognition that is contrary to existence.
By that [cessation], there is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the state of the intellect having the form "I am making this existent non-existent" is the contrariety (*pratīpatva*) toward existence.
By this, non-deliberative cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also explained.
Cessation has either the continuum as its object or the momentary instant of the continuum as its object;
first of all, the cessation of the continuum is not possible.

For it is the possessors of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) themselves— those characterized by the nature of arising and passing away— who are established as the continuum (*saṃtāna*) by way of the relationship between cause and fruit.
In that regard, there is that final possessor of the continuum,
through whose cessation the continuum must come to an end.
Does it initiate some result or not?
If it initiates one, then it is not the final [moment];
and in that case, there would be no cessation of the continuum.
If, however, there were no undertaking [of causal activity], it would be the last [category];
but it would be non-existent, because it lacks the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritā*), which is the defining characteristic of existence.

If that [continuum] does not exist, then its producer is also non-existent because it is a non-existent producer; by this sequence, all members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) are non-existent, and thus their continuum is utterly non-existent.
Therefore, of what could there be cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
Furthermore, a continuum is not merely the causal relationship between similar members of the continuum.
Its cessation is the arising of something heterogeneous, and the very moment that produces this heterogeneous [state] is the final moment of the continuum.
If that were the case, then when a cognition of taste or the like arises within the flow of a cognition of form, it would follow that the continuum is severed.
Or, even if there is some degree of similarity, because it exists at least in terms of its ultimate existence (*sattā*) despite being of a different nature, there is no cessation of the continuum.
With this intention, he said: "In all continua, because the relationship of cause and effect among the members of the continuum is uninterrupted, the interruption of the continuum is impossible.

Furthermore, the two types of cessation—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—are not possible as objects of existence.

In this regard, first of all, there is indeed a refutation: for a phenomenon that has just arisen and has not yet begun to function, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is impossible, because it does not depend upon human effort.
Nevertheless, he states another fault regarding both types of cessation with the words, "for [it is not] of phenomena... and so forth.

Since destruction without a continuity (niranvaya-vināśa) is not possible, therefore even that which is indefinable (nirūpākhya) is not possible; for even a thing that has perished remains definable by means of that very form which possesses continuity. He states the reason for the absence of destruction without continuity: "In all states whatsoever," and so forth.
Whatever possesses the nature of persistence is that which exists in the ultimate sense.

However, the various states—designated as specific modifications and characterized by arising and passing away—are all ultimately indefinable; therefore, they do not possess ultimate reality in themselves.
However, their reality is precisely that which persists;

and because that [reality] is recognized everywhere, it does not perish. Thus, since the possessor of the states does not perish, there is no destruction of the states without a persisting substrate (*niranvaya-vināśa*), because their persisting reality is uninterrupted everywhere.
This might be so:
in all cases such as a lump of clay, clay, a jar, or a shard, let it be thus because of the recognition of the essence of clay (*mṛttattva*).
But what persisting form is there to be recognized in a drop of water that has fallen and vanished upon the surface of a heated stone?
Lest there be a destruction of this [substance] without any continuity (*niranvaya-vināśa*), he says: "even in cases where recognition is indistinct.

Here too, it is to be inferred that those waters are led by fire toward the solar orb to become clouds, because one observes the uninterrupted persistence of the underlying continuants (*anvayin*) such as earth and so forth.
In this regard, it can be said: "The state of being water does not differ in a drop and in the ocean;
even when the drop has perished, its continuity remains in the sea."
Therefore, it is established that there is no destruction whatsoever that is without a causal continuity. //22//
START BsVBh_2,2.4.23:
And because there are faults in both cases. BBs_2,2.23:

The equipment (parikara) is the causal complex for right knowledge, consisting of the restraints (yama), the observances (niyama), and so forth, as well as hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana), and so forth.
The paths consist of the meditations on momentariness, selflessness, and so forth; the rest is self-evident. //23//
And [the atoms would have to exist] in space as well, because there is no distinction [between them]. This he explains with the words: "And that which belongs to them... and so forth.
Even for those who disagree with the authority of the Vedas, it must be stated that space (*ākāśa*) is inferable from the quality of sound.

For instance: since sound is distinct from generality, particularity, and inherence by virtue of possessing a genus (*jāti*), and since it is intangible yet perceptible by a single external sense organ, its status as a quality (*guṇa*) is inferred—just like odor and other such qualities.
Furthermore, this [sound] is not a quality of the self (*ātman*), because it is an object of an external sense organ.
For this very reason, it is not a quality of the mind,
because its qualities are imperceptible;
nor is it a quality of earth and the other [elements], because...
Because its qualities, such as odor and so forth, are not perceived in association with it;

therefore, having become a quality, like odor and the rest, that substance which is inferred from being perceptible by a specific sense organ is the fifth element, the entity called space (*ākāśa*). Moreover, they maintain that space is the absence of obstruction (*āvaraṇābhāva*).
A negation, whose own determination is dependent upon the determination of the locus of that which is to be negated, cannot be determined if the determination of its locus is non-existent.
And that locus of the absence of obstruction is space (*ākāśa*), which is a real entity (*vastu*). The rest is self-evident. //24//
And because of recollection (anusmṛti).
He analyzes [the opponent's position]: "Furthermore, the nihilist [claims] that for every entity..."

But for one who is not satisfied, thinking that memory may still be possible because of the cause-and-effect relationship within a single continuum despite this difference between the perceiver and the rememberer, he states the contradiction with the perception known as recognition: "Moreover,
[there would be] a single agent of seeing and remembering."
The meaning is that one should understand the statement "then I saw" to signify: "I remember, but another saw.
The subsequent section is an elaboration on the contradiction with the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
"From birth until the final exhalation" means until death;
furthermore, recognition is not based on similarity.
Since that [recognition] is possible only in the absence of a single [entity] that perceives both the preceding and succeeding moments, he raises an objection: "This is similar to that.
The meaning is this: this is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*).
Furthermore, conceptual construction determines its own internal form as being external;
it does not, however, grasp the preceding and succeeding moments or their similarity in reality.
Therefore, how can there be the consequence of a single, stable entity that perceives many?
He refutes this: "No;

because [the cognition] 'this is by that' involves the apprehension of distinct entities. This conceptual construction (vikalpa) first manifests as an appearance of a sentence-meaning composed of various word-meanings; therefore, one who asserts that these various word-meanings do not manifest therein would contradict their own self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).
Furthermore, it is not possible for a single cognition to possess multiple forms,
because that would contradict its unity; nor is it logical to claim that there are as many distinct cognitions as there are forms.
If that were the case, since cognitions would terminate with each individual form and because they lack any mutual communication, there would be no such thing as "manifoldness" (*nānātva*).
Therefore, it must be stated that cognition has as its object both preceding and succeeding moments along with their similarity;

and this is not possible without a single knower who persists through the states of the preceding and succeeding moments—thus follows the undesirable consequence of the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

If it should be argued that in this conceptual construction there is the employment of two words— “this” and “is similar to that”— but what is intended here is not two referents as the loci of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) and their similarity,
but rather that the cognition itself is imagined to have such a form;
To this he says: "For when a thing is well-known in the world... Dispute (*vivāda*) is the acceptance of two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum.
In that case, one person establishes his own position, while the other refutes that proof.

And all of this would not be possible if conceptual constructions did not have external objects as their objective supports, nor if they did not possess meanings established by worldly convention; for if they were merely forms within cognition, then since the properties appearing in conceptual constructions—

such as permanence and impermanence— would lack a single common object, there could be no contradiction between them, given that the cognitions themselves, which serve as the subjects (*dharmin*), are distinct.
For those who assert both the eternity of the self and the non-eternity of cognition do not contradict one another.

Nor does one who, intending to express the omnipresence of the self by using the word "eternal" in its non-worldly (alaukika) sense, contradict another who uses the word "eternal" for the self in its worldly (laukika) sense.

Therefore, by one who wishes to establish his own position and intends to refute the arguments of the opposing side, it must be stated that conceptual constructions possess meanings established in the world and have external objects as their basis.

If it were argued that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have two kinds of objects—the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*)—wherein the internal form is the apprehended object while the external is the determined object; and that in this way, the contradiction characterized by the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, as well as the status of having well-known referents, becomes possible—then [the author] says: "That alone which is ascertained as 'this very thing is the meaning' [is the object]."
To say anything else than this would merely demonstrate one's own prolixity.
This is the intended meaning: what is this "state of being determinable" (adhyavaseyatā) for an external object?
If it is "being graspable" (grāhyatā), then there is no twofold division [between perception and conceptualization].
Now, let another [objection] be considered:

has it not already been stated by those very [opponents] that activity occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within what is merely its own appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), which is actually non-objective? Furthermore, what is this "determination" of the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Is it an instrument (*karaṇa*), or a conjunction (*yojana*), or a superimposition (*āropa*)?
It cannot be an instrument,
for one thing cannot be made into something else.
Indeed, even a thousand artisans could never turn a jar into a cloth,
nor could they join an internal part with an external one;
moreover, if that were the case, there would be the cognition that it is "joined."
Furthermore,
as for this superimposition (āropa), does it occur when the external object is being perceived or when it is not being perceived?
If it occurs when it is being perceived, then does it occur through conceptual construction (vikalpa) or through a non-conceptual cognition (avikalpaka) arising at that same time?

To begin with, conceptual construction cannot have as its object a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is incapable of being associated with verbal expression, that does not conform to conventions of verbal designation, and that is not shared across space and time;
as they say: "The nature of pleasure and so forth is such that it cannot be the object of convention, for it is not shared by anything else."
Therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression.
Thus,

when an external object is being grasped by a non-conceptual cognition occurring at that time, but is not grasped by a conceptual cognition, it is not possible for that conceptual cognition to superimpose its own form upon it.
For it is not possible for a cognition of silver to superimpose silver upon an object standing before one that does not appear in the cognition of silver.

If the external object were not being apprehended, there would be only "its own form" and not "the external"; and in that case, there would be no superimposition. Furthermore, does this conceptual construction, while being self-cognized, first grasp its own form as a real entity and subsequently superimpose the external?
Now, when it grasps its own form, at that very moment it superimposes [the object].
Since cognition is momentary and devoid of succession, successive acts of grasping and superimposing are not possible for it.
Therefore, one must say that at the very moment it grasps the non-objective form of itself, it simultaneously superimposes the object.
And this is not tenable;
for one's own form (*svākāra*) is extremely vivid due to its being directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*),
whereas the external object being superimposed is indistinct and must therefore be something other than that [vivid form], rather than the superimposed form being one's own form.
Nor can superimposition be designated merely by the non-apprehension of difference,
because it has been stated that the apprehension of difference consists in the forms of clarity and lack of clarity.

Furthermore, if activity directed toward an external object occurs through the non-apprehension of its difference from a non-external particular (svalakṣaṇa) while the external object itself is not being apprehended, [then the following would ensue].
Well then, since no distinction from the three worlds has been apprehended by this [cognition], it would apply to anything whatsoever without distinction.
By this, the superimposition of externality even upon light—which is merely the form of cognition—is refuted.
Therefore, it was well said: "To speak of something other than that would only reveal one's own prolixity."

Furthermore, conventional usage is based on similarity; it is grounded in a cognition of the form "this is similar to that," and not in a cognition of the form "this is that very same thing. Thus he says: "And this conventional usage does not arise from similarity. [Objection:

But in cases such as a flame, even when there is no cognition of similarity, conventional usage is observed to be based on the apprehension of its continued existence due to similarity; so it should be here as well.
Fearing that this might not satisfy the reader’s previous objections, he says: "It might even happen with regard to an external object.
To illustrate: common people mock a Pāśupata who, while entering a city through a gate crowded with various folk, makes a unique mark for himself to distinguish his identity from other men. //25//
START BsVBh_2,2.4.26:
"Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed" (BBs_2,2.26).
For this reason as well, the doctrine of the Nihilists is untenable.
The nihilists (vaināśika), who desire the production [of effects] from the unstable, effectively assert that the production of entities arises from non-existence itself;
this has already been stated above.
If the production of an effect were independent [of causes], human effort and karma would be rendered futile.

Furthermore, since a moment cannot be assisted by dependence because it is indivisible, and since there can be no dependence upon that which provides no assistance, it follows that [the entity] would be non-momentary.

Moreover, because the negation of either dependence or independence is inseparable from the affirmation of the other, there is no other alternative; thus, an entity does not arise from an unstable entity.

The meaning is that, since the position of momentariness implies the non-existence [of the cause], it follows by implication that the arising of an entity occurs from non-existence; this is not merely implied by the logic, for they also demonstrate it by stating: "because there is no manifestation without having destroyed [the cause]."
He analyzes this [point] with the words: "From what has perished, indeed, [the effect arises].
The particle *kila* indicates a lack of conviction.
If the effect were to arise from an immutable cause (*kūṭastha*), then everything would arise from everything.
This is the underlying intention: an immutable entity must either have the nature of producing an effect or not have that nature.
If it has the nature of producing an effect, then it would produce all its effects simultaneously, as long as they are to be produced, because it is impossible for a capable thing to delay.
But if it does not have that nature, it could never produce [the effect].
If it were argued that, although capable, it produces effects sequentially by means of successive auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*),
that is incorrect.
Because it cannot withstand such conceptual analysis:
do these auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide some benefit to it or not? If they do not provide any, then, being non-beneficial, one would not depend upon them as auxiliaries.
Even in the case of its production (*ādhāna*), they would have to produce either a distinct or a non-distinct benefit (*upakāra*).
If it were non-different, that very [nature] would be what is expressed, and thus its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) would be contradicted.

But if there is a difference regarding the benefit, then since the effect exists when that [benefit] exists and does not exist when it does not, the benefit—by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—[is established as the cause], even though the immutable [entity] remains.
Thus, that which performs an action is not a [permanent] entity; therefore, an entity does not perform purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*).
As it has been said: "What do rain and sun do to space? Their effect is upon leather. If [the entity] were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like space, it would have no effect."
Thus, it is well said: "If an effect were to arise from an immutable cause that is incapable of producing anything, then everything would arise from everything."
He summarizes: "Therefore, from those seized by non-existence.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Not from the non-existent, because it has not been observed."
An effect does not arise from non-existence.
Why?
Because it is not observed.
For the production of effects such as sprouts from a rabbit's horn is not observed.
If, however, the arising of an entity were to occur from non-existence, then, because there is no distinction in their being non-existent, a sprout would arise even from a rabbit's horn and the like;
for non-existence does not differ [in its nature].
The meaning is that if it were connected with a qualification, even that non-entity would be an existent thing (bhāva) and not something indefinable.
Having granted for the sake of argument that a non-entity can be connected with a qualification, he says: "Nor is a non-entity the cause of the arising of anything.
Furthermore, whatever is not connected with something cannot be a modification of that thing.
Just as jars, bowls, cups, and so forth, when not permeated by gold, are not transformations of gold;
and since these transformations are not permeated by non-existence,
they are therefore not transformations of non-existence.
"But for you, there would be a modification of the entity,
because the entity is inherent in that [non-existence]," he says with the words, "And if an entity arises from non-existence.
Having repeated the statement of the proponent of non-existence as the cause, he refutes it with the words, "As for what was said..."
Even a stable entity produces effects sequentially through the gradual conjunction of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Nor are these auxiliary causes non-beneficial;
yet the assistance (*upakāra*) conferred upon it by those auxiliaries is neither different nor non-different from it.
However, it is indeed indeterminable; and from that which is indeterminable, an effect that is likewise indeterminable arises.
Yet, this does not imply that the stable entity is a non-cause.
It has been stated that because the effect has that [cause] as its material basis, it is like the snake having the rope as its material basis;
and thus says the Śruti: "Only 'clay,' indeed, is real."
Furthermore, even for those who maintain that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are distinct in every respect, exist as real entities (*vastusat*),
why is it that from seeds of a certain kind only effects of the nature of sprouts are produced, and not effects of the nature of camels?
For there is no distinction whatsoever between one seed and another seed, or between them and a camel, insofar as they are absolutely dissimilar;
nor do the universals "seed-ness" and "sprout-ness" exist as ultimate realities, such that a real causal relationship could exist between these two.

Therefore, one must maintain that the rule for the production of a specific type of sprout from a seed of the same type— which is based on the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as a conceptual construct— is established;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference based on the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*).
Only a mere indication has been given;
however, since the detailed exposition was provided in the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā* and the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity. //26//
START BsVBh_2,2.5.27:
And thus there would be the accomplishment [of results] even for those who are indifferent.
BBs_2,2.27 / The commentary on this is easy to understand. //27//
START BsVBh_2,2.5.28:
"Not non-existence, because of perception" (BBs_2,2.28).
He states the connection with the preceding section: "In this way," etc.

He states the distinction of the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) over the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), on the grounds that it is the intended view of the Sugata, by saying: "It is said that for some...

Now, the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting knowledge (*pramiti*)—in these four categories, the totality of reality (*tattva*) is complete; for if even one of these were absent, reality could not be established.
Therefore, by this [proponent] who establishes reality as consisting merely of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), these four categories must be accepted.
And thus, the reality is not merely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

For it is impossible that there should be only consciousness and yet fourfold categories [of object, subject, means, and act]; therefore, he says: "In that doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), by way of a form mounted upon the intellect.
Even though, according to experience, there is no object of experience, experiencer, or act of experiencing other than experience itself,

Nevertheless, it should also be understood that this entire conventional operation of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and results, as well as the operation of the knower, exists only internally, mounted upon the intellect and constructed by the intellect;
the meaning is that it is not ultimately real.
And thus, [your argument] proves what is already established.
For the proponents of Brahman do not accept that cognition possesses forms such as blue and so forth; rather, they hold that blue and so forth are *anirvacanīya* (indescribable).

To explain: the very nature of consciousness, when associated with an unreal form, is the object of knowledge (*prameya*); the illumination of that object of knowledge is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*).
The capacity to illuminate that [object] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He states—“even though an external object exists”—that even for the two proponents of the external [world], the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, the conventional usage of the means of valid cognition and its result is intended to be merely conceptual;
for if the means of valid cognition and its result were based on different substrates, their relationship as such would not be possible.
For when an axe is directed toward a *khadira* tree, a splitting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree;
therefore, it must be stated that these two share a common substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). And how is that so?

If both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) reside solely within cognition, and cognition— which is a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) without parts— cannot be joined with two parts that exist as real entities,
then that very cognition is the result, being a portion of "cognition-ness" conceptually constructed through the exclusion of non-cognition (*ajñānavyāvṛtti*).
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that aspect of capacity which, being conceptually constructed through the exclusion of incapacity, has the power to illuminate both self and non-self;
its object of cognition (*prameya*), however, is strictly external.
This is likewise the case in the system of the Sautrāntika.

The conformity of cognition to the object (*arthasārūpya*)—that is, its having a constructed blue form through the exclusion of non-blue forms—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is the cause for establishing [the object].
And the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*), which is constructed through the exclusion of non-cognition, is the result (*phala*), because it is that which is to be established.
Thus they have said: "For indeed..."
It is logical that the very existence of a mental modification (*vitti*) constitutes the cognition of that object,
since it is without distinction in all cases; however, it is by entering into similarity (*sārūpya*) that this [modification], assuming a similar form, brings about the connection with that object.
He states the arguments for the non-existence of external objects by way of a question: "How, then, is this known?
For that external object, which is intended to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of consciousness, cannot possibly exist as an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Indeed, cognition appears as a single, gross, blue form; it does not appear as extremely subtle atoms.
Nor can that which has the appearance of one thing have another as its object,
because that would lead to the over-extension [of the principle] whereby, by having everything as its object, it would follow that everyone is omniscient.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that grossness is a property of the appearance itself.
Because it cannot withstand analysis:
is this a property of the cognition that appears, or is it a property of the object at the time of its appearance?
If it is the former alternative, [then...]
Certainly; for if that were the case, consciousness would have been admitted to have its own constituent part as its very object.
And in that situation, who could be considered adverse when one is acting in accordance with it?
If it is argued that it is the second [alternative],
it is as follows: the atoms of form themselves, when produced without interval and appearing in a single cognition, constitute grossness (*sthūlatva*).
And in this case, there is no error on the part of anyone;
for it is not that those atoms of form do not exist,
nor is it that they have not arisen without intervals.
Nor do they reside in a single cognition;
therefore, let it not be that [the atom] is a property of the atom like blueness and so forth,
because such [properties] do not exist in each individual atom.
However, for those things that have entered the state of appearing [to consciousness], there will be a conventional grossness, just like [the conventional] plurality and so forth.
As they say: "When many [atoms] are grasped by a single [cognition], some form is indeed grasped;
it is conventional and resides in the appearance, because [that form] is impossible within a single [atomic] self. (Verse 1)
Nor is that perception erroneous, because it apprehends various entities;
conventional apprehension is nothing other than this, and the apprehension of an entity is not an error. //2//
Thus [it is argued]; but that is not so,
because the appearance of continuity is an illusion.
For those atoms of form are interspersed with atoms of odor, taste, and tangibility; they are not contiguous.
