Therefore, we see that this cognition of grossness regarding atoms that are separated by intervals is merely an error—just like the cognition of a single dense forest in trees that are distant and separated by gaps.

Consequently, even if it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), the cognition of jars and the like lacks the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) because it is erroneous, just like the cognition of a yellow conch shell and so forth, provided that one accepts its objective domain to be atoms.
Thus it has been said: atoms cannot, for their part,
be the objects determined by cognitions such as those of a pillar.
Nor are the pillars and so forth, which are aggregates of those [atoms], composite wholes (avayavin).
If they were non-different from the atoms, they would be nothing but atoms;
and the refutation of that has already been stated.
But in the case of difference, there is absolute dissimilarity, like that between a cow and a horse, and thus there is no identity;
furthermore, inherence has already been refuted.
In this way, by means of the dilemma of difference and non-difference, one should also reject [the existence of] universals, qualities, actions, and so forth.
Therefore, since everything that appears is incapable of withstanding analysis,

and since there is no means of valid cognition for the existence of anything not appearing, cognitions do not have external objects as their supports. Furthermore, consciousness cannot perceive an object in a hidden manner, as the sense organs do.
For just as a sense organ generates a cognition whose object is the external thing, another cognition cannot likewise generate a further cognition;
for the same objection would apply there as well, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Nor is it capable of producing a result characterized by "manifestness" (prākaṭya) which has the object as its substratum.
Because that [perception] is impossible with respect to past and future [objects];
for it is not possible that a substratum (dharmin) be non-present while its attributes (dharmas) are present.
Therefore, the very perceptibility of the nature of cognition itself must be accepted as the perceptibility of the object.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction for one who always knows that [consciousness] as being without form (anākāra), how could it establish a distinction between objects? Therefore, in order to establish such distinctions, a distinction of forms must be admitted for this [consciousness].
As it has been said: "For it is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of its object, because that existence is indistinguishable in all cases."
"But that [cognition] would enter into conformity with its object and thus bring about a resemblance to it. Furthermore, this single form is experienced;

if it belongs to consciousness, there is no proof whatsoever for the existence of an external object. Thus he says: "Moreover, by mere experience, [there is no proof] of a cognition whose nature is common [to all]."
Moreover, regarding the principle of "the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyama*):
whatever is necessarily apprehended simultaneously with something else does not differ from that thing, just as a second moon does not differ from a single moon.
And since the object is necessarily perceived together with the cognition, this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

For the difference [between object and cognition] that is to be negated is pervaded by the lack of necessity in their simultaneous perception; just as the two Aśvins, being distinct, are not necessarily perceived together, since sometimes one or the other is perceived when they are covered by clouds.
Here, this necessity—which is the opposite of the non-necessity that pervades difference—is observed, and thus it excludes the difference which is pervaded by that non-necessity.
As it has been said: "Because they are necessarily perceived together, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof;
yet their difference is seen by erroneous cognitions, just as [the difference] in the case of the non-dual moon."
Thus,
this should be regarded as being like a dream and so forth: whatever is a cognition, all of that is without an external objective support.
Just as the cognition of dreams, illusions, and so forth, so too is this cognition under dispute; thus, it is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For the state of being a cognition is invariably concomitant with the lack of an external objective support, just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is invariably concomitant with the property of being a tree. Therefore, when the lack of an objective support is to be proven as that which is invariably concomitant with mere cognition-ness, the property of being a cognition [serves as the probans].
This is the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
At this point, the Sautrāntika raises an objection: "But how, if external objects do not exist, can the variety of cognitions such as 'this is blue' or 'this is yellow' be accounted for?
For he [the Sautrāntika] held that whatever occurs only occasionally, even when [a certain condition] is present, all such things depend upon a cause distinct from that [condition].
Just as when I do not intend to speak or desire to go, the cognitions that appear as speech and movement depend upon another mental continuum;

likewise, the six types of active cognitions under dispute, even while the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists, [depend on something else]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And that which is distinct from the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness, serving as the cause for these occasional varieties of active cognition, is the external object.
If it is argued that production occurs only occasionally because the maturation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is occasional, [we reply]:

surely, for the *ālayavijñāna*s belonging to a single continuum, the "impression" is the capacity to produce those active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); its "maturation" is the orientation toward the production of its own effect; and the "condition" for that maturation is the preceding moment within its own continuum, since we do not admit dependence on another continuum.
And thus, all [factors] falling within the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* would be causes of maturation;
or else, none at all would be, since there is no distinction in their belonging to the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna*.

If it is argued that there is a difference in capacity due to the difference between moments, and because that [capacity] is occasional, the effect is occasional—then indeed, for a single [moment], there would be both the capacity to produce the cognition of blue and the capacity to awaken that [cognition], whereas this would not belong to another moment. Or, if it does exist [in others], how can there be a difference in capacity due to a difference between moments? For all [moments] existing within the *ālayavijñāna* continuum are equally capable; thus, since the efficient cause is present, the non-production of the effect is untenable.

Since the occasional nature of that which is to be negated depends solely upon its own continuum, its opposite—perpetuity—is perceived; by this perception, the occasional nature being excluded, it is established that [the cognition] depends on another cause.
Thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is proven.
Nor is it dependent upon another stream of consciousness (*jñāna-saṃtānāntara*).

Even by the Vijñānavādins, it is not maintained that all evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) [are caused by external objects], but rather only by certain evolving consciousnesses that manifest as interrupted movement or speech.
Furthermore,
if those [consciousnesses] were caused by the mental continua of other sentient beings, they would not be occasional, because that cause would be constantly present.
For there can be no spatial remoteness of one sentient being's continuum from another's,

because in the Vijñānavāda school, no space is admitted apart from consciousness; and since consciousnesses are immaterial and lack spatial extension, there is no possibility of temporal remoteness either, as that would entail the consequence of the saṃsāra having a beginning and the admission of the manifestation of previously non-existent sentient beings,
neither of which is accepted.

Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintained that since the diversity of cognitions would otherwise be inexplicable in the absence of an external object, an external object must exist as something inferable.
The Proponent of Consciousness (Vijñānavādin) refutes them, stating: "Because of the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The underlying intention here is this: even if the occasional nature of cognitions is explained as arising solely from within one's own mental continuum, the logical reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the contrary case remains doubtful.
For instance— even if [cognition] were caused by external objects— why is there sometimes the cognition of blue and sometimes the cognition of yellow?
If you say it is due to the presence or absence of the external blue or yellow object,
then why does the cognition of blue not occur even when a yellow object is present?
If it is argued that there is yellow cognition because of its capacity for that [yellow] and its lack of capacity for the other,
from what, then, does this distinction between capacity and incapacity arise?
If it is argued that this is due to a difference in causes, then in that case, moments (kṣaṇas) will also possess a difference in capacity based on the difference in their own causes;
for moments are the members of a continuum (*saṃtānin*) that serve as the causes for the diversity of effects, and they differ with respect to each effect.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a single "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) that produces the moments [of existence], such that by virtue of its non-difference the moments themselves would not differ.
But was it not said that the difference or non-difference of capacities does not follow from the difference or non-difference of the moments,
because even distinct moments are observed to possess a single capacity?

Otherwise, since the capacity to produce the cognition of blue would exist in only a single moment, further cognitions of blue would not arise; for that which possesses such capacity would have passed away,
and subsequent moments would lack that capacity.
Therefore, even though there is a difference between moments, there is no difference in their capacity;
however, when there is a difference in the continuum, the capacity does differ.
That is not so.

If there is no single capacity among distinct continua, then alas, since even the blue continua— which are mutually distinct— would lack a single capacity for producing the form of blue, blue-cognition would not arise even when another blue continuum is in proximity.

Therefore, just as in the case of different mental continua, it must be stated that among other moments—which arise dependent upon the differences in their own causes—only some possess a particular capacity while others do not.

And so, among those moments falling within the continuum of a single person's stream of consciousness, there is for a certain moment of cognition a specific excellence of capacity, otherwise known as *vāsanā* (latent predisposition), which is produced by its own antecedent conditions;
from this, a functioning consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arises with a blue aspect, and not with a yellow aspect.

However, for some, that [external object] is of such a nature that cognition has the form of yellow and not the form of blue; thus, since the variety of cognitions is established solely from the variety of latencies (*vāsanā*) acquired through one's own internal conditions, we see that there is no proof whatsoever for the existence of an object distinct from that [cognition]. Latency is simply a cognition belonging to the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) that remains unperceived; from the variety of these latencies arises the variety of experiences of blue and so forth.

Furthermore, because the variety of past experiences of blue and so forth gives rise to a variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), these two—consciousness and its latent impressions—are beginningless.
Therefore, there is no possibility of the fault of mutual dependence, as in the case of the continuum of seed and sprout.

Moreover, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is the variety of latent impressions alone that is the cause of the variety of cognitions, not the variety of objects; thus he says: "Moreover, by positive and negative concomitance..."
This being the case, we reply:
"There is no non-existence, because [objects] are perceived.
Indeed, it is not possible to determine that external objects do not exist.

For that [external object] would be determined as non-existent either because of the absence of apprehension, or even if there were apprehension, because it does not have an external thing as its object,
or even if it did have an external thing as its object, because of the existence of a means of valid cognition that sublates the external object.
He states, preceded by a question— "Why?"— that it is not the case that there is an absence of apprehension in every respect, saying "because of apprehension.
The meaning is that when an apprehension is so clear as to be common to all people, its non-existence cannot possibly be asserted.
He takes up the second position: "But surely I do not speak thus. He refutes it: "Certainly you do speak thus.
For when perception is grasped by the witness who apprehends that perception, it is grasped precisely as having an external object, and not as mere perception alone—this is the meaning."
And the phrase "for this reason" (ataśca) refers to the logical argument that will be stated below;
it takes up the third position: "Surely, because an external object is impossible."
He refutes [this view], saying: "This determination is not correct.
The underlying intention here is as follows: jars, cloths, and so forth appear as gross (*sthūla*), and not as supremely subtle (*paramasūkṣma*).

In this regard, although this grossness—characterized by pervasion across various directions and locations—is, insofar as it is a form of cognition, defined by the presence or absence of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*);...

Although it is joined with the association of contradictory properties precisely because the limiting adjunct of cognition (*jñānopādhi*) is unobstructed, nevertheless, its resulting multiplicity— characterized by the association of contradictory properties such as being in that location versus not being in that location, being mobile versus immobile, and being colored versus colorless— cannot be prevented even by Śakra, even if it exists in the form of cognition.
Furthermore, the dilemmas regarding whether [atoms] exist as distinct or non-distinct entities, as well as the fact that atoms possess parts, have already been established in the *Vaiśeṣika-parīkṣā*.
Therefore, just as with external objects, the possibility of grossness does not exist even in cognition.
Nor can a single cognition have the appearance of so many atoms.
Because it is impossible for a single entity to possess a manifold nature; or else, because it would follow that the mental aspects (ākāra) must be one, due to their identity with cognition.
Nor is it the case that there are as many cognitions as there are aspects.
For that many cognitions would be mutually unaware of one another, which would entail the impossibility of the experience of a gross [object].
Nor is it correct to claim that a single gross conceptual construction (*sthūla-vikalpa*), consisting of a synthesis of the forms of all those cognitions, arises subsequently;
for that too, by virtue of having a form, cannot be considered gross.

As Dharmakīrti said: "Therefore, there is no appearance of grossness either in the object or in the cognition, because that [grossness] is denied in the case of a single [atom]; it is not possible even in the case of many [atoms]."
Thus,

even by you who seek to establish the grossness of the form of cognition, existence and non-existence must be accepted as being preceded by the operation or non-operation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And if that is so, it is impossible to deny the external world— which is the locus of "this-ness"— as distinct from cognition.

And as for the conformity to the object (*viṣayasārūpya*) which has been posited for the sake of establishing the determination of cognition with respect to each particular object—it is not possible to deny the object on this basis, because without an object, both that conformity and its determination would be untenable; thus he says: "Nor [is the object denied] because of the cognition's conformity to the object."
Furthermore, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) that was stated does not withstand scrutiny.

If the apprehension of cognition and the object occurs as a concomitance (*sāhitya*), then the reason is contradictory (*viruddha-hetu*) and cannot prove non-difference; for concomitance is pervaded by difference, which is its opposite, and such concomitance is impossible if there is non-difference.
Now, as for the restriction to simultaneous apprehension (*ekopalambhaniyama*):
the word "together" (*saha*) does not denote oneness (*ekatva*).
Furthermore, is it apprehension as one, or is it a single apprehension of both the cognition and the object? It is neither.
He says that there is apprehension as a unity [of cognition and object] because the object is perceived externally.
Now, if it is argued that there is a rule of their being apprehended together (*ekopalambhaniyama*), he replies:

"For this very reason, it must be understood that even the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) regarding the cognition and its object is caused by the relationship between the means and the end (*upāyopeyabhāva*), and not caused by non-difference."
For just as all visual objects, being permeated by the form of light and cognizable by the intellect, are invariably perceived by humans,
yet for this reason alone the form of a jar or similar object does not become identical with light;
rather, the rule exists because light serves as the means (*upāya*).
Thus, here too, because the object is apprehended by means of an experience witnessed by oneself (*ātmasākṣika*), there is a necessity for the simultaneous perception [of the subject and object].
Furthermore, where a jar and a cloth are both within the range of a single cognition, cognizers determine both the difference between the objects and the difference between the cognitions.
And this is not possible if they possess a single nature; thus he says: "Moreover, [there is] the cognition of a jar and the cognition of a cloth."

Thus, because a difference in cognition is observed even when the object is not different, he says that the object does not have the nature of cognition: "likewise, there is the perception of a jar and the recollection of a jar.

Furthermore, since a cognition that terminates in its own form alone is ignorant of the occurrence of another cognition, those two [cognitions] whose difference [is claimed] are not apprehended; thus, the difference residing in them is also not apprehended.
In this way, momentariness, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, are also to be established through the difference between various cognitions of propositions, reasons, and examples.

Thus, that which has its own unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*)—which is excluded from others—is established through multiple cognitions, namely, that which is excluded and that from which it is excluded.

Likewise, even a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), whether in the form of a positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpa*) or in the form of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha-rūpa*), is accessible through multiple cognitions. Similarly, the relationship between the perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfumer (*vāsaka*) is also accomplished by means of multiple cognitions.
Thus, by the power of the affliction of ignorance, there is the state of being a real or unreal phenomenon: for example, "blue" is a real phenomenon (*saddharma*),
"a human horn" is an unreal phenomenon (*asaddharma*),
and "formless" is both a real and unreal phenomenon (*sadasaddharma*).
For it is possible to say that a rabbit’s horn is formless,
and it is likewise possible to say that consciousness is formless—
as it has been said: "It is established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless latent predispositions."
The meaning of a word is a threefold property (dharma) based on existence, non-existence, and both.
Thus, the proposition regarding liberation—that he who is liberated, that from which one is liberated, and that by which one is liberated—is established through manifold knowledge.
Likewise, the proposition is for the purpose of instructing one who is mistaken; it is that which is instructed, that by which one instructs, and he who instructs.

The person who is the one to be instructed and the one who instructs—that [process] is accomplished through multiple cognitions; this is not possible unless there is a single synthesizer of the cognitions of multiple objects.
He says that all of this is untenable if consciousness has only its own part as its object: "Furthermore, regarding two cognitions at earlier and later times," and so on.
Moreover, the relationship between action and its fruit, which depends upon difference, cannot exist within a non-differentiated consciousness.
Indeed, it is not the act of cutting that is cut, but rather the wood;
nor is it the act of cooking that is cooked, but rather the rice grains.
Likewise, in this case as well, it is not cognition that is known by its own part within itself—since such self-operation is contradictory—but rather an object distinct from it.
"Just as rice grains are nothing more than their cooking," he says, preceded by a description of the arrangement of the elements: "Furthermore,
one should accept that consciousness is [merely] consciousness."
He objects: "Is it not the case that consciousness has an object of apprehension distinct from its own nature?
The meaning of this is as follows: if consciousness were to apprehend an object distinct from its own nature, then, being itself non-perceptual, it would have to make the object perceptible.
For, unlike the eye, it does not impart any excellence to the object by remaining hidden within it.
By which [cognition] one might perceive an object that is not itself perceived;
rather, the very perception of that [cognition] is the perception of the object.
As they have said: "For one whose apprehension is not perceived, the seeing of the object is not established."
If that [cognition] were to be cognized by another cognition, then being itself uncognized, it would not be able to make the cognition of the object manifest.
In this way, there would be an infinite regress of "that and that"; therefore, fearing such an infinite regress, it is better to accept that [cognition] has its operation upon itself.
Furthermore, just as a lamp does not require another lamp, [so too is the case here].
Thus, knowledge also ought not to require another knowledge, because they are equal;
[the opponent] refutes this as follows: "Both of those [objections] are incorrect.

Since the desire for the apprehension of the witness of consciousness does not arise at the very moment of the apprehension of consciousness itself, the suspicion of an infinite regress (anavasthā) is untenable."
This is the meaning: it is true that for a perception that is not itself perceived, the seeing of an object is not established;
however, another perception need not be sought in order to make that [first] perception manifest to the perceiver.

Rather, as soon as a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) arises from the contact between the sense organ and the object, both the object and the perception become manifest to the subject.
For an object, whose nature is inherently concealed, requires a specific modification of the internal organ—namely, experience—in order to become directly perceived by the knower.
Experience, however, although insentient, does not require another experience for the purpose of receiving the reflection of consciousness due to its own transparency;
were it so, there would be an infinite regress.
For it is not possible that there could be an experience that has arisen yet is not perceived by the cognizer, as is the case with blue and other such objects.
Therefore, just as a cutter pervades the object to be cut, such as a tree, by means of the act of cutting, but the act of cutting does not [pervade] another act of cutting;
Nor is the cutter itself the agent of cutting; rather, it is Devadatta or another who acts by his own power.
Or, for example, as a cook pervades the object to be cooked through the act of cooking—not indeed by means of one cooking through another cooking.
Nor is the act of cooking itself the cooker; rather, it is Devadatta and others who are so by their own nature.

Likewise, the knower pervades the object of knowledge, such as blue and so forth, through the act of knowing, but does not pervade that very act of knowing through another act of knowing, nor is the act of knowing itself the knower.
However, the knower (*pramātṛ*) is by its very nature the pervader of valid cognition (*pramā*).

Furthermore, there can be no requirement for valid cognition with respect to the knower, who is the immutable, eternal consciousness (*kūṭasthanityacaitanya*); for if the knower required another knower for his own valid cognition, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

Therefore, it has been well said: "Because at the very moment of the apprehension of the cognition, there arises no desire to apprehend the knower—the witness of cognition—who is the immutable, eternal consciousness."
Regarding what was stated— "because of their equality, the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is untenable"— he replies:
"And because of the difference in nature between the witness and the cognition, the relationship of the perceiver and the perceived is tenable."
Let it not be that the relationship of apprehended and apprehender exists between two cognitions due to their equality;
rather, it is indeed possible between the knower and the cognition because of their disparity.
Furthermore, the status of being the apprehended object for a cognition does not consist in its possessing a fruit produced by the act of apprehension, as is the case with an external object.
Because another fruit cannot arise from a fruit;
as they say: "Cognition is not considered a fruit, because it is itself the fruit.
Rather, it exists by virtue of its self-established manifestation for the cognizer.
Even the object of apprehension is manifest to the knower when consciousness exists, and consciousness itself is manifest.
As others have said: "There is no status as an object (karmabhāva) for this [consciousness].

It might be argued that whatever is manifested is manifested by another, as in the case of knowledge and its object; and since the witness is likewise so, there is no difference between the cognition and the witness. To this, he says: "And of that which is self-established..."
Because the witness cannot be denied;
for instance, it is only if this witness—being eternally free from doubt and error—is of the nature of constant direct perception that its luminosity can be established as non-accidental.

To explain: even when the knower is doubting, [the witness] is non-doubting; even when he is erring, it is non-erroneous; even when he is conceiving of an object as remote, it is immediate; and even when he is remembering, it is experiential.
This applies to every living being;
and this is not possible if consciousness were dependent on something else,
as the consequence of an infinite regress has already been stated.
Therefore, its self-established nature must be accepted even by one who does not wish it, because it is the very essence of the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, according to the sequence already stated, since cognition lacks the capacity for self-comprehension and if a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is not admitted, then by asserting that "consciousness manifests itself independently of any other illuminator, just like a lamp," one would be saying that consciousness is neither accessible through valid cognition nor possessed of a comprehender.
It is like the manifestation of a thousand lamps placed within a solid block of stone;
if it does not shine forth for anyone who might perceive it, then enough with the notion of perception, since [consciousness] is self-luminous.
Thinking that consciousness itself is the perceiver, he raises an objection: "Certainly, it is so."
"Because it is of the nature of experience.

[The opponent objects: "Since the fruit (phala) possesses neither agency nor objecthood, another agent must be sought for it, like a lamp; and thus, your argument does not prove what is already established. To this, he replies: "No."
"Of another cognizer.
Now, one might object: "Let our own intended consciousness simply stand in the place of the witness; thus, there is disagreement only regarding the name, not regarding the actual thing.

To this, [the author] replies by suggesting that the witness-cognizer is self-established: "By the one who proposes that the witness-cognizer is self-established, it must be intended that [consciousness] manifests of itself."
Regarding the claim that "consciousness is precisely this [the cognizer]," he refutes it, saying: "No.
For the properties such as arising and so forth are indeed admitted to belong to consciousness; and thus, since it functions as an effect, it cannot be understood as the cognizer.
Because the relationship between agent and fruit is contradictory in a single entity;
rather, the meaning is that it is like [the case of] a lamp and so forth. //28//
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like a dream and so forth.
(BBs 2.2.29) The difference in nature consists in the presence or absence of sublation.
The cognition of the dream state is sublated, whereas the cognition of the waking state is unsublated; you too must necessarily accept the unsublated nature of the waking cognition,
for it is by means of that [waking cognition] that the dream cognition is understood to be sublated and false.
If, however, the waking cognition were subject to sublation, it could not be the sublater of the dream cognition;
for that which is itself to be sublated cannot possibly be the sublater.
Consequently, the dream cognition would not be false, and thus the example "like a dream" would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Therefore, because there is a difference in nature due to sublation and non-sublation, it is not possible to determine that waking cognition is without an objective basis by using dream-cognition as an example.
The phrase "fatigued by sleep" is a designation for a defect in the instruments [of cognition].
To state another point of dissimilarity for the sake of the false view, he says: "Moreover, it is only memory.
For a cognition produced solely from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is indeed memory;

however, that which arises from a causal complex characterized by the presence of currently functioning sense-organ contact, inferential marks, words, similarity, or the non-arising of other possible means of knowledge, is [not memory].
Knowledge is apprehension.

Here, in the case of one who is asleep, because of the absence of other causal complexes, only the latent impression (saṃskāra) remains; therefore, because it is born from a latent impression, it is memory.
Moreover, due to the defect of sleep, that [dream-cognition] causes even a father or other relative who is actually existing in reverse order to appear as if they were present.
Therefore, there is a distinction between memory and perception; and since there is a reversal in that memory, the meaning is that there is a great difference [between them].
Moreover, once intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established, the fact that waking cognitions correspond to reality— which is established by experience— cannot be overturned by inference,

because such an inference cannot arise due to its contradiction with experience. Furthermore, the state of having an uncontradicted object is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as it is grasped by the causal complex that produces the inference.
And with the intention that an effect cannot possibly arise in the absence of its cause, he says: "Moreover, because it would entail a contradiction with experience. (29)
[The opponent says: "There is no [external] existence, because [objects] are not perceived. [Reply:

This is not so, because perception occurs only when there is an object, following the presence and absence as seen in the world; it does not occur in the absence of an object within the *vāsanā* (mental impression).
The meaning is that even for a latent impression (*vāsanā*), it is observed to be dependent upon the perception of an object.
Furthermore, a worldly latent impression is not tenable even due to the absence of a substratum;
nor can the momentary storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) serve as the support for a latent impression.

Because there is no relationship of container and contained between two things arising simultaneously—just like the left and right horns of a cow—and because if [the substratum] had already arisen, its momentariness would be contradicted since the contained would not exist at the time of its own production; with this intention, he says: "Moreover, as for what is called 'latent impression' (*vāsanā*)," and so forth.
The remainder of the text has its meaning self-evident. //30//

If consciousness with an aspect (sākāra-vijñāna) is possible, yet an external object— whether gross or subtle— is impossible through conceptual analysis, then alas, in this way, both the object and the cognition cannot withstand investigation as being existent.
Nor can they be non-existent, because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to appear.
Nor as both, because of contradiction, since existence and non-existence cannot coexist in one place;
nor as neither, because...
Because the negation of one thing is inseparable from the affirmation of its opposite;
therefore, let the very inability of things to withstand critical analysis be their true nature.
As they have said: "This is what the wise declare to be the power inherent in reality."
In whatever way objects are reflected upon and analyzed, in that very same way [they appear].
Thus.
The meaning is that they do not settle upon any position whatsoever.

Desiring to refute this, he says: "But the position of the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, no effort is made to refute it.
For worldly means of valid cognition have existence and non-existence as their respective domains."

Indeed, when that which exists is apprehended as "existent," it is established as reality (tattva) just as it is, without error; and when that which does not exist is apprehended as "non-existent," it is established as reality just as it is, without error.

Furthermore, by one who establishes that both the existent and the non-existent are incapable of withstanding analysis, everything becomes established as contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, because it is contradicted by all means of valid cognition, this establishment is not tenable.
If it should be argued: "By this analysis, the ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*) of the means of valid cognition is refuted, but not their conventional validity (*sāṃvyavahārika*)."

And thus, since their objects are different, there is no contradiction with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); to this he says: "Indeed, this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which is established by all means of valid cognition, cannot be denied without first apprehending another reality (*tattva*). For the means of valid cognition, when operating within their own respective domains, operate precisely with the thought, 'This is the reality.'"
However, the non-ultimate (atāttvika) nature of that object must be understood from some other subverting cognition (bādhaka).
People do not, however, act on the basis of the thought, "Our validity is merely conventional (sāṃvyavahārika) and not ultimate.
Furthermore, a subverting cognition would demonstrate their non-ultimate nature by revealing a reality that is the opposite of the object of those [cognitions].
Just as [one perceives] that "this mother-of-pearl is not silver," "the rays of light are not water," or "there is one moon, not two moons," and so forth—

in the same way here too, the unreality of these means of valid cognition must be demonstrated by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) that establishes another reality which is contrary to the entire range of objects of those means of valid cognition; for it is not possible to subvert the means of valid cognition by means of a reality that has not been established.

If it is argued that by establishing the reality of things as being incapable of withstanding analysis, one demonstrates the non-reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is this "incapability of withstanding analysis" which is intended as the reality of things?
Is that thing, in ultimate reality, one of the categories such as existence (*sat*) and so forth, yet merely unable to withstand analysis?
Now, [it might be argued that] because it cannot withstand analysis, it is simply devoid of reality (*niḥsvabhāva*).
In that case, it is a contradiction to say that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), it does not withstand analysis as being any one of "existent" and so forth;
for if it does not withstand analysis, it cannot be any one of "existent" and so forth.
If it is one of those [three], how does it not tolerate investigation?
On the other hand, if it is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), how can it be possible to speak thus without first establishing one of those [three] as reality?
Furthermore, the very state of being devoid of reality is not itself the reality of things.
For if one investigates, there would be an absence of reality; and you yourselves have stated that even that [reality] cannot withstand analysis.
Furthermore, [that which is] superimposed—
It must be negated.
Furthermore, superimposition is observed to have a real substrate, as in the case of silver being superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like;
if there were no reality whatsoever, of what would there be superimposition, and upon what?

Therefore, we consider it logical that Brahman, which is non-proliferated (niṣprapañca) and ultimately real, is superposed with the nature of an inexpressible proliferation (anirvācya-prapañca); and having established that reality, the conventional validity of the means of knowledge is rendered sublated by the realization of its lack of ultimate reality. //31//
START BsVBh_2,2.5.32:
"And because it is untenable in every respect" (BBs_2,2.32).
He analyzes: "What is the use of saying more? In whatever way this system of the Vaināśika is presented, both according to its textual form and its meaning..."
First, in terms of the literal expression (*granthataḥ*), there is the improper use of words such as *paśyati*, *tiṣṭhati*, *asiddha*, and *poṣadha*.

In terms of the meaning (*arthataḥ*), having accepted selflessness (*nairātmya*) while nevertheless accepting the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the substratum for all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), one accepts an imperishable self (*akṣara-ātman*).

Likewise, having accepted momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), one accepts permanence by saying, "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*) remain constant," and so forth; much more could be cited in this manner.
"Because it is impossible in one [substratum]" (BSBh 2.2.33). The doctrine of the Sugatas, who go about with their loincloths untied, has been refuted.
Now, the system of the Nirgranthas is being refuted.
He states that system both concisely and in detail:
"And these seven categories are accepted by them."
Regarding this, he states the summary: "In brief, however, there are only two categories of entities (padārtha):
the soul (jīva), whose nature is consciousness, and the non-soul (ajīva), which is the aggregate of the insentient.
They describe this further elaboration of those two, the soul and the non-soul, as appropriate.
He says regarding that: "The five astikāyas," and so on.
Regarding all of these, there are also intermediate subdivisions.
The jīvāstikāya is threefold: the bound (baddha), the liberated (mukta), and the eternally perfected (nityasiddha).

The categories of existence (*astikāya*) are sixfold: the four elements beginning with earth, both the stationary and the moving; the category of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), which is inferred from movement; the category of rest (*adharmāstikāya*), which is inferred from stability; and the category of space (*ākāśāstikāya*), which is twofold: the space of the world (*lokākāśa*) and the space beyond the world (*alokākāśa*).
Among these, the space within the worlds situated one above the other is the space of the world; the place of liberation situated above them is the space beyond the world.
For in that [realm], worlds do not exist.
Thus, the two categories of living beings (jīva) and non-living beings (ajīva) have been explained in five ways.
The three categories of influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), and shedding (nirjarā) [are as follows]:
The characteristics of active involvement (*pravṛtti*) are elaborated upon.
Active involvement is twofold: correct and false.
Among these, false active involvement is the outflow (*āsrava*).
However, when there is right engagement, there are restraint (*saṃvara*) and the wearing away of karma (*nirjarā*).
The activity of the senses is called *āsrava* (influx) because it causes the person to flow toward sense objects.
For, through the doors of the senses, the light of the soul (*pauruṣaṃ jyotiḥ*), touching the objects, transforms itself into the form of cognitions such as color and so forth.
Others, however, say that actions are the influx (*āsrava*);
for they flow toward and follow after the agent, pervading him, and thus they are called *āsrava*.
This is a false engagement, because it is the cause of misfortune.
Restraint (*saṃvara*) and the wearing away of karma (*nirjarā*) are the two forms of right conduct.
Among these, conduct consisting of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, is restraint.
For it restrains the gateway to the stream of inflow (*āsrava*); thus it is called restraint.

Nirjarā (dissociation), however, is the cause for the abandonment of merit and demerit that have been defiled by passions (*kaṣāya*) and have operated since beginningless time; it consists of practices such as climbing upon heated stones.
For it is called *nirjarā* because it "wears away" (*jarayati*) merit and demerit entirely through the experience of pleasure and pain.
*Bandha* (bondage) is the eightfold karma.
In that regard, the destructive karmas (ghātikarman) are of four kinds, namely:
knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), deluding (mohanīya), and obstructive (antarāya).
Likewise, there are four non-destructive karmas (aghātikarman).
Namely: that which is to be experienced (*vedanīya*), name (*nāmika*), lineage (*gotrika*), and lifespan (*āyuṣka*).

In this regard, the misconception that "right knowledge is not the means to liberation, for an object is not established through knowledge because that would lead to over-extension" is called the karma that obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karman*).
The knowledge that liberation does not result from the practice of the Arhat’s teachings is the karma of obscuration of vision (*darśanāvaraṇīya-karma*).
The failure to discern the distinction among the many mutually contradictory paths to liberation shown by various teachers is the karma of delusion (*mohanīya-karma*).
The cognition that creates obstacles for those engaged in the path to liberation is the obstructive karma (*antarāya-karma*).
These are called destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*) because they destroy spiritual excellence (*śreyaḥ*).
Non-destructive karmas (*aghāti-karma*) are as follows:
for instance, experience-producing karma (*vedanīya-karma*), which is the cause for the maturation of a pure person (*śukla-pudgala*); for that indeed—
Even bondage does not stand as an obstacle to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because it does not obstruct the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
There is a "nominal" (*nāmika*) karma that is conducive to the experience-initiating karma that brings about a pure person (*śuklapudgala*);
for that [karma] initiates the initial state of the pure person, such as the embryo-stage (*kalala*), the bubble-stage (*budbuda*), and so forth.
The *gotrika* is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); even more so than that, the *ādyam* exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).
As for *āyuṣka*, it is called "life-span" (*āyus*) because it expresses or indicates life through the means of its production; thus it is *āyuṣka*.
These [three] are non-destructive karmas (*aghāti-karma*), because they serve as the basis for the white person (*śukla-pudgala*) and others.
This aforementioned group of eight factors constitutes bondage because it binds the person (*puruṣa*).

According to some, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding of the self in a higher region— an self whose afflictions and their latent impressions have entirely dissolved, whose knowledge is unobstructed, and who is solely intent upon bliss.

Others, however, maintain that liberation consists in this: since the soul (*jīva*) has the nature of moving upward, it is bound by the categories of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharmāstikāya*); when it is released from those, it moves upward, and that indeed is liberation.
These seven categories, beginning with the soul, have been presented along with their internal subdivisions.
In every case, they apply here the logic known as the "sevenfold predication" (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*).
It may exist; it may not exist; it may both exist and not exist.
It may be inexpressible; it may be both existent and inexpressible; it may be both non-existent and inexpressible.
"It may be that it both exists and does not exist, and is inexpressible.
Indeed, this word *syāt* is a particle (*nipāta*) resembling a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), which illuminates non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
As they have said: "In sentences, [the particle] illuminating non-absolutism indicates each specific qualification according to what is intended."
The particle *syāt* may be a substitute for a verbal form because it conveys a meaning [equivalent to one].
"Thus:

if, moreover, this word *syāt* were not an indicator of non-absolutism (*anaikānta*), then in the sentence *syād asti* ('it may be'), the word *syāt* would be meaningless. This is what was stated: 'because it possesses a connection with the meaning. However, if it indicates non-absolutism, then [the phrase] *syād asti* means 'it exists in some respect'; thus, through the word *syāt*, the meaning 'in some respect'—which is not explicitly stated by the word *asti*—is understood, and so there is no lack of purpose."

And thus: "Syādvāda, through its abandonment of absolute one-sidedness (ekānta) by means of the particle 'kim' and the suffix 'vidhi', relies upon the sevenfold method of predication (saptabhaṅganaya) to distinguish between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted."

Indeed, when an interrogative particle (*kiṃvṛtta*) is present, this [doctrine of] *syādvāda*—by means of the rule for the indeclinable *cit*, through the total abandonment of absolute one-sidedness—is applicable for the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, being dependent upon that perspective which exists within the sevenfold one-sided positions (*saptabhaṅga*).
For instance: if a thing exists as an absolute certainty (*ekāntataḥ*) such that "it exists," then it would necessarily exist in every way, at all times, in all places, and in its entire essence.

Neither through the desire to obtain nor through the desire to avoid would anyone ever, anywhere, or in any way, engage or desist from action; for there would be nothing to be obtained that has not already been obtained, and the abandonment of what is to be abandoned would be impossible.

However, under the view of non-absolutism (anaikānta), since existence occurs somewhere, at some time, for someone, and in some manner, the abandonment and acquisition [of things] are possible for discerning people.
He refutes this sevenfold method (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) by stating: "Because [contradictory properties] cannot coexist in one [thing].

He analyzes: "For it is not possible for properties such as existence and so forth—which exist in an ultimate sense and whose natures are mutually exclusive—to coexist simultaneously in a single substrate that exists in an ultimate sense.
What is meant is this: it is true that what exists...
In reality, that [ultimate reality] exists indeed in every way, at all times, everywhere, and in its entirety as an indefinable form,
just like the inner self (pratyagātman);
whereas it is said that something exists in some place, in some manner, at some time, and by some nature, [that is merely conventional].
Just as conceptual proliferation exists through conventional usage and not from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it cannot withstand analytical investigation.
Nor does mere conditionality establish reality, for that would entail the consequence of silver, water, and so forth—perceived in mother-of-pearl, desert mirages, and the like—also being real.

If, however, reality were established merely by non-sublation for worldly people, then since the conceit of the body as the self is also uncontradicted for them, it would follow that this too is ultimately real; thus, there would be the consequence of falling into the materialist (Lokāyata) doctrine and becoming a nihilist.
However, for those who appear to be wise, the sublation of the conceit of the body being the self through inquiry is equal to that of the manifold world (prapañca), which is itself indeterminate.

Furthermore, since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, there can be no conjunction of them; thus, there would be an alternative (vikalpa). And an alternative is not possible regarding a real entity (vastu).

Therefore, just as in the case of the cognition "Is it a post or a person?", when there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the sevenfold or fivefold nature— of the result which is the determination of that sevenfold or fivefold nature, of the cognizer who is the knower, of the means of knowledge which is the instrument for that, and of the object of knowledge which is the sevenfold or fivefold nature itself—
the sage has rightly established his status as a Tīrthaṅkara through his self-proclamation.

And since a definitive determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) exists exclusively where there is absolute being, the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) does not apply everywhere; thus he says: "These which are the seven categories. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //33//
START BsVBh_2,2.6.34:
"And thus there is non-omnipresence of the self" (BBs_2,2.34).
The phrase "and thus" (evañca) indicates a conjunction (samuccaya) by means of the word "and" (ca).
For if the self were of the same size as the body, it would follow that it is incomplete and limited;
and thus it would be non-eternal.
For whatever is limited is all non-eternal, just like jars and other such things, and so too would the self be.
He states this very point: "Just as in the case of a single substratum (dharmin).
And he says that this other [point] is indicated by the term "incompleteness" (*akṛtsnatva*): "And because the dimensions of bodies are not fixed.

For a living being (*jīva*) whose dimension is that of a human body cannot pervade the entire body of an elephant due to its smallness; thus, because the self does not pervade the entire body, there is incompleteness.
And thus, it does not have the size of the body.
Likewise, when one discards the body of an elephant and becomes the body of an ant, the self would not be fully contained within that ant-body; therefore, the self is not of limited size.
The rest is easy to understand.
He objects: "This might be so; [the soul] has infinite parts.

For just as a lamp situated inside a small jar or a great palace possesses contraction and expansion, so too does the individual soul (jīva) within the bodies of an insect and an elephant—this is the meaning.
Having thus formulated this alternative, he refutes it with the words: "Of those, moreover, which are infinite...
First of all, a lamp cannot serve as an illustration here.
Because it would follow that [the lamp] is impermanent; for the parts of a lamp are indeed subject to disintegration,
and the lamp as a composite whole possesses the nature of arising and ceasing at every moment.
Therefore, because it is impermanent, one must accept that the living being (jīva) is not stable and that its parts are likewise unstable;
thus, the two-fold refutation mentioned regarding the alternatives applies.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the parts of the living being are infinite, that is even more untenable, as he says: "Moreover, [it would be] merely the size of the body. (34)
He introduces another sūtra preceded by a doubt, beginning with "Now, by way of a synonym.
To that as well, it is said:
START BsVBh_2,2.6.35.
Nor can there be non-contradiction even through figurative interpretation, because of [the necessity of] transformation and so forth.
The eight types of karma have been mentioned, beginning with knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya).
Furthermore, if the eternity of the self is admitted, then for those qualities that come and go...
The sense is that because there is no knowledge of the self due to the determination of the limited number of parts, there is no liberation.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "because of the consequence of such defects and others," we shall state the defect indicated by the inclusion of the word "and others" (ādi).
Furthermore, would these parts of the living being be conscious individually or as a collective?

If they were conscious individually, then because there is no rule ensuring that many conscious entities share a single intention, the body might at some point be destroyed by their contradictory movements in different directions.

If, however, consciousness belonged to the collective, then when the body of an elephant became the body of a gnat, the living being—consisting of only two or three remaining parts—would not be conscious.
Because there is no whole [as a distinct entity], [the soul resides] in the body of an ant by means of that which has dissolved from the collection of many [atoms].
Or else:

having raised the objection regarding the impermanence of the living being (*jīva*) as suggested by the preceding sūtra, and fearing it might be like the Buddhist view of the permanence of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), this sūtra states: "And even through modification there is no contradiction, because of change and so forth."

Nor is there a lack of contradiction regarding bondage and liberation on the grounds that, although the size [of the self] does not remain constant due to its various states, the self is eternal because one accepts the existence of a continuum.
Why?
Because of defects such as transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth.

If the continuum (*saṃtāna*) were a real entity (*vastu*), it would undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*), and consequently, defects such as impermanence would follow, just like leather. If, on the other hand, it were not a real entity, the defect of falling into the position of selflessness (*nairātmya*)—as indicated by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—would follow. Thus, they are "naked" (*visica*), meaning they are without clothing (*vivāsana*). //35//
START BsVBh_2,2.6.36:
And because of the persistence of the final state and because both are eternal, there is no distinction.
(BBs_2,2.36) For in this way, the dimension of the living self (*jīva*) existing in the state of liberation would be eternal.
If it were not the case that [something] comes into being after having not existed,
then because things such as jars— which come into being after having not existed— are impermanent,
how could it be that [the self] does not come into being after having not existed? [It would follow that it] must have existed even previously.
Furthermore, when it is constrained by a different magnitude, it cannot become something new.
Therefore, the final magnitude must have existed previously as well; thus, there is no difference [between the states].

Consequently, there would only be the magnitude of a single body, and no attainment of bodies that are increased or decreased in size, because this would contradict the admission that the soul possesses the magnitude of the body.
And here, the construction is: "because it would follow that both dimensions [of the self] are eternal.
And the phrase "only the dimension of a single body" is intended as an illumination.
But in the second explanation, the construction is: "in both states."
The point is not that it possesses the same size as a single body, but rather that it possesses a single magnitude—whether minute or large; this is the distinction. //36//
Regarding the sūtra *patyur asāmañjasyāt* (2.2.37):
To dispel the misconception that this [sūtra] refutes the doctrine of God as the cause without distinction, he says "kevala" (only).
Those who rely upon Sāṃkhya and Yoga, such as Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others,
have declared that *pradhāna* is [the cause];
the *puruṣa* is the power of seeing, the witness of the mental modifications.

And that Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct person who is untouched by the various afflictions (kleśa), karmic results, and latent dispositions (āśaya); he is other than both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
There are four types of followers of Maheśvara: the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, [the Kāpālikas, and the Kālāmukhas].
The Kāruṇikasiddhāntins and the Kāpālikas—
these four are all Māheśvaras, as they follow the established doctrines (siddhānta) composed by Maheśvara.
The cause is Īśvara;
the effects are those derived from Pradhāna, such as Mahat and the rest;
and yoga consists of meditation on the syllable Oṃ and the like, as well as concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth.
The *vidhi* (prescribed method) begins with the three daily ablutions and ends with the practice of living in concealment;
*duḥkhānta* (the end of suffering) is liberation (*mokṣa*).
The *paśus* (individual souls) are those beings, and their *pāśa* is bondage; the release from that is the end of suffering.

This is their intention: indeed, for a conscious supervisor such as a potter, there is only the status of being a *nimitta-kāraṇa* (efficient cause) regarding an effect such as a jar, but not the status of being the *upādāna-kāraṇa* (material cause) as well.

Therefore, it follows that here too, God is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the causes of the world as its supervisor, and not also the material cause (*upādāna*), because it is contradictory for one and the same entity to be both the supervisor and the supervised. This is the position reached.

This being the case, it is replied: "On account of the inconsistency of [the doctrine of] the Lord" (Patyurasāmañjasyāt). The underlying intention here is as follows: Is the status of God as a mere efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) asserted on the basis of scripture (āgama), or on the basis of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara)? As for that other means of valid cognition, would it be inference (anumāna) or presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)?
It cannot be from scripture; for...
It has been stated more than once that this [text] is intent upon demonstrating that [the self] is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Therefore, one must rely on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this matter.

In that regard, inference is first of all not possible; for it proceeds in accordance with what is perceived, and in accordance with that, there is inconsistency. Thus he says: "inferior, middling," and so forth.
This is what is meant: when the existence of God is established through scripture (*āgama*), one need not follow after what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*).
For when heaven, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth are understood through scripture, there is nothing among them that is perceived.
Indeed, scripture does not function by way of similarity to what is perceived.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing what is heard (śruta), even if one postulates very many unseen things whose nature is contrary to what is seen, they do not incur the "odor of iron" (lohagandhitā), because they possess valid means of cognition (pramāṇa).

Any conformity to what is seen that is made therein is done merely out of friendship [toward the tradition]. However, an inference that functions independently of scripture (āgama) and proceeds by way of similarity with what is seen is far more afraid even of a chaff-like contradiction than it is of a contradiction to what is seen.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the Lord] depends upon the karma of living beings, we say no.
Why?
Because if karma and the Lord were to act as the impeller and the impelled respectively toward one another, it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

The meaning is this: if the Lord were subject to compassion and free from passion, then he would not cause living beings to engage in evil action (*kapūya-karman*), nor would he preside over such action even once it has arisen, since the suffering of living beings would not arise by that much alone.
For people are not dependent on God [in such a way that] they would be unable to perform a base action through their own independence;
nor can a base action, unguided by Him, produce its fruit.
Therefore, one must postulate a reversal of what is observed: that even though God is independent, He is impelled by actions.
And thus, this further "pustule upon a boil," namely the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya), would result:
that the Lord is to be impelled by karma, and karma by the Lord.
[The opponent] objects: "If you say it is not so, because of beginninglessness (anāditva)..."

[The opponent argues: "Past karma is set in motion toward present action by that Lord, and by that Lord, the present action is then set in motion toward its own effect. [The author] refutes this: "Not as in the case of the present time.
Now, how can past karma—which was not previously set in motion by the Lord—perform an action characterized by being set in motion by the Lord?

In that case as well, since it was set in motion by Īśvara, who was himself set in motion by prior karma, there is the fault of a blind succession (*andhaparamparā*). For a sighted person leads the blind, not one blind person another;
likewise here, since both are to be set in motion, who could set whom in motion? This is the meaning.
Furthermore, he states "moreover" (*apica*) because the Naiyāyikas' claim that God is faultless contradicts their own tenets;
the implication is that this is not our tenet.
But surely, one is seen to act out of compassion as well, and compassion is not a fault; therefore, he says: "and [he acts] only when impelled by his own interest.
For when compassion exists, suffering arises for that person, and because of that, he acts to eliminate it; thus, even those possessed of compassion act only when impelled by their own interest.

[Objection: "But let [the Lord] act being motivated solely by his own interest; even so, what is the fault? To this he says: "Because the Lord possesses his own interest. This means because of his desire. And since the neutrality (audāsīnya) of the Puruṣa is admitted, there is no real activity [on his part]. //37//
Furthermore, he states another refutation based on observation:
"And because a relationship is untenable. (BSBh 2.2.7.38; BBs 2.2.38)
For conjunction is indeed observed among things that possess parts and are not all-pervading.
Conjunction is the attainment of what was previously unattained; it is impossible for all-pervading things because there is no prior non-attainment and because they lack parts.
Indeed, the nature of conjunction is to exist without pervading its entire substratum.
And it has already been stated that the non-pervasive occurrence of conjunction is not possible in partless entities.
Therefore, the sense is that because the pervader—non-pervasive occurrence—is absent in conjunction, there must be the absence of its pervaded, namely conjunction.
Nor is [conjunction] characterized as inherence.

For that [inherence] is accepted as the relation which is the cause of the notion of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of container and contained.
And there is no mutual relationship of container and contained between primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), and God (*īśvara*); this is the meaning.
Nor is there a relation characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*) that is to be inferred from an effect; thus he says: "nor any other."
For the status of the *pradhāna* as the cause of the *mahat*, the *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth, is not yet established;
thus he raises an objection—"by the proponents of Brahman"—and refutes it: "No."
Why?
Because, according to his view, a relationship characterized by identity with the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) is established.
Furthermore: [apiceti].
For scripture, in its operation, does not depend upon an illustrative example; thus, it is capable of functioning even with respect to what has never been seen before and what is contrary to it.
Inference, however, follows what has been observed and cannot function in such a manner. He raises an objection: "Even for the opponent... [and so forth].
He refutes this, saying "no.

Our position, however, is that since both God (Īśvara) and the sacred tradition (Āgama) are beginningless, there is no contradiction in the tradition having God as its source; such is the intended meaning. //38//

START BsVBh_2,2.7.39 adhiṣṭhānānupapatteśca / BBs_2,2.39 / Furthermore, inference proceeds according to what is observed and does not have as its object that which is beyond the world; this must not be forgotten here either.
The rest is easy to understand. //39//
If it is argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, it is not so, because of [the existence of] experience and so forth;
[He is] devoid of form and the like.
The meaning is that its form is unmanifest (*anudbhūta-rūpa*).
For it is observed that the body, which is the instrument and locus of the person, is employed only for the sake of one's own experience and so forth, and not elsewhere.
Indeed, no one is ever found employing an external tool, such as an axe, without it being perceived.

Therefore, the sense is that for the Lord who employs an instrument devoid of form and other qualities, there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain (bhoga), and thus He would lack lordship (anīśvaratva). He states another alternative: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
Previously, "presiding" (*adhiṣṭhiti*) was the presiding [act]; now, however, "abode" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is said to be the body, which is the locus of experience.

Thus, while non-sovereignty was previously established through the consequence of experiencing enjoyments and so forth, the distinction here is that non-sovereignty is now stated by virtue of the consequence of possessing a body due to the experience of enjoyments and so forth. //40//
[The opponent faces] the consequence of being finite or lacking omniscience.

Furthermore, for one who accepts inference as the sole means of valid cognition, it must be inferred that even *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, and *īśvara* possess numerical distinction and finitude, because they are substances, or because they are objects of knowledge while possessing numerical difference.
Consequently, there would either be finitude or a lack of omniscience.
Our point, however, is that regarding an object accessible through scripture (*āgama*), inference has no power because its subject matter is sublated by that scripture.
Furthermore, the dimension of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-parimāṇa*) refers to whatever size a thing may have—whether minute, large, infinitely large, long, or short.
Now, lest this fault should arise, there is the subsequent alternative:

for one who has an end, the non-perception of that end would entail a lack of omniscience; but for one who has no end at all, the non-perception of such an end does not bring about a lack of omniscience.
The point is that one does not become ignorant simply from the non-cognition of things such as a rabbit's horn.
He refutes this with the word "tataḥ" (from that).
It has been stated that inference, independent of scripture, makes known their finitude. //41//
START BsVBh_2,2.8.42:
Because of the impossibility of [the soul's] arising (utpattyasaṃbhavāt). BBs_2,2.42:
Except insofar as it does not contradict the Vedas, that portion in which there is contradiction is rejected.

He states that [particular] portion: furthermore, as for what is said—that from Vāsudeva arises Saṃkarṣaṇa, the individual soul (jīva)—if the individual soul were to possess a cause, it would be non-eternal;
and if it were non-eternal, due to the absence of one who goes to the next world, there would be no next world.

And consequently, since it would follow that heaven, hell, and liberation do not exist, this results in nihilism; such is the meaning. Furthermore, he states that the birth of the soul is untenable—this he will refute later. //42//
And there is no instrument for the agent. (BBs 2.2.43) Even if one who is proficient in many crafts were to fashion an axe and then cut a palāśa tree with it, [the axe would still not be the agent].

And even if, through effort, one perceives the self and its objects by employing the instrument of knowledge characterized by the contact between the senses, their objects, the self, and the mind, nevertheless, how could Saṃkarṣaṇa— who is himself without an instrument— produce the mind called Pradyumna as an instrument? Or, if one who lacks an instrument possesses the power to fashion an instrument, then what is the point of fashioning an instrument at all?
The meaning is that all effects are accomplished simply by non-action. //43//
Or, if they exist as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that [nature]. (BBs 2,2.44) These,
such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, are indeed Vāsudevas— faultless and devoid of defects such as ignorance.
They are without a basis and without any material cause;
for this very reason, they are irreproachable, being free from defects such as impermanence.
Therefore, the meaning is that the impossibility of their arising is not a fault, because it is consistent [with the nature of reality].
To this it is replied: "Even so.
Let there be no fault by way of [our] admission;
nevertheless, the fault arises spontaneously through another mode.
He states another alternative preceded by a question: "How so? If, first of all...
These various Lords, being distinct from one another, cannot possibly possess mutually contradictory intentions.
Furthermore, if their will were obstructed, the effect would not arise;
if their will were unobstructed, then since each one possesses lordship individually, the act of ruling would be accomplished by one alone, rendering the others purposeless.
And if they were to rule collectively, no single, pure Lord would exist.
Furthermore, there would be an abandonment of your own tenet,
because you have accepted that the Blessed One alone is Vāsudeva, the ultimate reality;
therefore, another interpretation must be adopted.

Considering that there is the fault of the impossibility of origination (*utpattyasaṃbhava*) in that case, [the author], intending to present another alternative interpretation, refutes it by means of the impossibility of origination, stating: "Now, this is the intended meaning.
The rest is easy to understand. //44//
And because of contradiction:

Having indeed spoken of qualities such as knowledge as distinct from the selves who possess those qualities, [the scripture] then declares their non-distinction, saying, "These venerable ones are Vāsudevas themselves."

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), another [contradiction] is subsumed: having stated the difference of Pradyumna and Aniruddha from the Self by characterizing them as mind and ego, there is the subsequent statement of their non-difference from that very Self, which is contrary to that [previous claim].
Thus, the contradiction with the Vedas has been explained. //45//
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhagavatpādabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter, titled "Demonstration of the Faultiness of the Doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Others.
The Third Quarter of the Second Chapter begins.
START BsVBh_2,3.1.1
"Not ether, because it is not heard.
Previously, the contradiction of the Śruti with other means of valid cognition was refuted;
now, however, the mutual contradiction among the Śrutis themselves is being refuted.
In this regard, he states the mutual contradiction among the scriptural texts concerning creation: "In the Vedāntas, here and there.

Just as it was established that the positions of others are not to be relied upon due to contradictions in scripture, so too is one's own position [not to be accepted] due to such scriptural contradictions.
The "clarity of its meaning" consists in the demonstration of the true nature of reality through the removal of fallacious appearances.
The fruit of this [inquiry] is the removal of the doubt regarding the independence of the world’s cause being Brahman within one's own school.

For here, in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), a mutual contradiction among the scriptural texts is demonstrated, whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is no contradiction.

In this regard, the statement of a certain proponent of a partial conclusion (siddhānty-ekadeśin) is: "The ether is not produced, because there is no scriptural text [to that effect]. His intention is as follows: although there is a scriptural text in the Taittirīyaka regarding the production of the ether, nevertheless, due to its contradiction with other means of valid cognition and its conflict with many other scriptural texts, that text must be understood figuratively.
Thus, since the ether is eternal, creation begins only with fire (tejas).
And thus, there is no contradiction among the Śrutis.
This has been stated: first, having recourse to the ether, it is considered whether this ether has an origin or not.
If it does not, then there is no apprehension of contradiction with the Śrutis.
The meaning is that, since there is thus a contradiction with the Śruti, another effort must be undertaken to resolve it. //1//
START BsVBh_2,3.1.2 Therein is the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "But it exists" (asti tu). BBs_2,3.2.
For in the Taittirīya, within the section on creation, the first creation is heard to be that of space alone;
and in the Chāndogya, the first creation is that of fire alone.

Nor is it proper to assume that what is understood from another Śruti to be unaccompanied should be considered as having accompaniment, because that would contradict the cognition of its being unaccompanied.

Indeed, what has not been heard is postulated for the sake of establishing what has been heard, and not to the detriment of it; moreover, the state of being without assistance is set aside by the state of having assistance once the hearing is postulated.
Furthermore, there can be no option between these two—like that of rice and barley—when they are independent of one another.
For it is the performance that is subject to conceptual differentiation, not the reality itself;
indeed, the conceptual differentiation between a post and a person finds no footing in the actual object.
Nor is a systematic distinction established by means of different creations.
Because the past creation was exactly like the present creation;
for it is certainly not the case that in this creation curd is produced from milk, while in another creation milk is produced from curd.
Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning creation, being mutually contradictory, cannot serve as authoritative evidence for this matter—this is the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa). //2//
START BsVBh_2,3.1.3:

A proponent of a particular view within the established doctrine (siddhāntyekadeśin) reveals his own intention by means of the sūtra: "Because [the primary sense] is impossible" (gauṇyasaṃbhavāt). BBs_2,3.3.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because this scriptural statement regarding the origin of space is figurative, due to its impossibility [in a literal sense] on account of conflict with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and conflict with many other Vedic texts.
He states the conflict with other means of valid cognition: "For not of space... [and so forth].

For the production of an effect is necessarily dependent upon inherent causes (samavāyi-kāraṇa), non-inherent causes (asamavāyi-kāraṇa), and instrumental causes (nimitta-kāraṇa); in their absence, it cannot come to be, just as smoke cannot exist in the absence of fire.
Therefore, space is existent, causeless, and eternal. Furthermore,
regarding those things that arise, their experience and causal efficiency are not perceived prior to their arising, but are seen once they have arisen,
as is the case with fire and so forth.
Furthermore, space does not possess such a distinction between arising and non-arising;
therefore, he says "and of those things that have origination" [to show] that it does not arise.
Illumination is the act of making manifest, having as its objects things such as pots and cloths.
"And because of its dissimilarity to earth and the rest.
By the inclusion of the word "and the rest," it is understood that space is eternal, like the self, because while being a substance, it lacks the quality of touch.
[The phrase] "in the spaces of the forest" [is used].
Even in the Veda, the multiplicity of the single ether is due to its limiting adjuncts. //3//
