START BsVBh_2,3.1.4 Having thus stated that [the term] is figurative because it contradicts other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he states that it is also figurative because it contradicts another scriptural passage (śruti):
"And on account of the word" (śabdāt). BBs_2,3.4.
This is easy to understand. //4//
And it may belong to a single [word], like the word "Brahman";
it is the word that is supplied, not the meaning of the word.
For that [term] is primary in some instances and figurative in others, depending on the possibility or impossibility [of its literal application]; thus there is no contradiction.
He raises two objections with the word "how.
He resolves the first objection with the words "first of all, it is one alone."
The family home; vessels; bowls, jars, saucers, and so forth.
The meaning is that this restrictive determination is relative and does not apply to all objects.
He states another argument: "And not even by space," where the word "even" (api) indicates a concession.
The meaning is that even if [the world] depends on everything, there is still no fault. And "prior to its arising"— the word "of the world" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He refutes the second objection with the words, "And for this very reason, by means of the knowledge of Brahman.

This is because space is non-different from Brahman due to the absence of any difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, space does not exist apart from location or time, and it is non-distinct from Brahman as well as from the effects of Brahman, which possess a nature inseparable from it. Therefore...
He says that just as when a few drops of water are thrown into a jar of milk, once the milk and its effects are known, the sky is also known—thus:
"Moreover, every effect as it arises... (verse 5).
When the opponent has thus reached a position that accords with one part of our own established doctrine, [the Sūtra] says this:
"There is an abandonment of the thesis because of the words expressing non-difference. (BBs 2,3.6)

Since the world has the nature of being an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, and since that modification is in reality non-different from Brahman, knowledge [of the world] is logically established once Brahman is known.

For the true essence of the world is not other than Brahman. Therefore, space (*ākāśa*) also, being a modification as an illusory manifestation of That, becomes known through the knowledge of That, and not otherwise.
If, however, there were no modification, then that other reality would not become known when Brahman is known.

For two distinct things, even if they lack a difference in defining characteristics and even if they are non-different in space and time, the knowledge of one does not result in the knowledge of the other.
Indeed, when milk is being drawn from a jar full of milk, even though drops of water are present, there is no cognition regarding the reality of water within that consciousness.

Therefore, since milk is not known when [the other elements] are known, one must—against one's will—accept the production of space (*viyat*) in order to avoid contradicting the accumulation of propositions and examples.

Thus, when the proponent of a partial doctrine has been refuted, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states a distinction regarding his own position: "It is true that [the objection] has been shown;
however, for that very reason, it is contradictory."
He states the essence of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "This is not a fault;
[it refers] to the creation of light in the *Taittirīyaka*.

Between two scriptural passages (*śruti*), one that can be explained otherwise and one that cannot be explained otherwise, the one that cannot be explained otherwise—the *Taittirīyaka* scripture—is the stronger.
Furthermore, the Chāndogya Śruti is weak because it can be interpreted otherwise.

Now, it was argued that fire, being understood as initially without accompaniment, is contradicted by its having accompaniment; to this he says: "For this Śruti does not have the production of fire as its primary purport.
The connection with creation is what is directly stated by the scripture (śrauta), whereas the distinction [of fire from water] is merely implied (ārtha).
And that [creation] is sublated by another scriptural passage (śruti) which contradicts it, because it is of inferior authority;
nor is its state of being without assistance [independent of Brahman] scripturally established, as is the case with the connection to the creation beginning with fire.
However, [the sequence] is obtained through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Nor does the contradiction of that [sequence] by what is directly stated (śruta) entail the impossibility of the creation of fire as stated;
this is what was meant by the phrase "having the production of fire as its primary [subject]."
This might be so:

if a single sentence cannot have multiple meanings because it is impossible for one [agent] to possess two simultaneous operations, then, alas, how is it not contradictory for a single creator to possess multiple operations? To this, he says: "But the creator, though one..."
The capacity of a word is determined by its observed usage by elders.
Furthermore, it is never observed that a single, non-repeated word functions toward multiple objects through both sequential and simultaneous operations.
However, it is indeed observed that even a single agent possesses multiple functions through both sequential and simultaneous means; this is the meaning.
And it is not the function of a single sentence regarding this matter, but rather that of distinct sentences; thus he says, "Nor by us...
This is easy to understand.
He raises an objection: "But [it is] for the purpose of enjoining tranquility (*śama*)."
"The meaning of a word is that which the word aims at;
and this [passage] does not aim at creation, but rather aims at tranquility (*śama*).
He refutes this by stating: "Not indeed by conforming to the priority of fire (*tejas*)."
The meaning is that because the sequence is subordinate and secondary, its abandonment is improper due to the conflict with the primary elements mentioned in the revealed text (*śruti*).

Following the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) method of argumentation, he says, "Moreover, in the Chāndogya," in response to the proponent who maintains that space is not produced, and regarding the alternative way in which the initial proposition was established.
He refutes that [position] with the words "As for what was said":

because the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) must conform to the illustration (dṛṣṭānta), and since the latter consists of the nature and its transformation, the former [the subject] must likewise be of such a nature.
Furthermore, this statement, "one only, without a second," is based on error— like the cognition of milk in water—
or it is figurative— like [saying] "the boy is a lion.
Regarding this, he states that it is not, first of all, based on error, by means of the analogy of milk and water.

The meaning is that since error and the intention to deceive are attributes of a person, they are impossible in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Nor is [the term "one"] figurative; thus he says: "And this [statement] is definitive. Granted, let there be oneness through figurative usage.
The two terms, "exclusivity" (avadhāraṇa) and "secondless" (advitīya), are not tenable [if taken metaphorically].
For worldly people do not say, when applying the metaphor of "lionhood" to a boy, that "there is not even the slightest boy other than the lion.
Therefore, the Śruti intends the absolute identity of the world with Brahman, and not a merely metaphorical one.

The meaning is that in repetition, there is indeed an increase in the object's magnitude, not even a decrease, let alone a figurative one. Nor is [the word "all"] used with respect to its own function; the word *sarva* (all) naturally denotes the entirety, and unless there is a contradiction with another scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is not appropriate to restrict it to a single part. //6//

Having restated the objection that there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the origination of space (*ākāśa*), [the author] replies: Since that other means of valid cognition is itself rendered invalid by its own contradiction with another means of valid cognition, it lacks the power to establish that [the statement regarding space] is merely figurative.
Therefore: "But wherever there is modification, there is division, as in the world" (BSBh 2.3.7).
This is the formal argument: space, the directions, time, mind, and atoms are subject to modification,
because, while being distinct from the self, they are divisible, just like a jar, a bowl, a water-pot, and so forth.

The statement that "every effect is without self" means that it would be without a material cause; thus, the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda) is refuted by the Śruti itself when it introduces [the argument]: "How could being be born from non-being?"
And the refutation of that [objection] has already been established below.
Precisely because it is the Self, there is no possibility of doubting the refutation of the inner Self (pratyagātman).

What is meant is this: if the effect possesses a material cause (upādāna), then since the Self alone is mentioned by scripture as the material cause, it is impossible to postulate any other material cause.

It might be argued: "Let it be that the self is the material cause of this world; however, there may exist another material cause for that [self], even if it is not heard of. To this, he says: "For the self is not adventitious, nor is it something to be produced by any other material cause."
Why?
Because it is self-established;
for its existence or its manifestation is established by itself.
Regarding that, he states the non-accidental nature of the perfection (*siddhi*) which consists of luminosity: "For the Self does not [depend on anything else for its own illumination].
This has been established: because it is not the locus of doubt, error, or mediacy, the Self is never dependent on another for its manifestation;
rather, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth that depend upon it for their manifestation.
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
And the negation of such [an entity] is not possible;
for even a negation, which derives its own existence from that [entity], cannot arise as something contradictory to it—this is the meaning.
He states that the existence of this [cognizer] is not adventitious: "For thus I myself know even now.

Although the means of knowledge (*pramā*), the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) exist in the present, past, and future, the cognizer is experienced as always being present; therefore, for one whose nature is never lost, existence is not adventitious.
For adventitiousness is pervaded by limitation to the three times.
Because it is excluded from that cognizer who is always present, the state of being adventitious (*āgantukatva*), having taken its own pervader (*svavyāpaka*) as its basis, ceases to exist;
thus, even when [the object] becomes otherwise, it is to be known.
By means of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the alteration of both the cognition and the object of cognition is demonstrated.
[Objection: "Granted that there may be no change for a living cognizer, but it will certainly occur for one who is dead. To this, he says: "In the same way, even when reduced to ashes.

Indeed, if something is established by experience as having an existent nature (*satsvabhāva*), its being indeterminable (*anirvacanīyatva*) must be understood from some other subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
And the subverting factor in the case of jars and the like is their deviation from their own nature, as brought forward by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, for one for whom that [object] does not belong to the self, such a conceptualization is not tenable; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the conceptualization of an indefinable nature in what is established by uncontradicted experience as having the nature of existence.
This is what was stated: "it cannot be conceived."

Having thus refuted the inference for the non-arising of space by means of a counter-inference through this continuous argument, he further refutes it on the grounds of its being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). As for what was stated—that [the cause] is of the same genus—it is not the case that a single material cause (*upādāna*) initiates only a manifold effect (*upādeya*).

For where milk transforms into the state of curd, one must not admit that there is the causal status of multiple constituent parts; rather, it is the single milk already taken as a cause that transforms into the state of the effect, which is the curd.
Just as, for those who maintain that atoms are partless, a milk-atom [transforms] into the state of a curd-atom;
the rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //7//
By this, the case of the wind (mātariśvan) has been explained.
If, through repetition, there is an increase in the meaning and not a decrease, then figurative usage (*upacara*) is far removed from being possible.
Ah, sir! This would entail the consequence that air is eternal.

For, after stating the immortality of both [air and space] in the passage, "Air and the intermediate space—this is immortal," the text then speaks specifically of air: "This deity, namely air, is never-setting.
Therefore, due to this repetition, it follows that the immortality of air is not merely relative, but rather innate.
This has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Because of the denial of setting [of the sun] and because of the scriptural hearing of immortality and so forth.
By the word "and" (ca), which serves the purpose of conjunction, repetition is indicated.
This being the position reached, it is said: because of the proposition that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all.
Because the meaning of the statement of the thesis (pratijñā) is primary, and because other statements serve to establish that [thesis],
and because among those [other statements] there are many found that establish non-duality as well as those that establish the sequence of the origination of Mātariśvan.

Because these two scriptural passages are stronger due to their primary status and their greater number, the two prohibitions regarding immortality and non-setting must be interpreted as being relative in accordance with them;
thus, in comparison with the more numerous scriptures, both of those two scriptural passages are merely figurative expressions. //8//
START BsVBh_2,3.3.9:
But the non-existence [of the Self] is impossible, because it is not logically tenable for that which exists [to arise]. BBs_2,3.9:

Now, since there is a scriptural statement regarding the existing Self that "there is no creator of this," and thus its lack of a cause is established, how can there even be a suspicion of its arising?

Nor is it logical to claim that the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is established without seeing the [contrary] statement, for it would be impossible for one who has studied the Vedas not to perceive the qualification for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*). Therefore, he says: "In the case of the ether and the air.

For just as the scriptural statements regarding the immortality and non-setting of the ether and the air are interpreted as being merely relative (*āpekṣika*), due to their contradiction with other scriptural passages; so too [is this case].

Thus, the scriptural statement regarding the Self being without cause must be explained as being relative, because it contradicts the scriptural statement using the analogy of sparks from a fire and because it contradicts other means of valid knowledge.

Furthermore, the idea that if the Self were to possess a cause, it would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā) which brings the scent of iron—that is, the charge of logical fallacy—is unfounded, because the succession of cause and effect is beginningless.
The same applies to the phrase "from modifications" (vikārebhyaḥ).
The contradiction with other means of valid cognition has been shown.
This being the case, it is said: the arising of that which possesses a single, eternal nature is impossible.
Why? Because it is logically untenable.

For Brahman is heard in scripture to have a single, uniform nature; therefore, in the absence of a subverting factor, that [nature] must not be altered. This has been stated: although modifications are perceived as existent, they are seen to perish after the lapse of a certain period of time; thus, because they are delimited by the three periods of time, they are indeterminable (anirvacanīya). But the Self is not like that, for it is well-known—both from scripture and from experience—to possess a single, uniform nature existing in the present. Regarding this, he says: "Brahman is indeed pure Being (sanmātra)."

This is what is meant: that which deviates from its own nature is unreal (anirvacanīya), and it is logical that it should have something real (nirvacanīya) as its material cause; the reverse is not the case.
For example, a snake has a rope as its material cause, but a rope does not have a snake as its material cause.
Furthermore, between two things that are indefinable and do not deviate from their own nature, there can be no relationship of material cause and effect, as in the case of a rope and mother-of-pearl.
Nor is there such a thing as an illusion without a substratum; thus he says: "Nor from what is non-existent."

Nor can there be an infinite regress of errors without a substratum; thus he says: "Because, if the fundamental primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) were not accepted, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.

For a real causal relationship that is beginningless is not vitiated by an infinite regress. However, it has been established in the section refuting the Madhyamaka school that a superimposition of a modification cannot have a superimposed thing as its material cause;
this should not be forgotten here.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is not appropriate to justify error by means of a non-existent substrate through its beginninglessness.
Furthermore, the scriptural passage concerning sparks of fire is to be interpreted with reference to the form of the fuel.
The remainder has a self-evident meaning.

However, those who have described this section as concerning the production of space, time, and the qualities [of sound] must explain the sūtra "because of the impossibility of the existent" with great difficulty;
furthermore, they must state its logical connection within the context of establishing non-contradiction,
for no scriptural passage is found that teaches the production of space, time, and so forth, in the same manner as water and the other elements.
Let that suffice for now. //9//
START BsVBh_2,3.4.10:
Fire [arises] from that, for thus he says:

"Even though in the phrase 'from air, fire,' the ablative case [denoting] the source (*apādāna*) is a *kāraka* case ending, and it is a principle that 'a case ending based on a *kāraka* is stronger than a case ending based on a word-meaning (*upapada*)', this [ablative] cannot properly be taken as referring to immediate succession."

Nevertheless, despite the contradiction with the *bahuśruti* (multiple scriptural passages), the genitive case-ending (*upapadavibhakti*) alone is more appropriate here, even if it is weaker [in force].

Consequently, this scriptural statement, "From air, fire," is intent upon showing immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Furthermore, when direct birth from Brahman is possible, it is not proper to resort to an indirect lineage-based birth by way of being a descendant of that [air].
The prima facie view is that it should be like the sacrificial post for the animal sacrifice in the Vājapeya.

This being the position, it is replied: It is appropriate that in the case of the animal sacrifice and the Vājapeya—which are distinct as subordinate and principal elements—one resorts to an indirect connection through a series because of the direct lack of connection with the Vājapeya.
But here, since even air, though a modification of Brahman, is in reality non-different from Brahman, [the connection] is indeed direct when air is the material cause.

The final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that it is logical to restrict the scriptural texts—which are compatible with both interpretations—to the one [the effect being Brahman] according to the maxim of "eating from a bronze bowl" (kāṃsyabhojinyāya), since the instrumental case-ending is more powerful than the justification for Brahman being the material cause.

As for the phrase "even though produced through a succession," this refers to the conceptualization of difference; for he speaks of ultimate non-difference when he says, "Brahman having attained the state of air."

Just as in the case of "her [milk] has been boiled," the illustration is based on a similarity in the mere sequence of transmission and not on a similarity in every respect; thus, everything is clear. //10//
START BsVBh_2,3.5.11 Water. BBs_2,3.11.
This has been explained by the commentary through an explanation that requires no further elaboration (nigadavyākhyāta). //11//
START BsVBh_2,3.6.12:
*Pṛthivyadhikārarūpaśabdāntarebhyaḥ* (BBs_2,3.12).
This word "food" (*anna*)—both by its etymological derivation and by common usage—applies to rice, barley, and the like, as well as to their derivatives such as boiled rice (*odana*).

Moreover, direct scriptural statement (śruti) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa), and that [statement] is reinforced by the supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa): "Wherever it rains. Therefore, what is intended here is that edible things such as rice and barley alone are produced from water;
for even the blackness of certain inedible things is possible.
For even the earth is not exclusively black, since it is observed to have red and other colors as well.
Consequently, there is a contradiction with another scriptural passage, such as "from water [comes] earth, from earth [come] plants," and so forth; this is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.

When there is a conflict between two scriptural passages (*śruti*), since an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*) regarding the actual entity is untenable, one passage must be interpreted in conformity with the other. In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) in the phrase "from water, earth" should be taken to mean "food," or whether the word "food" (*anna*) in the phrase "it created food" should be taken to mean "earth"—given the context of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the prevalence of the black color [of the earth], as well as the subsequent statement, "That which was the froth of the waters... [it is concluded that the latter is the case].

And because the scriptural statement must be followed, and since the remainder of the passage can be explained otherwise, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the word "food" refers to the earth, which is the cause of food. //12//
But by meditating on that very [Brahman], through its characteristic mark, he [attains it];
for in the sequence of creation, the non-contradiction regarding the elements has been stated.

Now, a question arises: do the deities presiding over the elements, such as space and the rest, proceed toward the successive creation of the elements independently, or are they dependent upon the Supreme Lord?

In this regard, since their own scriptural statement—"from space comes air, from air comes fire"—shows them to be independent, and since there is no evidence for their dependence on another conscious being when they themselves are conscious, and because the introductory context and the indicative marks can be reconciled with Brahman, the ultimate cause, even through an indirect succession; therefore—

It might be argued that since space and the other elements are themselves independent causes of air and the rest, this contradicts the principle that the entire world has Brahman as its source (*brahmayonitva*).

This being the position reached, it is replied: the statements such as "from space, air" describe space and the others merely as material causes (*upādāna*), but not as independent presiding agents (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).

Furthermore, the claim that conscious beings possess independence regarding their own effects is not absolute, for they are frequently observed to be dependent on others, like servants, apprentices, and so forth. Therefore, for the sake of consistency with the presentation of the inferential mark (liṅga), it is logical that it is indeed the Lord who, existing as the material cause in various forms such as space and so on, presiding over them himself as the instrumental cause,
creates those respective transformations such as air and the rest.
Otherwise, both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the introductory context (*prastāva*) would be rendered problematic.

[The phrase] "by virtue of the penetration (*āveśa*) of the Supreme Lord" means that the Supreme Lord himself, having entered [the individual soul] in the form of the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is the beholder (*īkṣitṛ*).

Therefore, it is established that for the entire range of effects, the Supreme Lord alone is the direct presiding cause as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and not [the Lord] having attained the state of ether and so forth;
rather, [the Lord] having attained the state of ether and so forth is the material cause (*upādāna*). //13//

But the reverse order is therefore logical. (BBs 2,3.14) Regarding the arising of the great elements, a specific sequence is heard in scripture, whereas regarding their dissolution, only dissolution in general is mentioned.
In that case, when a fixed rule is possible, there can be no lack of rule; for such a state is devoid of systematic order,
and when systematic order exists, a lack of systematic order is not tenable.

In this regard, when there is a need to determine the sequence, the question arises: should the observed sequence of dissolution in the case of jars and other objects be the regulator of the sequence of the dissolution of the great elements, or should it be the scriptural sequence of origination? On this point of doubt, the scriptural [sequence] is more worthy than another scriptural [sequence], because of its belonging to the same class and thus being present to the mind.
It is not seen [to be so], because they belong to contradictory classes.

Therefore, it might be argued that the order of dissolution is restricted by the very same order of origination mentioned in scripture; to this, it is replied: indeed, the order of origination would be the regulator only if there were a requirement for an order of dissolution, but there is no such requirement for an order of dissolution.
For the sequence of dissolution, even as it follows the Vedic revelation, is sublated by the specific sequence established through perception and inference;
for if that [sequence] were the case, it would follow that the effect exists even when the material cause has ceased,
but this is not so.
Therefore, because it is obstructed by the observed sequence that is contrary to it, there is no expectancy at all for another sequence, as such a thing is incapable of being perceived.
This very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "And it is logical" (*upapadyate ca*).
The author of the Bhāṣya also says: "And this [dissolution] is not required [as the order of meditation] because of its unsuitability.
Therefore, the statement that the order is the reverse of the order of origination is said to be based on reasoning (nyāyamūla) and is a traditional teaching (smṛti). //14//
START BsVBh_2,3.9.15:
If it is argued that the intermediate consciousness and the mind arise sequentially because of their respective signs, we say no, because there is no distinction [between them].

Having thus examined the origin and dissolution of the elements as they relate to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the author] now examines the sequence of the intellect, the sense organs, and the mind.
And here, by the etymological derivation "that by which one cognizes" (*vijānāti*), the word *vijñāna* denotes both the sense organs and the intellect (*buddhi*).

In that context, when there is a requirement for a sequence among these, because [the *vijñānas*] are mentioned between the self (*ātman*) and the elements (*bhūtāni*), the order is determined by that very textual recitation.
Therefore, there would follow the undesirable consequence of violating the previously established order of origination.
Since it is understood that the organs arise from the Self and the elements arise from the organs, it follows that "from the Self [arises] space.

Furthermore, since the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *annamaya* does not signify a modification (as it does in *ānandamaya*), this being the position reached, it is replied: first of all, because the mind and the other organs are distinct [from the Self].

Since there is scriptural evidence in passages such as "the mind consists of food" (*annamayaṃ manaḥ*) that indicates a dependence on a cause, it is appropriate to take the suffix *mayaṭ* here in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), in order to state the required meaning;
otherwise, something unnecessary would have been stated.
And even that [unnecessary statement] is not tenable.
For just as a sacrifice cannot consist of food alone, so too an abundance of food cannot exist for the mind.

Thus, it is logical that the mind and other organs, having manifested their modifications, arise beyond the primary elements (*bhūta*). Having accepted this [position] for the sake of argument, he says: "But suppose they are non-material (*abhautika*)."
Let it be that the self itself arises from the instruments;
indeed, it does not follow from this that the self must not arise from the primary elements (bhūtas).
And thus, there is no consequence of violating the stated sequence.
It is distinguished, differentiated, or, in other words, divided. //15//

But the designation [of the Self] as "moving" or "non-moving" must be figurative, based on its dependence upon the body, because it occurs when that [body] exists. For instance, names such as "Devadatta" belong to the individual self (*jīvātman*), not to the body.

Because it is impossible to perform *śrāddha* and other rites for a body that bears that name [only figuratively]. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) belongs to one who considers the designation "Devadatta died" and "Devadatta was born" to be primary;

however, since such primacy would render impossible the connection with the fruits of heaven and so forth mentioned in the scriptures as occurring in the hereafter, and because this would contradict the scriptures, the worldly designation must be explained as being secondary (*bhākta*).
Devotion consists in the production and destruction of the body, and from that follows its conjunction [with the self].

Furthermore, rites such as the *jātakarma* (birth ceremony) are for the purpose of purifying the sins of the living being arising from the embryonic seed, and not for the purpose of destroying the sins produced by the birth of the living being itself.
For this very reason, they record in their tradition: "In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb comes to rest.
Therefore, it is established that the birth and death of the individual soul (jīva) do not coincide with the birth and destruction of the body.
And this discussion is conducted on the assumption that worldly designations are rooted in non-delusion.
However, it has been stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* that this [superimposition] is rooted in error. //16//

This [section] is commenced to dispel another doubt: that although gross production and destruction may not occur for this [jīva] through the arising and passing away of its body, it will nevertheless undergo production and destruction at the beginning and end of a great cycle of creation (mahāsarga), just like space and other such elements.
"Because it is not heard [in scripture] and because of its eternity, [the self is not produced]; for those [scriptures].
He states the seed of the doubt that is the root of this inquiry: "because of conflicting scriptural statements. He demonstrates that very point: "in some scriptural passages..."
He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "In that regard, it follows...

First of all, the individual selves (*jīvas*) are distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) because they possess contradictory attributes, such as being characterized by having sins removed versus not having sins removed.
If these [individual selves] are not modifications (*vikāras*), then their status as a different reality would contradict the numerous scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*).
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the proposition that through the knowledge of Brahman all things are known.
Therefore, transformation is authorized by the Śruti texts.
Moreover, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated here: "Because it is differentiated, like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth."
Furthermore, the scripture "as from a fire tiny sparks fly forth" directly shows that individual souls (jīvas) are modifications of Brahman.
And the passage "as from a well-kindled fire" directly shows both the origin and the dissolution of the souls from Brahman.
[Objection: But it is understood that the origin and dissolution of entities proceed from the Imperishable (akṣara).
It is not [the case] for individual souls; therefore, he says "of the individual selves" (*jīvātmanām*).
This might be asked:
why is the origination of individual souls not mentioned in the scriptures on creation, just as the origination of ether and the other elements is?
Therefore, because that which is fit for being recorded in scripture is not so recorded, we understand its non-existence; to this he says: "And there is no non-hearing anywhere.

For if this were the case, there would be no inclusion of the subsidiary parts belonging to other recensions (śākhās) for a rite that is recorded in one particular recension along with only a few of its own subsidiaries.

Therefore, due to the contradiction with many scriptural passages, the scriptural statement regarding entry must be explained as referring to the production [of the self] through a state of modification.

Therefore, it might follow that individual souls (jīvātman) arise like space; to this, it is replied: this would indeed be so if the souls were distinct from Brahman, but this is not the case. For there are scriptural texts on non-differentiation, such as "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" and "By this living soul," and because their difference is merely due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the association of contradictory attributes is possible, just as in the case of space within jars, water-pots, and the like.

Furthermore, because numerous scriptural passages such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) refer to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and because other scriptures concerning eternality, birthlessness, and so forth are observed; and because the dissolution of the adjuncts along with the one characterized by them is established in many ways through both questions and answers; and because non-distinction is declared by scripture itself in the passage, "The one God is hidden in all beings"—the eternal individual selves (*jīvātman*) are not modifications.
Thus it is established that there is no contradiction with the thesis of non-duality (advaita).
Furthermore, the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa has already been explained above, and therefore it is not explained here. //17//
Therefore, [the self] is indeed a knower. For the meaning of "knowing" is pervaded by action; in the absence of that [action], it does not occur, just as smoke does not exist in the absence of fire.
Furthermore, in states such as deep sleep, because the object of knowledge is absent, there is an absence of the cognition that pervades it.
Thus, consciousness is not the essential nature of the self, since consciousness is excluded even while the self persists.

Therefore, because the presence and absence of cognition follow the presence and absence of the sense organs and other factors, this consciousness—which is produced by the contact of the sense organs and so forth—is an adventitious attribute of the self, not its inherent nature.
For this very reason, the sense organs and so forth possess purposefulness;
otherwise, the sense organs would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, the scriptural passages concerning eternal consciousness must be interpreted as referring to potentiality.
For souls possess an innate capacity for the production of knowledge;
it is not the case that knowledge fails to arise because of a lack of contact with the senses and so forth, as is the case with space.

Thus, when it is argued that souls are indeed insentient (*jaḍa*), it is replied: that adventitious knowledge which is insentient by nature is sometimes indirect (*parokṣa*), sometimes doubtful (*saṃdigdha*), and sometimes erroneous (*viparyasta*).
Just as in the case of a jar or similar objects, it is not so with the self;
for even when one is engaged in inference, [the self] remains immediate.
Even while remembering, he is one who possesses direct experience;
even while doubting, he is free from doubt; even while erring, he is not mistaken—the Self of all.
And thus, it has that as its intrinsic nature;
nor is there an absence of consciousness which has that as its intrinsic nature, because of its eternity.
Therefore, the mental modifications (*vṛtti*), being of the nature of action, possess objects; in the absence of an object, as in deep sleep and similar states, they cease.
By this, it is established that consciousness is the very nature of the Self.
Consequently, the scriptural texts proclaiming eternal consciousness do not require any forced interpretation whatsoever.
And since the sense organs possess their purposefulness only when there arises a functioning directed toward objects such as odors, everything is clearly explained. //18//
START BsVBh_2,3.13.19: [The Sūtra says:
"Because of the departure, the going, and the returning" (BS 2.3.19).
Even though the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) belongs to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself without modification, and thus it does not possess the dimension of an atom;

Nevertheless, this section is intended to resolve the contradiction between the scriptural statements regarding departure, going, and returning, on the one hand, and the direct hearing of its atomic dimension, on the other; thus he speaks by means of an objection and its resolution, beginning with "But surely...
He takes up the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "In that regard, what first presents itself is...
For the production of disjunction and conjunction is indeed the result of departure and so forth.
And those two do not exist for that which is omnipresent, because it is impossible for them to exist in something that is either eternally present everywhere or whose nature is everything. //19//
And by its own nature, [the term applies] to the two subsequent [stages]. For "departure" (utkramaṇa) is firmly established as referring to death.
And that [agency] is possible even for one who is motionless while remaining there, through the cessation of ownership over the body; it is not, however, [possible] through going and coming.

For those two, which are established as involving motion and whose action resides in the agent, are impossible in the case of an all-pervading [self]. Thus, the intermediate dimension—that is, the magnitude—is that of the body alone.
And this has been refuted in the *Arhatparīkṣā*.
Since going and coming cannot occur in that which is infinitely great, the soul's atomicity is established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

Furthermore, since its localized nature is established through going and coming, it is proven that death is simply the soul’s departure from the body, rather than merely the cessation of its ownership over the body while remaining therein; thus he says: "And since going and coming are real..."
Furthermore, he states that the departure from the body is indeed the death of the individual soul (jīva) by saying, "of the parts of the body.
Therefore, the meaning is that even the departure (utkrānti), which involves going and coming, has a point of departure (apādāna) and thus serves as a proof for its atomicity (aṇutva).
This is not only because of the scriptural mention of the point of departure;
He says that the scriptural statement regarding the exit from another part of that body is also exactly like this: "He [takes] these particles of light... (20).
"If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of scriptural statements [to the contrary], we say no, because of the context of the other [passages].

(BS 2.3.21) Since the atomicity of the individual souls has been established by scriptural texts concerning their departure from the body and so forth, they are therefore distinct from the all-pervading Supreme Self, being its modifications.

Thus, the meaning is that scriptural passages concerning magnitude, infinity, and so forth, refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman) and not to the individual soul (jīva); therefore, there is no contradiction. One might object: "If the souls are atomic (aṇu), then how is it that the embodied self is referred to as being connected with magnitude in the passage, 'He who consists of knowledge among the vital breaths'? To this he replies: "The reference is made from the perspective of the scripture—that is, from the ultimate standpoint—just as in the case of Vāmadeva."

For just as the individual soul Vāmadeva, while still in the womb, realized his identity with Brahman through the vision of ultimate reality, so too, because modifications are in reality non-different from their material cause, they are designated by its measure; this is the meaning. //21//
START BsVBh_2,3.13.22:
And by means of its own word and by measure. BBs_2,3.22:
He analyzes the term "its own" [as follows]: "directly indeed."
He analyzes *unmāna* (measurement by comparison): "In the same way, *unmāna* also...
*Unmāna* is measurement by extraction (*uddhṛtya mānam*). It is the hundredth part extracted from the tip of a hair; and from that hundredth part, again the hundredth part extracted—that is *unmāna*.
Measurement extracted from the tip of a needle is merely the size of the tip of a needle. //22//
In order to introduce another sūtra, he raises an objection: "But if [the self] were atomic" (nanvaṇutve sati).
The meaning is that if the self were atomic, it would not pervade the body, and consequently, there would be no perception of coolness extending over all limbs.
There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood (BBs 2.3.23).

For the living being is conjoined with the skin, and the skin pervades the entire body; thus, the connection of the self, through its pervasion of the skin, is capable of perceiving coldness throughout the whole body—this is the meaning. //23//
If it is argued that [the experience of pleasure] is due to a difference in the location [of the application], we say no, because it is admitted [to be so] in the case of the heart;
for, having perceived through direct perception the smallness of a drop of sandalwood paste, the conceptualization [of its pervasive effect] becomes logical.

The meaning of the objection is this: for one whose atomicity is doubtful yet whose effects are perceived throughout all parts of the body, this conceptualization cannot find room unless its inherent pervasiveness is abandoned.

Furthermore, he states "nor is there an inference here," because an inference of the soul's atomicity based on the example of a drop of sandalwood paste is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as counter-examples are possible.
He removes this doubt with the words "To this it is replied.
Although the atomicity of the Self is established by the previously cited scriptures, nevertheless, another scripture is adduced for the sake of its comprehensive scope. //24//

Or [the soul's pervasion of the body] is due to its quality, as in the case of the world. (BS 2.3.25) However, while the pervasion of the body by a drop of sandalwood is possible through the movement of atoms because it possesses parts, the movement of atoms within the partless self is not possible.

Therefore, regarding those who think there is an inequality [between the soul and its qualities], this is said in response: "Or, due to its quality, as in the world. He analyzes this: "Consciousness," etc. Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, nevertheless its quality—consciousness—pervades the entire body.
Just as, even when a lamp is small, its quality [of light] pervades the entire interior of the house. //25//
Having also refuted this by way of an objection, he states another example:

The conjunction of the large and the small obstructs the small, but not the large;
for the conjunctions of jars, water-pots, and the like never encompass the space of the sky, but rather only the small [objects] such as jars and water-pots;
otherwise, wherever there is space, there would be the perception of jars, water-pots, and so forth everywhere.
They too would consequently follow as being of the same dimension as space;
furthermore, it is not possible for a minute soul (*jīva*) to experience sensations extending throughout the entire body.
Even if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were minute, nevertheless, because it is connected to the skin and the skin pervades the whole body, [the sensation] occurs in one part [of the body].

Even if the skin is presided over [by the soul], it is as if it were not presided over; thus, the soul, which pervades the body, is able to experience coldness throughout all its limbs via the sense of touch in the Ganges.
However, if the soul were atomic (aṇu), it would experience that [cold] only in that specific part of the body where it resides, and not throughout all the limbs.
Because that [pleasure] does not pervade all parts of the body, whereas the prick of a thorn, being localized, does not result in a perception that pervades all parts; this is the difference.
For it is indeed a quality (guṇatva) alone...
For this indeed is the "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) of qualities: that they occupy the same location as the substance (*dravyadeśatva*).

For this very reason, just as in winter, when an extremely dense cold touch belonging to water-substances with closely packed parts is being experienced, their unmanifest color (*rūpa*) is not perceived;

so too, when the extremely dense fragrance of musk and the like—whose subtle parts are dispersed by the carrier of scent—is being experienced, neither color nor touch is perceived. What is the reason for this?
This is because those two [taste and touch] are non-manifest, whereas odor is manifest;
furthermore, there is no consequence of the exhaustion of the substance,
since it is replenished by the addition of parts from another substance.
For this very reason, by virtue of the passage of time, its scent of death is perceived.
Furthermore, that which is called consciousness is not a quality of the soul, for qualities belong to things;
rather, it is its very nature.

Furthermore, if the nature [of consciousness] is all-pervasive, it does not follow that the entity is non-pervasive, for that would entail a loss of its true essence; thus he says: "And if consciousness...
In this way, since the soul's identity with the Supreme Self is established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa through its immutability, [the objection is refuted].

Likewise, regarding its supreme greatness [established] from scripture and other sources, those scriptural passages concerning its atomicity must be explained in accordance with that [greatness] as being based on the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus he says: "Because its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*).
He explains this [sūtra] as follows: "Of that intellect... (*tasyā buddheḥ*).
At that time, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) because the self is presented by the intellect (*buddhi*) with which it is connected;
for the true nature (*tattva*) of the self, which is pure, awakened, and liberated by nature, is not experienced by those in transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*).
Rather, it is precisely this [self] which is attached to false knowledge, aversion, and so forth, that falls within the range of individual experience.

Furthermore, since the individual self (*jīvātman*), whose true nature is Brahman and who is changelessly eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*), cannot by its own nature be associated with desire and aversion, these qualities—which actually belong to the intellect (*buddhi*)—are superimposed upon it through the superimposition of non-difference.
This is just as the reflection of the moon superimposed on a bowl of water is perceived as trembling when the water trembles; this has been established in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*.

Thus, its status as an individual soul (*jīvatva*) is produced by limiting adjuncts such as the intellect; and because the intellect, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is atomic (*aṇu*), the self also comes to be designated as atomic.
Just as a hailstone placed in the sky [is not perceived] because it is of the same size as the sky,
so too is the occurrence of departure and the other stages [of the soul]. The rest has been explained by the very words of the text.
At the time of departure [from the body], there would be either non-existence or a lack of transmigratory state;
consequently, there would follow the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done. //29//

START BsVBh_2,3.13.32:
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other.
(BBs_2,3.32) This might be so.
Even if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) exists, since it is eternally present, why do constant perception and non-perception not result?

If it is argued that this consequence does not follow because the capacity of the internal organ is sometimes obstructed and sometimes unobstructed due to the occasional ripening of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*),
then let that [obstruction] belong either to the self (*ātman*), the internal organ, or the sense organs, while the internal organ itself remains present.
He raises the objection: "Then what is the use of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is like a useless tumor? with the words, "Or rather, [it belongs] to one or the other self.
The phrase "or rather" sets aside the established conclusion (siddhānta). The proponent of the conclusion replies: "And it does not belong to the self."
Attention is indeed the desire to understand or the desire to hear;
and these two are not attributes of the Self, because the Self is changeless.
Nor are they the sense-faculties, because we observe blind people and others even when individual sense-faculties are absent;
furthermore, those [faculties] cannot exist as external objects while being experienced as internal.

Therefore, there exists some internal factor distinct from those, and it is this that constitutes their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This is what was meant by the statement: "of which [there is] the application of attention" (*yasyāvadhāna*).
Regarding this very point, he shows the scriptural authority (śruti) with the words: "And thus" (tathā ca). //32//
START BsVBh_2,3.14.33:

The soul is an agent, because the scripture has a purpose. (BBs 2,3.33) Now, one might object: since the soul's status as both agent and enjoyer has already been established by the very statement "because its essence consists of those qualities" (tadguṇasāratvāt), the further explanation of that is redundant. To this, he says: "by way of the section on its essence consisting of those qualities."
This is an elaboration of that very point: for those who perceive that the Self is solely the enjoyer and not the agent, this [text] is intended to refute that view.
The venerable Jaimini said, "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic," meaning it belongs to the performer, the one who carries out the practice.
"By the agent" means up to that point.
"The fruit of the scripture" refers to heaven and so forth.
Why?

Because the scripture is characterized as a means for achieving the fruit of the agent, injunction (*vidhi*) consists in being a means required by the agent. If cognition (*buddhi*) is the agent and the self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer, then that which is the enjoyer does not possess the agency of that which is the means required by the enjoyer. Whose [is the agency]? [It belongs to the self.]

Furthermore, since agency does not require [external] means, what connection could there be between "what" and "by whom"? Thus, the scripture would be purposeless, its subject matter non-existent, and consequently, it would be devoid of utility.

Just as its status as an enjoyer—though not a real entity—is merely conventional due to its having the qualities [of the intellect] as its essence, so too its agency is merely conventional and not real.
And it has been established in the Introduction to Superimposition (Adhyāsa-bhāṣya) that the scripture has as its subject matter those who possess ignorance; thus, everything is clear. //33//
START BsVBh_2,3.14.34:

Movement (vihāra) is transition (saṃcāra), which is action (kriyā).
In that regard, independence is not possible for one who is not an agent;
therefore, for this reason as well, the individual soul (jīva) is the agent. //34//

Because of appropriation (upādāna).

BBs_2,3.35: Therefore, regarding these vital breaths and sense-faculties, the act of taking up—that is, appropriating—the consciousness by means of the consciousness of the intellect (buddhi), meaning the capacity for grasping—is what is meant by "appropriation" (upādāna). Independence in this regard is not possible for one who is not the agent. //35//
START BsVBh_2,3.14.36:
"And because of designation; if [it is argued] that it occurs in action, there would be a reversal of the instruction. (BBs 2,3.36) This is merely an additional argument; it is not a valid proof.
Consciousness is the agent that performs the sacrifice;
for everywhere else, the intellect, being of the nature of an instrument, is designated as such by its very status as an instrument and not as an agent,
but here it is [designated] as an agent.
In designating that [consciousness], there would be a misconception;
therefore, the self itself is designated as consciousness, and by that [designation], it is called the agent. //36//
To introduce another sūtra, he raises an objection: "Here he says, 'If...
A wise person, being independent, would bring about what is desired for himself, not what is undesired.
Furthermore, the attainment of what is undesirable is also observed for him;
therefore, he is not independent, and thus he is not an agent.
The meaning is that this is because his characteristic is such.
The answer to this is:
"There is no such restriction, just as in the case of perception" (upalabdhivad-aniyamaḥ).

The agent employs other causal factors, such as instruments and so forth, but he himself is not employed by those other causal factors; this much alone constitutes his independence. It does not mean, however, that he does not depend upon other causal factors in the performance of the action.
Thus, such independence does not even belong to the venerable Lord; therefore, the agent would be one whose discourse has ceased to exist.

Furthermore, by the power of the maturation of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), one who desires to obtain what is desired might, through a confusion regarding the means for its accomplishment, employ a method that leads to the undesired and thereby incur the undesired; thus, there is no contradiction between agency and the lack of necessity (aniyama).
Because its sole purpose is the conceptualization of objects.
Indeed, for the Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness, the instruments such as the senses present their respective objects;
therefore, consciousness as delimited by the object is designated as "modification" (*vṛtti*) and as "cognition" (*vijñāna*).
And in that regard, he possesses independence; such is the meaning. //37//
START BsVBh_2,3.14.38:
Because of the reversal of the case endings [indicating] causal agency (śakti). BBs_2,3.38: Previously, the reversal of the case endings expressing the cause was stated.

Now, this is not a redundancy because it concerns the reversal of the capacities of the factors of action (*kāraka*). However, if one were to postulate another instrument (*karaṇa*) in order to avoid such a reversal, there would be a contradiction regarding the name [of that factor]. //38//
And because of the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
[In this context] "meditative concentration" indicates self-restraint (*saṃyama*).
For concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are indeed to be designated by the term "saṃyama" (mastery).
As it has been said: "The three together in one place constitute saṃyama.
In this context, the instruction to "listen" and "reflect" is the teaching on concentration.
"One should meditate upon" (nididhyāsitavya) is the instruction for meditation (dhyāna);
"one should see" (draṣṭavya) is the instruction for meditative absorption (samādhi).
As they have said: "That very meditation, when it appears as the object alone and is, as it were, devoid of its own form, is samādhi."
The meaning of the aphorism is this: when this self, which is the agent here, is instructed regarding meditative absorption (samādhi), it realizes its own agency. //39//
And just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways (yathā ca takṣobhayathā).
He states the intermediate connection (avāntarasaṃgati) with the words: "In this way, first... (evam tāvad iti).
He reflects: "That, moreover...
He adopts the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "In that regard...
For the reasons such as the purposefulness of the scripture (śāstrārthavattva) and so forth establish the agency of the self.

Furthermore, since natural agency is possible and there is no sublation [of it], it is not logical to claim that it is adventitious through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does the consequence of the absence of liberation serve as a sublater of this [agency];

for just as one whose nature is knowledge does not cease to be a knower even in the absence of an object of knowledge, so too one whose nature is agency does not cease to be an agent even in the absence of engagement in action.
Therefore, when it is argued that its agency is indeed intrinsic, it is replied as follows:
Brahman is repeatedly heard in scripture to have an essence that is eternally pure, conscious, and free;
thus, its consciousness is logical even in the absence of anything to be known.
Just as fire possesses the quality of being a burner even when there is no object to be burned— since it is understood to have that nature—
its agency, however, is to be understood from its immersion in action.
Furthermore, it is not possible for that which is eternally indifferent, immutable, eternal, and repeatedly heard [in scripture] to have such a connection;
for since there is no contact with anything at any time, how could there be a conjunction with its power? This is because a power without an object is impossible.

Thus, if one were to admit an entry into activity directed toward that object in order to establish that [power], then, because there would be no destruction of the nature of that which is of such a nature, it would follow that the entity itself is destroyed.
And there is no connection with action for one who is liberated;
because action is suffering, liberation would not be a state of supreme bliss in which all suffering has vanished. With this intention, [the author] says: "Agency is not inherent to the Self.
Failing to understand this underlying purpose, the opponent objects: "But even while [the Self] remains..."
He refutes this, saying: "Not so; even for signs.
Power, which depends upon both the capable and the incapable, necessarily implies the capable by its very existence.
And thus, the sense is that what is implied by that [means] must always be possible.
He objects: "But surely [it is not so], because of the prescription of the means for liberation. He replies: "No."
Regarding the phrase "dependent on means of accomplishment" (*sādhanāyattasya*):
for us, however, liberation is not something to be accomplished; rather, it is the very nature of Brahman, and that is eternal.
He reveals the intended meaning: "Moreover, [it is said] 'eternally pure'.
He raises an objection: "In that case, the transmigrating being must be something other [than the Self].

This is the meaning: if the transmigrating being were something other, then upon the dissolution of its ignorance and liberation, all would be liberated simultaneously, because there would be no distinction.
Furthermore, it would follow that all of saṃsāra must be utterly annihilated.
If [the self] were other than the aggregate consisting of cognition and so forth,
then liberation and saṃsāra would belong to that very aggregate alone, and not to the self.
He refutes this, saying: "No, because they are established by ignorance.
Thus, liberation and saṃsāra do not belong to the supreme self.
Because it is eternally liberated;
nor can it belong to the aggregate of intellect and so forth, because that is insentient.

However, due to the diversity of the aggregates such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, which are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self—though one, pure, and [inherently] free from impurity—appears as if divided and as if impure when conditioned by the distinctions of each respective aggregate of intellect and so on. Consequently, upon the disappearance of a particular aggregate of intellect and so forth, it appears as if liberated therein and as if bound elsewhere; just as a single face appears differently according to the distinctions of the adjuncts such as a jewel or a sword.

Just as [a single face] appears diverse— as long, as round, as dark, or as fair— depending on the removal of this or that particular adjunct (*upadhāna*), such that it seems "liberated" in one place while "constrained" in another,
there is no liberation of all upon the liberation of one; therefore,
neither birth nor transmigratory existence belong to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Nor is [the soul] a mere aggregate of intellect and so forth; rather, the ultimate truth is that it is the very nature of the Self, conditioned by intellect and the rest, which has attained the state of a living being (jīva).
In this very context, he demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) through scriptural passages with the words "And thus.

Furthermore, he states that the conditionality [of the soul's attributes] is established because scripture shows its submergence and emergence following the submergence and emergence of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), with the words "Likewise, in the states of dreaming and waking."
Regarding this very point, he explains the Sūtra by saying "He said this":
*saṃprasāda* is deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
This might be so.
The carpenter possesses hands and other limbs, and by employing tools such as an axe through them, he may indeed experience suffering;

however, the Supreme Self is without parts, so by what means could it employ the mind and other faculties? To address this disparity with the example of the carpenter, the text says: "And the example of the carpenter.
Just as the carpenter is happy while remaining indifferent [to the labor] by means of his own body, [so too is the Self].
One who employs instruments such as an axe and so forth becomes miserable;
likewise, one who remains indifferent to his own self through his own self becomes happy.
However, one who employs instruments such as the mind and so forth becomes miserable—it is only in this respect that there is similarity between them, but not in every way.

Just as the self (*ātman*) and the living being (*jīva*), without depending on other parts, set their own body into motion, so too do they set other instruments such as the mind (*manas*) into motion; since this is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is improper to subject this to questioning or objection.
Having restated the reasons for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes them with the words "As for what was said":
"For that which is the ultimate purpose of a scripture is alone the meaning of that scripture."
That [injunction] is intent upon the cultivation of the means required by the agent; it is not intent upon the true nature of the agent.
Therefore, by relying on an agent as established in common worldly experience, it does not have the power to convey an innate agency belonging to the person.
Consequently, because it would contradict such instructions as "That thou art," that [agency] remains understood as being produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).
He objects: "Is it not the case that [the soul] exists in the intermediate state?
The meaning is that agency, being dependent on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), is not possible when those adjuncts have departed; therefore, it is logical that it must be inherent (*svābhāvika*).

Furthermore, he says, "Likewise even in the case of taking up [a body]," because even where instruments exist, the agency of the self alone is heard of in scripture; thus, it is logical that it is indeed inherent.
He refutes this as follows: "First of all, it is not the case that [the adjuncts] cease in the state of deep sleep (*saṃdhyā*).
The meaning is that the removal of the adjuncts is unproven, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serves as the adjunct, persists even in the state of deep sleep.
Furthermore, he states, "And the movement (*vihāra*) there is also of the same nature as the cognition," meaning that in dreams, the movement is of the same kind as the cognition itself.
The same applies to the case of the instrument (*upādāna*).

Although the agentive case-ending is heard when applied to the agent alone, nevertheless, this agency of his is produced by the proximity of the object and the instrument; it does not belong to him in isolation.
For one who cuts with the aid of an axe is not a "cutter" in the absolute sense.

Now, if it were the case that agency belongs not to the [self] alone, but only to that which is accompanied by instruments and so forth, then the agentive case-ending would also apply to the instruments and the like; yet this is not observed. Thus he says: "In common usage, it does not occur."

The meaning is that even in the case of instruments and so forth, the agentive case-ending (*kartṛvibhakti*) sometimes indeed occurs by virtue of the speaker’s intention. Furthermore, this scriptural mention of "appropriating" (*upādāna*) is intended merely to denote the cessation of the operation of the instrument, not its independence; the agentive case-ending, however, is figurative. This is because the cessation of the operation of an instrument without prior conscious intent is observed, as in the expression "the bank wishes to fall. Thus he says: "Moreover, in this 'appropriating'..."
As for this designation [of agency] which we have stated to be merely an incidental elaboration, it arises from this very point:
"of all causal factors indeed.
For in their own respective operations, all [factors] are agents, as in the cases: "the rice grains soften," "the wood pieces burn," and "the pot bears [the food]."
Regarding agency:

is it that the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors possess only agency and not the status of instruments? To this he says: "But their status as instruments is relative to perception. Now, if this is so, might the self’s agency be inherent in that very [perception]? To this he says: "And even in that perception, its agency is not inherent. Why? Because the self has the nature of eternal perception."
The meaning is that there is no activity of an entity within its eternal intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, it has been stated that this [self] does not possess an inherent agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to perception.

Nor is the agency of cognition and so forth superimposed upon the self in the same way that the agency of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth residing therein [is superimposed]; for he says: "Even agency preceded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) cannot belong to the perceiver."
Why?
Because the ego (ahaṅkāra) is also perceived [as the agent].
For that which is the object of motion in a particular action cannot itself be the mover in that very same action.
This is what is meant: if cognition were itself the act of apprehension, then one would attribute the status of being the apprehender to it within the self;
but this is not the case.
Because it is perceived as being insentient, it is impossible for it to be the agent of perception.

And when the intellect (*buddhi*) is not the agent in perception, then that which was said—that if the intellect were the perceiver, another instrument would have to be postulated, and thus there would be a mere disagreement over names—does not hold true; he says this because, such being the case, there is no need to postulate another instrument since the intellect lacks the status of a perceiver.

In that case, would it not follow that the intellect (*buddhi*) is non-active while the self (*ātman*) is inactive with respect to perception? To this he replies: "Because the intellect is admitted to be an instrument (*karaṇa*).

This is the intended meaning: since consciousness (*caitanya*), which is perception, is the very nature of the self and is eternal, the self has no agency therein, nor does the intellect possess the status of an instrument.
However, it is consciousness itself, when delimited by an object, that is designated as both "modification" (vṛtti) and "apprehension" (upalabdhi).

Regarding its modification through the delimitation of various objects, it is logical that the intellect and other factors function as instruments (karaṇa), while the Self functions as the agent (kartṛ) through the mediation of those [instruments], preceded by the sense of ego (ahaṅkāra). //40//
But [the agency] comes from another, because of the scriptural statement to that effect (BS 2.3.41).

As for this agency of the individual souls (*jīvas*) which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), since it exists through passion (*rāga*) and other factors characterized by impulsion, one need not postulate another, namely Īśvara, as the impeller.
Because this would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Furthermore, a Lord who is devoid of hatred and partiality cannot be expected to impel living beings toward good and evil actions,
by virtue of which the diversity of the world would arise in dependence upon merit and demerit.
For if he were independent and compassionate, he would surely impel living beings toward Dharma alone and not toward non-Dharma;
consequently, all beings impelled by him would be exclusively righteous and thus happy, rather than suffering.

However, it is logical that beings who are independent, being impelled by passion and other afflictions as they act, accumulate both merit and demerit and thereby experience the diversity of worldly existence.

And thus, injunctions and prohibitions possess purpose; otherwise, however, since living beings would be entirely dependent on another and would be impelled by the Lord alone, injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered useless.
For instruction is not meaningful for one who is being driven by a powerful torrent of wind and water.

Therefore, since the scriptural passages such as "He indeed makes him perform good action" and so forth contradict all the scriptures concerning injunctions and prohibitions and contradict worldly experience, they must be interpreted as having the purpose of praising the Lord's sovereignty—this being the position reached.
It is stated:
"For this very one causes [the soul] to perform good deeds," and so forth. These scriptural passages declare that in all activities, living beings are dependent upon the Lord;
therefore, in the absence of any contradiction, it is not appropriate to interpret them as being intended merely for the purpose of praise.
Furthermore, that which is established by scripture is not something to be postulated,
such that its postulation would be contradicted by the existence of passion and other factors that incite activity.
Nor is it logical to argue that if [the world] were dependent on God, then because of merit alone, living beings would experience only happiness and there would be no diversity.

Although this Lord is free from passion, nevertheless, by impelling beings toward merit and demerit in dependence upon the karma of each preceding being, He is neither partial through hatred or favoritism,
nor is He merciless;
nor is there a beginning to the accumulation of karma, because saṃsāra is beginningless.
It is not correct to say that for one who is dependent on Īśvara, injunctions and prohibitions are purposeless;
for Īśvara does not impel living beings like a violent wind, but rather acts by conforming to their consciousness through the medium of the presentation of passion and so forth.
In this way, for those who seek to obtain what is desired and avoid what is undesired, injunctions and prohibitions become meaningful.
With this intention, it was said: "Even though agency depends on another, the individual soul (jīva) indeed acts.

Therefore, because there is no contradiction with the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, because people perceive only superficially, and because of such scriptural passages as, "For he alone causes one to perform good action," and "This ignorant creature is not its own master regarding its pleasure and pain," [the soul is said to act].
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or indeed to a pit.
Thus, from this Smṛti it is established that the agency of living beings belongs only to those who are dependent on the Lord, and not to those who are independent.

For if the Lord alone were to be appointed as the locus for injunctions and prohibitions— such that the fruit of injunctions and prohibitions were produced by the Lord independently of the merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) established by them— then injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered purposeless.
He says "likewise, one who performs what is enjoined" because not only would there be pointlessness, but the opposite would also follow;
furthermore, the previously mentioned fault—the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done—would result. The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //41//
But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise prescribed and prohibited actions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons. (2.3.42)
START BsVBh_2,3.17.43:
"A part [of Brahman], because of various designations, and also otherwise; for some record that He has the nature of fishermen, kitavas, and so forth" (BS 2.3.43).
He states the intermediate connection: "between the individual soul and the Lord."
The relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary is the relationship between the instigator and the instigated.

Here, it was stated that there is no fixed certainty because, at first glance, there is no reason for a definitive determination. Then, observing what appear to be fallacious reasons for certainty, he adopts the position of differentiation and says, "Alternatively."

The relationship of ruler and ruled, the relationship of seeker and sought, the relationship of knower and known, the relationship of controller and controlled, and the relationship of substratum and superstratum are not possible if there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Nor can scriptural passages such as "Brahman is the gambler, Brahman is the thrower of dice" (*brahmadāśā brahmakitavāḥ*), which aim to establish that the gamblers are Brahman and the throwers of dice are Brahman, be reasonably explained if there were a difference between the individual souls and Brahman.

Furthermore, these scriptures—which aim to establish both difference and non-difference—along with the Vedic verse directly proclaiming the status of being a part (*aṃśatva*), such as "All beings are one foot of Him" (*pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni*), [establish this very point].
Furthermore, from the Smṛti passage beginning with "A portion of My very self," it is established that individual souls (jīvas) are portions of the Lord.

Moreover, through the possession of unsurpassed limiting adjuncts (upādhis) and the yoga of majesty (vibhūti), it is logical that the Lord rules even over those portions of Himself whose adjuncts are inferior.
Indeed, the individual souls cannot be literal parts of the indivisible Lord.

Furthermore, if individual souls (*jīva*) were parts of Brahman, then the sensations experienced by them would belong to Brahman, just as sensations occurring in the feet and other limbs belong to Devadatta.

Consequently, for one who has attained the state of Brahman, there would be the undesirable consequence of experiencing all the sensations belonging to every soul; therefore, worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) itself would be preferable to liberation, since in that state one experiences only the sensations pertaining to oneself and not so much [as in the other case].

[If the soul were partless,] it would experience suffering; however, since the liberated [soul] would then share in all the sensations of every living being, liberation—being fraught with such manifold evils—would have to be avoided through effort.
Likewise, because identity and difference, which are mutually contradictory, cannot coexist in one place, the souls cannot possess parts.
Nor is it tenable that Brahman alone is real while the individual souls (jīvas) are unreal,
for that would entail the absence of the established order of pleasure, pain, liberation, and saṃsāra, as well as the impossibility of injunctions and prohibitions.
Therefore, the individual souls alone are ultimately real, not the one non-dual Brahman.

Regarding the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śruti*), it might be argued that they are merely figurative (*upacāra*) due to the absence of distinctions in genus, location, and time; to this, we reply: valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—and verbal testimony (*śabda*) in particular—function to make known an object not previously apprehended.
In this regard, since difference (*bheda*) is already established by worldly experience, it cannot be the primary object of verbal communication.
