However, since non-difference (*abheda*) is not so established, it is fit to be communicated by way of restating the difference that has already been apprehended.

The purport of a statement lies precisely where it begins, is referred to in the middle, and is concluded at the end. Since the Upaniṣads begin with non-duality, refer to it in their midst, and conclude with it, they are rightly understood as being solely devoted to non-duality.
Furthermore, it is not logical that what a text is devoted to should be considered merely figurative.
For it has been stated that through repetition, there is an increase in the reality of the object, not its diminution, much less its status as merely figurative.

Therefore, since non-duality is established as real, the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) for that Brahman arises from the differentiation caused by the substrate of beginningless and indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*). Just as a single original form appears as various reflections due to the differences in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as mirrors, so too are worldly and Vedic injunctions and prohibitions, as well as the systematic arrangement of pleasure, pain, liberation, and saṃsāra, rendered logically consistent.
Furthermore, liberation does not involve an abundance of misfortune;

for, just as reflections possess qualities such as darkness or brightness, it is only the individual souls (*jīvas*) who are connected with various experiences, whereas Brahman, like the original object (*bimba*), is not so connected.
And just as when the mirror is removed, that reflection remains in the state of the original object and no longer exists as a reflection in a sword.

Thus, it is established that upon the removal of the veil of ignorance, the individual soul (jīva) attains the state of Brahman; the intended meaning is that the jīva is like a part of Brahman by virtue of its dependence on Him, but it is not actually a part. //43//
And from the wording of the mantra: "And from the wording of the mantra" (mantravarṇāt). // 44 //
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti: BBs_2,3.45 // 45 //
Like light and so forth, the Supreme is not thus. 46. (BBs_2,3.46)
And they record:
"A collection or group measured by the number seventeen is called 'the seventeen' (saptadaśaka)."

Namely: the ten external organs of cognition and action; the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is a single entity when the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas)—though distinct only through their different functions—are unified; the body; and the five objects [of the senses]. Thus, there is a group consisting of seventeen [principles]. //47//
START BsVBh_2,3.17.48:
Permission and prohibition [apply] due to the connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.
(BBs_2,3.48) "Permission" is intended here as an injunction (*vidhi*), and not as an instigation to action for one who has already begun acting.
In the case of that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), it is impossible for there to be compliance with the intention of an author;
furthermore, in the case of the Agniṣomīya slaughter, which serves the purpose of the ritual (kratvartha), the instigation of one already engaged in the act is untenable.
Even regarding the human goal (puruṣārtha), since activity occurs in respect to the restrictive portion (niyamāṃśa), what indeed is this connection with the body?

The intention [of the objection] is this: for the self (*ātman*), which is immutable and eternal, there can be no conjunction with the body, nor inherence, nor any other kind of relationship whatsoever, because it transcends all attributes (*dharma*).
The reply is: "This aggregate consisting of the body and so forth arises as a false cognition (*viparītapratyaya*) within the self, such that one thinks, 'I am indeed this [aggregate]'.
The meaning is this: it is true that there is no ultimate (*pāramārthika*) relationship between the self and the body and its adjuncts; however, [the error arises from the following].

However, there is a contrary mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding the self, produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, which takes the form: "I am indeed this aggregate of the body and so forth.
In this [modification], the aggregate of the body and so forth appears through identity with the self.
The meaning is that this relationship, characterized by identity, is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtta*) and not ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
One who harbors a hidden intention objects: "In that case, for one who possesses right vision... The reply is: "No;
for him..."

If it is held that right vision consists in the realization "I am Brahman, one only without a second," wherein the aggregate of the subtle and gross bodies and so forth is shown to be [merely] presented by ignorance, then indeed injunctions and prohibitions are entirely purposeless with respect to one who possesses such a vision.
He clarifies this very point with the words: "Of the rejectable and the acceptable."

The accuser reveals his hidden intention: "It is only for those who perceive [the self] as distinct from the body that there is eligibility for performing rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* which have fruits in the next world. To this he replies: "No;
because of the conceit of its being composed of those [elements]."
He analyzes this [point] with the words "It is true":

for one who knows the self to be non-different from the body composed of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*), but does not know it to be non-different from the entire aggregate of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—
He has authority over the fruits pertaining to the next world;

however, one who perceives the complete distinction from the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, and is thus devoid of the conceit of being the enjoyer of karma, has no authority over action. Consequently, there is no acting according to one's own whims, because for such a person, even that [whim] is absent due to the lack of conceit. //48//
And because there is no continuity [of the self], there is no confusion [of karmic results]. (BBs 2.3.49) // 49 //
And it is merely an appearance.

For those Sāṃkhyas or Vaiśeṣikas who maintain that there are many all-pervading selves and who desire the arrangement of pleasure and pain to be ultimately real, for them alone does this confusion result.
In that regard, he first states the contradiction [with the Sāṃkhyas] by means of a question: "How so?

Since the connection with the *guṇas* is of such a nature that it is indistinguishable with respect to all *puruṣas*, the pleasure and pain produced thereby must be indistinguishable for all. Nor can there be a systematic distinction based on *karman*.

Because action is material in nature and primordial matter (prakṛti) is common to all, the lack of a fixed order remains as it was. He raises an objection with the words, "It might be so," the meaning of which is this:
primordial matter does not act for the sake of proclaiming its own manifestations.
But [it acts] for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

And toward that person for whom the two goals of the person—enjoyment and liberation—have been accomplished through effort, [Prakṛti] ceases activity because its office is fulfilled; however, toward other persons, it continues to act because its office is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, since the distinction between the liberated and the transmigrating is established, he refutes [the objection] that the distinction between pleasure and pain would also follow, by saying "no."

Because all *puruṣas* are omnipresent and because *pradhāna* is common to all, there is no basis for saying that "this purpose has been accomplished for this particular *puruṣa*" by means of this [activity].
Therefore, a fixed order must be established without a cause, namely, by virtue of a specific purpose;
however, that is untenable due to the absence of a cause—this is the meaning.
Let there be no fixed rule for the Sāṃkhyas, because the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) inheres in the Pradhāna,
and the Pradhāna is common to all.

For the followers of Kaṇāda and others, however, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) inheres in the self and is unique to each individual self; and the relationship between the self and the mind, characterized by the status of owner and owned, is beginningless because the various types of unseen forces are beginningless.
Thus, even though the conjunction of the self [with the mind] is common to all, the arrangement of intentions and so forth is indeed possible due to the uniqueness of the owner-owned relationship.
Furthermore, the conjunction itself is not common [to all].
For the conjunction of that mind with other selves is not the same as its conjunction with its own master,
because a conjunction of selves differs according to the distinction between each respective conjunct.
Therefore, since the oneness of the self is established by scripture, [the mind cannot belong to another].

Furthermore, since it is logically possible for the systematic arrangement to be unitary, there is no need to postulate that it consists of multiple natures, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava) and contradict the scriptures.
Furthermore, if one were to postulate difference based on the possession of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*):
for that [particularity] would be postulated only when there is difference, and difference would exist only because of that [particularity].
This very point constitutes the refutation of the Kaṇāda doctrine.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, out of a desire for bold argumentation (prauḍhavāditā), has applied such sūtras as "because of the lack of restriction regarding the unseen" (adṛṣṭāniyamāt) even against the followers of Kaṇāda;
yet some prefer to hold that these [sūtras] are intended solely to refute the Sāṃkhya doctrine—let that matter rest for now. //50//
START BsVBh_2,3.17.51 Because there is no restriction regarding the unseen (adṛṣṭa). BBs_2,3.51 // 51 //
And the same applies to intentions and so forth. (BBs 2.3.52) // 52 //
If it is argued that [the whole exists] because of its spatial location (pradeśa), we say no, because [that location] is included within [the parts]. (53)
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, composed by the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the third quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Resolution of the Apparent Contradiction Regarding the Scriptural Passages on the Five Great Elements and the Living Self.
The same applies to the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

Although the scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths at the beginning of creation should—given the promise that "by knowing Brahman, everything is known," the contradiction with the explanatory passages, and the contradiction with the numerous Śruti texts on non-duality—be interpreted in some other way, just as the passages concerning the non-remembrance of the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth were interpreted; nevertheless:

Nevertheless, not knowing how [the matter] might otherwise be interpreted, and thinking that even a single scriptural statement that is otherwise inexplicable could justify the alteration of many others, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) argues as follows.
In this context, he recalls the reasons for the prima facie view regarding the ether (*viyat*) due to its extreme height, beginning with the words "In that regard, first...

Since the origination of the great elements is to be understood solely through the authority of scripture, wherever the scriptural statement ceases, the absence of those elements is understood there due to the absence of that means of knowledge.
The meaning is: "just as in the case of the nature of the dharma consisting in the worship of a caitya and its ritual action.

Here, having raised an objection based on an initial misunderstanding of the scripture and a resulting lack of certainty, he introduces the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) stated with the words "or rather" (athavā).
His intention has been shown.

In the aphorism "And the [penance for] drinking [liquor] is like that," what is referred to is the similarity to the meaning of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument in the section concerning the "sacrifice upon receiving a horse" (aśvapratigraheṣṭi) and others.

However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: this would indeed be so if the scriptural statement regarding the existence of vital breaths (prāṇa) at the beginning of creation were established as not being otherwise possible;
but rather, it is established in quite another way.
For it must be stated that at the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*), there is a creation of the means for fire; this opening passage is intended for that purpose.

In that context, the sovereign person Prajāpati remains entirely undestroyed while only the three worlds have dissolved; therefore, with respect to his vital breaths (*prāṇa*), that scriptural statement is logically consistent. Consequently, [the subsequent section] is for the sake of favoring the majority of scriptural texts and for the sake of establishing the promise of "knowing all."

If, however, the context were secondary, it would follow that the subject matter is irrelevant due to the absence of conformity with the promised topic; thus, even the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) would be mere modifications of Brahman, like space.
Nor is it the case that there is no scriptural mention of the origin of the vital breaths at all, as is the case with the worship of a shrine (*caityavandana*) and similar acts.
Indeed, in some places their origination is not heard of, yet in various other places their origination is shown;
therefore, there is a disparity [between them] and such practices as the veneration of caityas and the poṣadha observance.
"Because a figurative sense is impossible.
(BBs 2.4.2) Some explain the sūtra "because a figurative sense is impossible" by means of the commentary on the section concerning space (*viyadadhikaraṇa*):
the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is figurative, because their origin is impossible.
That is incorrect, because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
For instance, it would be untenable for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) to have as their self the unmodified Brahman, just as it is with the individual soul (*jīva*).
Or [it may mean] as being a distinct principle from Brahman.
First of all, these [elements] do not have the nature of unmodified Brahman like the individual soul (jīva), because they are insentient.
Therefore, it must be accepted that their non-origination is due to their being a distinct principle.

And thus, there would be a contradiction of the proposition that "by the knowledge of Brahman, all is known," as well as a subversion of the entirety of the Vedānta; this is what he states in the words: "for in the section concerning the ether (viyadadhikaraṇa)... //2//
START BsVBh_2,4.1.3:
"And because it is heard before that [word]. BBs_2,4.3: The commentary on this is explained by the word itself (nigada). //3//
START BsVBh_2,4.1.4:
"Because speech is preceded by that" (BBs_2,4.4).
The term "speech" (*vāk*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for speech, vital breath, and mind.

The meaning is this: even in those cases where you claim that the creation of the vital breath (prāṇa) is not mentioned during the creation of fire and the other elements, we maintain that it is indeed mentioned there as well.

For instance, in the context where the fact that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by food, water, and fire is recorded in the passage beginning with "For [the self] consists of food" (annamayaṃ hi), etc., [the creation of prāṇa is also implied].
In that regard, if it is taken in its primary sense, then the creation of all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) has been stated;

if, on the other hand, it is taken in a secondary sense, even so, considering the beginning and conclusion of the manifestation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākriyā*) as having Brahman as its agent, and because of what is well-known from other scriptural passages, the statement regarding the "watery nature" (*āpomayatva*) of the vital breaths and so forth is indeed already explained as being for the purpose of elaborating upon the fact that they are effects of Brahman.
In that case as well, it is established that there is the creation of the vital breaths. //4//
START BsVBh_2,4.2.5:
"And because the destinies have been specified" (BBs_2,4.5).
He states the intermediate connection: "In the context of arising."
He states the cause of the doubt: "because of the contradiction in the scriptural texts.
*Viśaya* means doubt.
In some places, there are seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Namely: eye, nose, tongue, speech, ear, mind, and skin.
In some places, eight are proclaimed as vital functions (prāṇa) by way of grasping, binding, and quality;
namely: nose, tongue, speech, eye, ear, mind, hand, and skin.

These are the *grahas* (seizers), while their objects are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers), which are likewise eight, as stated in the textual passage beginning with, "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed a *graha*; it is seized by the out-breath (*apāna*) as its over-seizer, for by the out-breath one smells odors.
In some places, they are nine.
It is as follows: there are seven vital breaths (prāṇas) located in the head and two directed downwards.
The two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the one speech—these are the seven.
Alternatively, the anus and the generative organ, or the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas), are the two directed downwards; however, this is not so.
In some places there are ten;
indeed, it is said that there are nine vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, with the navel as the tenth.
In other places there are eleven: "These ten are the vital breaths in a person."
Namely: the five sense faculties beginning with the nose, the five action faculties beginning with the hands, and the self as the eleventh;
it is called the "self" (ātman) because it pervades [the body] by means of its presiding presence, and that is the mind (manas), making eleven.
In some places, there are twelve.
Regarding the statement, "The skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations," these are as follows:
the skin, nose, tongue, eyes, ears, mind, heart, hands, feet, genitals, anus, and speech.
In some contexts, these same vital organs (prāṇas), augmented by the ego (ahaṅkāra), are thirteen.
Thus, the Vedic texts are in disagreement regarding the number of living beings.
Here, he first presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of a question: "What, then, is the conclusion?
That there are exactly seven."

There are exactly seven vital breaths (prāṇas). Why? Because of their movement and because of our understanding; for there is understanding from the scriptures, such as "The seven prāṇas come forth," and so on.
It is not only from scripture that this understanding arises.
He says that it is exactly so even because of the qualification: "And because they are specified," [as in the passage] "There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.

When it is stated that those seven which are in the head—the ear and so forth—are the vital breaths, it is understood that the others, such as the hands and so forth which are not in the head, are not vital breaths.
Just as when it is said, "he sees with the right eye," it is understood that he does not see with the left;

this is what is meant: although there is a contradiction with the Vedic revelation, and although subsequent numbers cannot be contained within preceding numbers, nevertheless, since it is impossible for many numbers to function as qualifiers [simultaneously], when only one must be postulated, [the lower number is chosen].

It follows that sevenfoldness alone is logical, because it is primary and concise; however, eightfoldness and so forth should be understood as intended merely to indicate different modes of functioning. Thus is the prima facie position. //5//
This being the position reached, it is said:
"But since the hands and so forth exist [as faculties] when [the body] is present, it is not thus."
"But since [the body] exists, it is not thus with respect to the hands and so forth.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not only seven; rather, the hands and so forth are also vital breaths (prāṇas).

Since it has been established by another means of valid cognition that there are eleven vital breaths (prāṇas), [the objection] "this being so" is not correct; here, the suffix -tasi is used in the sense of all case endings.
It is not thus.
The literal meaning is that there are seven [categories] because of their brevity and their priority.

What is meant by this is as follows: although the Vedic scriptures are independent as they are intrinsically authoritative, nevertheless, due to mutual contradictions among them, they are not sufficient for determining the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, in the case of an established entity, an option (*vikalpa*) is not possible, as it is in the case of a ritual performance.
Therefore, they are established by virtue of objects brought forward by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For instance,

regarding the rule "one should cut off [the portion] with the *sruva* ladle," since it is impossible to cut off meat or a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) [with that ladle], [it is understood to apply to clarified butter].
Furthermore, because there is the possibility of offering liquid substances, it is established that "liquids" refers to those offered with a *sruva* ladle.

Likewise here as well, from the establishment of the five effects—the cognitions of form and so forth—there follows the establishment of the five instruments, namely the sense-faculties of sight and so forth.
For the blind and others do not perceive forms and so forth, even when the other [faculties] such as the nose exist and their presence is inferred by the perception of odors and so forth.

Likewise, from the establishment of the fivefold effects characterized by speech and so forth, there follows the establishment of the fivefold organs of action characterized by speech, hands, and so on.

For indeed, the mute and others do not possess the capacity for speech and the like, even when the feet and other organs of action, as well as the sense organs, exist and their presence is known through activities such as walking.
In this way, the internal organ is inferred through the establishment of functions such as volition (*saṃkalpa*), which cannot belong to either the organs of action or the sense organs.
Moreover, even a single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) can perform multiple functions,
just as a single lamp is the cause for the illumination of forms, the modification of the wick, and the drying of the oil; therefore, there is no plurality of internal organs.

The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is indeed one; however, it is designated as "mind" (manas) because of its function of deliberation, as "ego" (ahaṅkāra) because of its function of self-identification, and as "intellect" (buddhi) because of its function of determination.
Although it is non-different, it is figuratively treated as if it were threefold due to the difference in its functions.
In reality, however, it is only one, as there is no evidence for its division.

Thus, because there is a fixed arrangement of eleven functions, the scriptural statement that "there are eleven prāṇas" is direct and primary. Other scriptural passages, however, must be interpreted in accordance with this.

In that regard, the scriptural mentions of the numbers seven, eight, nine, and ten are merely restatements of parts (avayuti-anuvāda), just as the statements "he chooses one," "he chooses two," are made in conformity with the statement "he chooses three."

As for the scriptural mentions of the numbers twelve and thirteen, these must somehow be interpreted as being directed toward meditative worship (*upāsanā*) and the like, with the intention of expressing a distinction based on a difference in function (*vṛtti-bheda*).

Therefore, it is established that there are indeed only eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and no others. Furthermore, even the statement regarding the sevenfold nature of the breaths located in the head must be restricted to four alone.
Because it would contradict another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for there are not indeed two eyes, since the effect characterized by the perception of form is non-dual.
However, for one whose single eye is covered, the perception of form is not such as it is for one with both eyes intact;
therefore, there is only one eye, which is merely figuratively treated as if divided by the difference in its physical locations.
Even for a blind person, perception occurs through a portion of the eye located within a single eyeball.
By this, the nose and the ear are also explained.

This is another interpretation of the two Sūtras: "The seven vital breaths—the eye, nose, tongue, speech, ear, mind, and skin—would be those that depart," because the movement of only seven is specifically mentioned in scripture. To explain this, he raises an objection: "But does not the word 'all' also apply here?"
The answer to this is: "Because they are specified.
For it is the organs beginning with the eye and ending with the skin that are specified in the context of departing.

Therefore, since the word "all" (sarva) refers back to what is under discussion, it follows that only the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) depart, and not the hands and so forth. This is the prima facie conclusion.
He objects: "But surely here consciousness is the eighth"?
This was introduced by the statement, "They say it does not cognize. He replies: "This is not a fault."

He states the established conclusion: "But other vital breaths, such as the hands and so forth, are understood to be subject to departure, because of the scriptural statement regarding the hands and others being 'seizers' (grahas). Indeed, the traditional teaching of their status as seizers would only be appropriate if they were to bind the self until liberation; otherwise, like the six-sheathed body, their status as seizers would not have been taught."
For this very reason, the Smṛti declares that these [elements] constitute the limit of liberation, stating "by means of the puryaṣṭaka.
Likewise, the Atharvaṇa Śruti also speaks of the departure (utkrānti) of these eleven.

Therefore, because of other Śrutis, because of the Smṛti, and because there is no restriction on the meaning of the word "all," it remains established that all [the elements] depart; thus, what was stated—that there are only seven—is incorrect.
However, it is established that the number seven is for the sake of illustration. //6//

START BsVBh_2,4.3.7 aṇavaś ca / BBs_2,4.7 / Here, according to the Sāṃkhyas, because the sense organs are derived from the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-principle) and because the *ahaṃkāra* pervades the entire cosmic egg (*jagadmaṇḍala*), the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are omnipresent.
They hold that their function is localized because it resides within the region of the body, and that the scriptural accounts of their going and returning are based upon that localization;

in response to them, [the author] says: "And the prāṇas are atomic. Their atomicity consists in the non-manifestation of color and touch, due to their being difficult to perceive, but it is not the state of being a *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom), for that would entail the impossibility of producing effects that pervade the body.
It has already been stated that there is a perception of cold touch extending over all limbs in one who is afflicted by heat while submerged in a cool lake.
This is what is meant: if the sense-faculties were all-pervading (*sarvagata*), it would follow that there would be perception of objects that are obstructed or distant.

If it is argued that even though they are all-pervading, their status as instruments (*karaṇatva*) belongs only to those portions delimited by the body, and therefore there is no consequence of perceiving obstructed or distant objects—well then, since their status as instruments and their nature as sense-faculties (*indriyatva*) is established only for those parts delimited by the body through the distinction between what is reached and what is not reached, the sense-faculties cannot be omnipresent.

Thus, there is a discrepancy only in name and not in substance; we call it "that sense-organ" (tadindriya), whereas you call it "function" (vṛtti). Consequently, it is established that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are atoms (aṇavas). //7//
And the best [breath] as well:
not only are the other vital breaths transformations of Brahman, but this one is too.
And [the opponent] thinks that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not a modification of Brahman, because it is the most excellent;

because in the *Brahmasūkta* known as the *Nāsadāsīya*, which proceeds under the heading "Non-being was not," the activity of the vital breath is heard in the phrase "breath existed" (*prāṇo 'nīd*) prior to creation, and since activity is impossible when something does not exist, the vital breath must exist; and because of the scriptural statement regarding its being the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*). Thus, he maintains that the vital breath is not a modification of Brahman.
Furthermore, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position arises for one who, despite the contradiction with many scriptural passages, sees no way to reconcile these two Vedic texts.

The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is that precisely because of the contradiction with many scriptural passages, the word "anīt" does not intend to describe the function of the vital breath;
rather, it means "it breathed," "it lived," or "it existed," referring to the cause of creation.

Therefore, it should be understood that this [scriptural passage] is intent upon establishing the actual existence of that [prāṇa], and that its status as "the eldest" is relative to hearing and the other senses.
Consequently, in accordance with many scriptural passages, it is established that even the primary prāṇa is a modification of Brahman. //8//
"Neither air nor function [is the prāṇa], because of the separate teaching. (BS 2.4.9) Now, the true nature of the principal prāṇa is being determined.

For here, from the scriptural statement "That which is prāṇa is vāyu," it appears that prāṇa is indeed vāyu. Alternatively, since prāṇa is heard of as distinct from vāyu in the passage "Prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it [shines] with vāyu as its light," there is a contradiction between these two. Rather than accepting this contradiction, it is better to follow the view of other systems (tantrāntarīya). Thus, let prāṇa be simply the general function of the organs (sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti), and let the two scriptural passages be interpreted in some way so as not to have contradictory meanings.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that even here, there is no contradiction with the scriptural enumeration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as distinct from the organs, because of the difference between the function (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses the function (*vṛttimat*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the vital breath is not the common function of the sense organs; for it would have to be either the combined function of the organs taken together or the function of each one individually.
It cannot be the combined [faculties], because in the absence of one, two, three, or four faculties, their non-existence would necessarily follow;
for indeed, the red quality produced by the conjunction of turmeric powder and lime cannot exist if either of those two is absent.
Furthermore, the carrying of a palanquin, which requires many porters, cannot be accomplished by two or three;
nor can it be accomplished by the skin alone,
for if that were the case, it would be impossible for [the quality] to function as a universal.

Furthermore, when causal factors acting in concert produce an effect, they do so only through intermediate operations that are consistent with the primary operation; for example, the individual actions of birds are consistent with the movement of the cage as a whole.
However, when the primary operation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is to be produced by the sense organs, there exists no such intermediate operation consistent with it.
Moreover, the cognitions of form and so forth are not consistent with it.

Therefore, *prāṇa* is not a common function of the sense organs; likewise, it should not be understood that there is a separate teaching [of *prāṇa*] based on a desire to express some kind of distinction between the function and the possessor of the function.
Consequently, *prāṇa* is neither an action nor merely air.
But it is simply a specific division of air that, having entered into the internal self, is called the fivefold prāṇa. //9//
It might be argued as follows:

just as the eye and other organs are subordinate to the living self (*jīva*), and because the living self is preeminent, it alone is independent; so too, because of its importance and preeminence, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) should likewise be independent.

Furthermore, since it is not possible for two independent [souls] to have a single unified purpose within one body, the body would be torn asunder by their simultaneous and contradictory movements in different directions.
To this objection, it is replied:
"But [the soul is] like the eye and other organs, because of its being taught together with them, and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 2.4.10).

Although the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses superiority and preeminence in comparison to the eye and other organs, nevertheless—due to its being a composite, its lack of sentience, its material nature, its being taught alongside the eye and others, and its subservience to the purpose of the person—it must be dependent upon the person, just like a bed, a seat, or similar objects.

And so, just as a minister, though the chief among other officials appointed by royal command, is not independent in relation to the king, even so the vital breath, though the chief among the eye and other organs, is not independent in relation to the living soul (jīva). //10//
START BsVBh_2,4.5.11 It might be argued that if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is an instrument together with the eyes and other organs by means of the teaching [of scripture], then,
this being the case, another object must be stated for it, just as there are objects such as form (*rūpa*) for the eyes and the other organs.
Nor can that be asserted;
and [the author] avoids the fault of contradicting the enumeration of eleven instruments by stating:
"And because it is not an instrument, there is no fault; for so he shows. (BBs 2.4.11)

We do not accept that the *prāṇa* is an instrument for functions such as delimitation or retention, by which it would require a separate object; nor would the elevenfold nature of the instruments be thereby disturbed. Rather, the *prāṇa* is the cause that sustains the body and the senses, a function impossible for the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
And this has been demonstrated through a series of scriptural passages; its function is not merely the maintenance of the body and the senses. (11)
Furthermore:
It is designated as having five modes of activity, like the mind. (BBs 2.4.12)
"Error is false cognition not established in its own form," such as the cognitions of water and so forth in relation to mirages and the like.
Furthermore, the state of "not being established in its own form" exists even in doubt, because that [doubt] is not established in a single [aspect].
Therefore, that too is included.
"Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows from verbal cognition and is devoid of a real object.
Although the state of being devoid of a real object exists even in false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), nevertheless, it lacks the status of being a cause for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

However, this [conceptual construction], despite its inability to withstand the scrutiny of the learned, certainly possesses the status of being a cause for linguistic usage due to the power of verbal cognition.
As in the expression "the consciousness of a person" (*puruṣasya caitanyam*),
there is no relation denoted by the genitive case here, because such a relation is based on a distinction [between two entities].
This is because consciousness is absolutely non-different from the Puruṣa.

Furthermore, although a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having non-existence as its objective support is not admitted here, nevertheless, a mental modification characterized by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of distraction certainly exists; thus, everything is clear. //12//
And [the opponent argues that] it is atomic;
however, because of the scriptural statement regarding its all-pervasiveness— "equal to the three worlds"— the vital breath (prāṇa) is all-pervading.

As for the scriptural passages beginning with "equal to a flea," they will apply to the omnipresent [Self] through its limitation [by the body], just as the omnipresent ether (ākāśa) attains equality with a pot or a water-jar through its limitation by those objects. To this objection, he says: "And it is atomic.
Because of the scriptural statements regarding its departure, movement, and return, the internal vital breath (prāṇa) is limited and not omnipresent.

It has been stated previously that because it is difficult to perceive, the term "atomic" (aṇutva) is applied figuratively even to that which pervades the body, but it does not actually possess atomicity.

As for the measurement [of the prāṇa] based on its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva), that refers to its form as the *sūtrātman*—the cosmic totality and its individual manifestations in the divine realm—and not to its internal (ādhyātmika) form.

Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "equal to a gnat" indicate that the equality of the prāṇa with the body pertains only to its functional state within the body; it should not be interpreted in any way as being like the space within a jar, which is merely a limitation imposed by an external adjunct (*upādhi*).
But the presiding over fire and the other elements is by Him, because of the scriptural teaching concerning Him.

For it is a general rule that whatever is seen performing an action does so by its own power; however, its being presided over by another may occur due to the force of some other stronger means of knowledge.

If it is argued that, because we observe non-conscious tools such as axes and the like performing their functions when presided over by carpenters and others, one must likewise postulate presiding deities for the sense organs on account of their non-consciousness—this is not so;
for there already exists a conscious presider in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
Nor is it appropriate to accept that the deities themselves are the presiders, based on scriptural passages such as, "Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth."
For if one were to admit multiple presiding deities, no effect whatsoever could arise due to contradiction, as there would be no cause for regulating their intentions toward a single purpose.

Moreover, since the presider over the sense organs would himself be the enjoyer, the deities would possess ownership by virtue of being the enjoyers of the body; thus, the living self (*jīva*) would neither be the owner nor the enjoyer.

Therefore, it follows that the metaphorical designation of Agni and others with respect to speech and the other organs must be understood through some secondary cause, such as their quality of illuminating, rather than through the actual entry of the deities Agni and the rest into the mouth and other parts of the body in their own essential form.
This being the case, it is said in reply: In various Śrutis and Smṛtis, it is understood here and there that deities such as Agni preside over speech and the other organs.
And it is not proper to explain this through forced interpretation when no such contradiction exists.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to be the presiding deity of the senses if it lacks knowledge of the specific nature and functions of those organs.

However, it is possible for deities—who have directly perceived [the truth] through the primordial knowledge (*ārṣajñāna*) of the senses and so forth—to possess the specific knowledge of the distinct natures and the distinct functions of those [senses].

Therefore, it is logical that those very deities are the presiding controllers (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) of their respective instruments, and not the individual soul (*jīva*). Or, even if the individual soul were the controller, there would still be no fault.
There exists a single Supreme Lord, the inner controller (antaryāmī) and regulator of many presiding deities; by His power, even those who might otherwise disagree are unable to dissent.
Thus, through this unity of purpose, there is no obstruction to the production of their collective effect.
Nevertheless, this does not imply that the deities possess the status of enjoyers within this body.
For even though a charioteer stands upon a chariot, he is not the enjoyer of the victory or other results achieved by it, but rather the owner alone;
likewise, although the deities are the presiding agents, they are not the enjoyers, since only that much is heard regarding them.
The enjoyer, however, is the individual soul (jīva) alone.
Furthermore, deities, who consist of bliss, do not deserve enjoyment that is full of suffering and suited to the bodies of humans and the like.
Therefore, it is established that there are deities presiding over the vital breaths; the rest of the meaning is not obscure. //14//
Because it is heard from one who possesses breath. (BBs 2.4.15)
And because that [space] is eternal. 16. bsVBh_2.4.7.16. bs_2.4.16. // 16 //

Those [others] are the sense-faculties (indriya), because they are designated as such, with the exception of the "best" one (the vital breath). Let it not be that the vital breath is merely a function (vṛtti) of the sense-faculties.
The sense organs themselves will be the functions (vṛtti) of this Prāṇa, who is both the eldest and the best.
That the existence and non-existence of the sense organs follow the existence and non-existence of that [Prāṇa] is established by both scripture and experience;
thus, there will be no improper multiplicity of meanings for the single word "prāṇa."
This is because the modifications cannot be a different principle from that which possesses the modifications;
for if the sense organs were a different principle,
it would follow that the word "prāṇa" has multiple meanings.
Or [it might be argued that] there is a figurative sense (lākṣaṇikatva) regarding the senses;
however, when a primary sense is possible, a figurative sense is not appropriate because it is inferior.

Furthermore, a designation by distinction is not a proof of actual difference; for if it were, then since there is also a designation of the mind as distinct from the senses in such passages as "From Him is born the vital breath" (prāṇa), it would follow as an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the mind is not a sense organ.

However, because they are designated as sense organs by virtue of their dependence on memory (smṛti), and because there is the Śruti text—"O, let us assume his very form"—which indicates that even though the sense organs are mentioned separately from the vital breath (prāṇa), they possess the nature of the vital breath;
therefore, based on both reasoning and scripture, it follows that the eleven sense organs are merely functions (vṛtti) of the vital breath itself and not distinct principles (tattva).
To this prima facie view, it is replied: the sense organs are distinct principles from the primary vital breath.
Because there is a designation of difference in various instances;
because of the scriptural teaching of the association with contradictory properties characterized by having attained or not attained death;
and because of the difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For the maintenance of the body is for the sake of the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), while the perception and reflection belong to the sense organs; yet,
the fact that these [latter] conform to the presence or absence of that [breath] does not entail their subsistence within it,
because there is a deviation with respect to the body.
For the vital breaths and so forth follow the presence and absence of the body, whereas the self does not;
and as for the Vedic scripture which declares that the sense organs have the nature of the vital breath,
the Commentator has stated that upon examining the preceding and following passages, their distinctness alone is perceived.

Therefore, because it contradicts numerous scriptural passages and because it involves an internal inconsistency between earlier and later statements, the description of the sense organs as being "of the nature of breath" (prāṇa) must be understood as figurative, based on their dependence upon the vital breath.
As for the mind, its status as a sense organ being established by tradition, its occasional mention as distinct from the sense organs follows the maxim of the "cow and the ox.
Alternatively, the distinction is made because the sense organs have only present objects as their domain, whereas the mind has all three periods of time as its range.
Nor is it appropriate to interpret the abundance of references to differentiation regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) in that manner;
for a transition has already been shown based on the scriptural hearing of its nature as the vital breath.
Likewise, since the word "prāṇa" is primary when applied to the eldest [breath], it is logical that the word "prāṇa" is used figuratively for the sense organs and for other principles beyond them.

Moreover, it is not logical to establish identity between two things whose difference has already been apprehended merely out of deference to their primary [literal] sense; let there be no identity between the Ganges and its banks, for instance.

Others, however, fearing the need to supply the word "difference" (*bheda*) and fearing the redundancy of the phrase "and because of the scriptural mention of difference," have explained it otherwise, since the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the immediately preceding "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the doubt as to whether only the eleven beginning with speech are the sense organs (*indriya*), or whether the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also one: a sense organ is that which is a mark (*liṅga*) of Indra, who is the Self (*ātman*).

Thus, like speech and the others, the vital breath also possesses the status of being a mark of Indra. Furthermore, being a sense organ does not consist in being an instrument for the perception of objects such as form;
for if it did, light would also have to be considered a sense organ.

Therefore, since the sense organ is that which is elemental and possesses the mark of Indra, it follows—just as in the case of speech and the others—that the vital breath (prāṇa) is also a sense organ.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the sense organs are speech and the rest, other than the preeminent vital breath.
Why? Because they alone, speech and the rest, are designated by that term "sense organ" (indriya).
For the word "indriya" is not observed to be used in its primary sense for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Its derivation as "the mark of Indra" (*indraliṅgatā*) is merely a basis for etymological analysis, just as [the word] "cow" (*go*) is derived from "that which goes.
However, the actual ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the state of being an instrument for the perception of color and so forth, while having the body as its locus.
Furthermore, this [prāṇa] has the body as its locus insofar as it is benefited or harmed by the benefit or harm of the body;
thus, there is no consequence of light (āloka) being an organ.
Therefore, it is established that, according to conventional usage, only speech and the others are organs, not prāṇa.
The section belonging to the author of the Bhāṣya, however, is to be understood as applying to the sūtras beginning with "Because of the scriptural statement of difference" (bhedashruteh). //17//
Because of the scriptural teaching of difference. (BBs 2.4.18) // 18 //
And because of their difference in nature. (BBs 2.4.19) // 19 //
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the scriptural instruction;

for in the section concerning the evolution of Being, after prescribing the creation of fire, water, and food through the textual sequence beginning with "That fire thought," it is taught: "This [triple-natured]..."
The Deity thought: "Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms; let me make each one of them threefold.
The meaning of this is: the purpose of the aforementioned desire to become many has not yet been fully accomplished in every respect; therefore, [the Deity] again reflects.

Having accomplished the purpose of becoming manifold, she thought: "Ah, how now may I enter these three aforementioned deities—Fire and the others—by means of this individual self (jīva), the sustainer of life, which was previously created and is now brought to presence through memory;
having entered them as a mere reflection, like the image of a face in a mirror or the image of the moon in water, within the subtle elements consisting of intellect and the rest?"
"I shall differentiate name and form; I shall make this clear, such that 'this is its name' and 'this is its form.
Of those three deities, I shall make each single deity threefold, consisting of the three—fire, water, and food.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is this differentiation of name and form performed by the individual soul (jīva), or is it performed by the Supreme Lord?

If it were created by the individual soul (jīva), then there would be uncertainty due to contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form. However,
if it were created by the Supreme Lord,
then there is no contradiction.

In this regard, since we observe the living being (jīva) acting as the agent in the creation of names such as "Ḍittha" and "Ḍavittha," and in the creation of forms such as jars and cloths, there is a possibility here as well that the living being is the agent in the tripartite creation and the creation of name-and-form;
thus, by virtue of its fitness, the phrase "by this living being" is connected with the principal action, "I shall manifest," and not with the immediately preceding phrase, "having entered."
For the direct connection with the principal word-meaning is the general rule for all subordinate word-meanings, because they exist for its sake;
however, when that direct connection is impossible in certain cases, recourse is taken to an indirect (paramparā) one,
and the possibility of a direct connection has been demonstrated by way of semantic fitness (yogyatā).
But is it not the case that the supreme Lord's agency is heard in the passage, "This deity [thought]...?
True;
however, that will be so by way of being the instigator.

Just as in the world one might say, "Having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, I shall gather it together," if, on the other hand, the jīva were itself the agent of direct realization, the phrase "by this living soul" would be redundant;
for the jīva cannot otherwise function as an instrument.

The agent who directly performs the action becomes the instrument for the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), because the instigator brings about the activity of the agent being instigated with a view toward the primary action.

Therefore, since there is a contradiction—namely, that the soul (*jīva*) possesses agency in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*), while elsewhere the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) does so—it follows that there is indecision regarding the matter.
To this position, it is replied: even here, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught to be the differentiator of names and forms, not the soul.
Because he is unfit for connection with the primary action [of creation].

If it is argued that—since agency is observed elsewhere in the case of objects named Ḍittha, Ḍavittha, and so forth, as well as in the case of objects such as jars and bowls—fitness might be possible here as well—the answer is no.

This is because the possibility is subverted by the absence of presumptive evidence (*arthāpatti*), which is determined by the incapacity [of a human] to construct things such as mountains, rivers, and oceans.
Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone whose agency as the creator is taught here, not that of the individual soul (jīva).
However, the connection of the word "having entered" with this [Supreme Lord] is appropriate because of their proximity.
Nor is there any pointlessness, for the mention of His entry is purposeful insofar as the threefold differentiation (trivṛtkaraṇa) is for the sake of the individual soul who is the enjoyer.
It might be argued as follows:

because the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when there is a common agent (in the sense that "having entered, I shall explain"), it is taught that the very soul (*jīva*) who is the agent of entering is also the one who explains; otherwise, if the Supreme Lord were the explainer and the soul were merely the enterer, [the rule would be violated].

He says "nor is there such a thing as a so-called individual soul" because the use of the suffix *ktvā* would be contradicted by the fact that the agents [of the two actions] would be different; the rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //20//

"Meat and so forth are of the earth; the other two are according to their names. (BBs 2.4.21). Here, the author of the Commentary has explained this sūtra as being intended to indicate its subject matter, serving as a supplement to the subsequent sūtra.
It is also possible to state that this [passage] serves the purpose of dispelling doubt.

For instance, regarding the statement, "That which is the subtlest part of food is the mind; but that which is the subtlest part of fire is speech," there is indeed a disagreement between the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) and the Sāṃkhyas. In that regard, the followers of Kaṇāda declare the mind to be eternal.
The Sāṃkhyas, however, say that speech and mind are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra).
The statement regarding their being "portions of food" (annabhāga), however, is intended to indicate their connection with food;
for when food is consumed, the mind becomes healthy.
In this way, one should infer the similarity in brilliance (*tejas*) even from the eloquence of speech.
In this regard, the following verse applies: "From meat," and so forth.

Although it should have been stated as "speech and mind" (*vāk-manas*), the use of the terms "meat" and so on is for the purpose of providing an illustration by presenting that which is yet to be proven (*sādhya*) alongside that which is already established (*siddha*).
Just as flesh and so forth consist of the elements earth and so on, in the same way, speech and mind also consist of fire and earth; this is the meaning.
What is intended is this: there is nothing whatsoever eternal apart from Brahman, because that would contradict the proposition that through the knowledge of Brahman, all things are known.

Furthermore, because it contradicts the teachings of those who are learned (*bahuśruti*), it cannot be derived from *ahaṅkāra* either, since the category of *ahaṅkāra* as postulated by the Sāṃkhyas lacks scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*). Therefore, in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), it is not appropriate to interpret the direct Vedic statement otherwise in any way. Having stated that there is some fault, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) points out that fault, saying: "If everything indeed... (verse 21).

"But on account of its predominance, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation. (BSBh 2.4.22) The meaning is that even though the process of triplication (*tribṛtkaraṇa*) is common to all, a thing is designated by that which is most abundant within it. //22//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* of the venerable Bhagavatpāda, composed by the illustrious Vācaspatimiśra. //4//
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Non-Contradiction," in the venerable Śaṅkara Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras.
